He, retreating a little behind a tree, sprinkled the clearest water into their throats, whence they stood still at once, as if astonished and subdued. Therefore, with the yoke fitted to their necks, he began to turn the earth with the plow and to scatter the dragon's teeth as seed. But as soon as this seed was covered under the earth, lo! armed men appeared, born according to the number of the teeth. When they rushed at Jason, he—as he had learned from Medea—withdrew slightly from their sight and struck one from a distance with a stone. This man, believing he was being beaten by the one next to him, <margin>One of the earth-born struck by a stone.</margin> pierced him with a drawn blade; and as one after another took revenge for the death, a mutual battle overwhelmed every last one of them. Once they were killed, and nothing more remained that could prevent the seizure of the Golden Fleece, he finally gained possession of it and returned safely to his homeland together with Medea.

# Book 2 of the Hieroglyphics

<margin>Mercury gilded the fleece.</margin>
...carried by the ram across the Hellespont, he reached Colchis, sacrificed the ram to Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes, the messenger god often associated with alchemy.</note>, and hung the fleece in the grove of Mars. This fleece, which Mercury had gilded, was sought by many in vain. But now, let us proceed to those notable matters concerning what has been narrated so far; first, let us consider how these things have been explained by others:

<margin>The interpretation of others.</margin>
Many, and indeed the more simple-minded among them, believe that these things truly happened just as they are told: that Jason was sent, that he went, fought with monsters, and returned home after they were defeated. By the "Golden Fleece," they understand either living sheep of a golden color, or gilded ones. Others believe they were not sheep at all, but rather gold-bearing minerals that were customarily cleaned in sheepskins <note>This refers to an ancient gold-mining technique where sheepskins were used to catch gold particles in rushing water.</note>. Still others think it was a book fashioned from sheepskin (which they call <term>parchment</term>), in which the <term>chemical art</term> <note>original: "artificium Chymicum"</note> of making gold by art was written. Some admit these stories are indeed fables, but they twist them toward I know not what moral teaching, as if such great and numerous coverings were fashioned for, or were useful for, the shaping of morals. There are others who take all these things as hieroglyphics and allegories, containing and involving not morals, nor common physics, but the most occult secrets of nature—the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapidem philosophicum," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> and the method and art of its preparation. They explain that just as a nut hides its kernel within its shells, so too does this story hide its truth. In addition to a hundred supporters of Chemistry testifying to this same thing, even the most bitter hater of this art, **Natalis Comes** <note>A famous 16th-century Italian mythographer whose works were standard textbooks in the Renaissance.</note>, affirms it, albeit according to the judgment of others:

<margin>Why was this opinion not refuted by Natalis, like most others? Perhaps because it is too clear?</margin>
For thus he says in Book 6, Chapter 8 of his *Mythology*: *"There were some,"* he says, *"who judged the things done in Jason’s voyage to be the mutations of chemical bodies, and the Golden Fleece—captured at last after so many labors—to be called the Philosopher’s Stone, which is produced finally after so many changes of those bodies."* We, not being led away by the prejudice of others, will not presume to believe this or that, or to deny that or this; rather, we shall weigh the opinions of each of these in the balance of reason and experience, so that we may finally arrive at the equilibrium of truth.

<margin>Response: History is not found beneath the Golden Fleece.</margin>
Regarding those who suppose the history of the first sort—who think that Jason went and returned—let them take this response: there are indeed places in the nature of things which such Heroes are said to have sought;

# Book 2 of Egyptian-Greek Lore

<page-num>67</page-num>

<header>Book 2 of Egyptian-Greek Lore</header>

<margin>A real location does not imply the truth of the event imagined to have taken place there.</margin>
...might be said; because since these places are perpetual and not as subject to change as the rest of the world, they have always been attached to allegories—lest they seem like mere fables. This is evident in almost all the inventions concerning Phrygia, Colchis, Delos, Cyprus, Rhodes, and other places produced in ancient times. For if a fable were presented without a specific location, it would lose its charm and immediately betray itself as a fiction. However, the timing, the characters, and the deeds performed by them—along with the other circumstances of Jason's expedition—do not agree with the truth at all. If the time is examined, it is indefinite, nor was it truly defined by any writer living at that time so that it could be recognized in histories. It does not escape me, however, that this timeframe is placed precisely in chronologies and historical collections. But this is done on the foundation that **Troy** is said to have been destroyed three hundred years before the founding of Rome, and that Jason’s expedition preceded the fall of **Troy** by nearly 100 years, because the sons of the Argonauts participated in the **Trojan** expedition. Yet both of these points are assumed rather than proven, as will be shown more extensively below under the section on **Troy**.

<margin>Fictional characters imply fictional events and not history.</margin>
But if one may draw a conclusion from the characters—since an event cannot happen without people—if the characters are removed, the event itself is destroyed. Since, therefore, all the Argonauts are fictional characters, just as there are characters in Comedies or Tragedies, or as are found in the poetry called *Amadis* <note>A reference to "Amadis of Gaul," a famous series of chivalric romances known for their fantastical and rambling plots.</note> (which recognizes neither head nor foot and produces and confirms events from events, persons from persons, and fictions from fictions in a continuous series);

<margin>All Argonauts are fictional characters and originate from gods.</margin>
indeed, since almost all of them derive their origin from gods (who were never either men or gods), how can the deeds believed to have been done by them be true? Even if someone were to excuse these figures in some way, how could Hercules—who is said to have lived in Egypt in the time of **Osiris** and was appointed governor of Egypt by him before his travels, which they fable happened 20,000 years ago—also have taken part in this Argonautic expedition? Or if it is permitted to make many versions of Hercules through distinctions (just as they make many versions of Saturn, the Sun, Apollo, Mercury, and the like), how, I ask, did Pollux take part in the Argonauts, when **Helen** <note>Helen of Troy.</note> was brought forth from the same egg with him? <note>According to myth, Pollux and Helen were siblings hatched from an egg after Zeus, in the form of a swan, visited their mother Leda.</note>

<margin>Absurdities of the literal or historical sense.</margin>
<margin>Incredible things contrary to nature.</margin>
...of the Trojan expedition. If you prove these characters were gods, I will not be able to contradict you; but if they were men, they seem far too long-lived. For Helen would be a toothless old woman of at least 120 years by the time all of Greece waged the Trojan War because she had not been returned. These details hold together like sand blown by the wind. Indeed, if the matter is considered as a historical event, only children, not men, should be persuaded that there are bulls that vomit fire, or that armed ranks of men spring from the earth in a sudden birth—growing faster than mushrooms or pumpkins—who, when struck by a single stone, all kill one another to the last man. What shall we say of the ever-watchful dragon, said to be the son of Typhon and Echidna, and of his sown teeth? What of Medea's drugs and counsels and countless other things? Shall we make history out of these? 

<margin>The explanation of others.</margin>
It is therefore a fable, and a dull one at that, to suggest that those sheep had golden or lemon-colored wool, or were gilded, and that such labor was undertaken by Jason just to possess them. Those who understood them to refer to gold mines—among whom **Strabo** is counted in his *Geography*—came closer to the truth. Still closer were those who interpreted it as a book or parchment containing the secret of <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <note>The alchemical art of making gold.</note>, as **Suidas** does. But no one would undergo such great and varied dangers for these things, nor would they have need of Medea’s drugs. Nor would Jason, whose name signifies a <term>healer</term> <note>original: "medicum"; the name Jason is etymologically linked to the Greek word "Iasthai," to heal.</note> and who was instructed by **Chiron** in practical experience, have been required for such a task—anyone else would have done. Nor would **Aeson** have been restored to youth by Medea.

<margin>The most true allegorical interpretation.</margin>
It remains, therefore, that we must adapt the whole matter from beginning to end to an allegorical interpretation. We do not apply it to moral lessons, properly and primarily, unless we wish to be mad ourselves, or accuse those who invented such great things for the sake of mere morals of madness. Secondarily, we do not deny that it can be bent toward that purpose, as can all other things. However, it should be applied not to the works of nature known to peasants, but to those most secret things proper to philosophers: namely, the **Golden Medicine**, which deals with the golden remedy for the mind and body. Those who preceded us think as we do (such as **Luigi Marliano**...

...[Guglie]lmus <note>Likely referring to Guglielmus Gratarolus, a 16th-century physician who published collections of alchemical texts.</note> in a complete volume published under the title of the **Golden Fleece**, and those who collected so many treatises on the **Chemical art**, arranged in various volumes and published in German under that same title, and countless others (whom we omit here for the sake of brevity) who accompany them—whose writings are in everyone's hands, so we will not cite them here: Now, we shall specifically demonstrate that the aforementioned voyage of **Jason**, with its dangers, deeds, persons, and all circumstances, pertains to <term>Philosophical Medicine</term> <note>In alchemy, this refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, capable of "curing" base metals into gold and restoring human health.</note>, and nothing else but the highest chemical artifice and the **Secret of Secrets**, translated from the Egyptians to the Greeks and described under this most beautiful allegory.

<margin>Who Jason is.</margin>
The character of Jason—his name, education, lineage, and deeds—proves this: For his name expresses a "medical" man, derived <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰᾶσθαι"</note> *from the act of healing* or from *curing*; for <gloss>healing</gloss> <note>original: "ἰάσεως"</note> is the art of curing. It is not enough to assert, as some do, that Jason was not a surgeon nor gave medicine, and who therefore interpret his story as a moral lesson. For even if he was not a literal physician or surgeon (since Jason himself never existed in the natural world), he is imagined and presupposed to have been one. Indeed, all signs agree with the name: He is educated by **Chiron**, who instructed him in medicine—the same who also educated **Hercules** and **Achilles**, youths of the same character and family: the latter as an invincible Hero for the Trojan war, the former as most fit for taming monsters.

<margin>Chiron and Medea assisted in educating Jason.</margin>
Thus, Jason drew manual experience from Chiron, just as he received from **Medea** the counsel and perfect **Theory** necessary for the completion of the work. From these things, a point worthy of note occurs: that some kind of manual handling, learned from Chiron, must precede the perfect Theory instilled by Medea in the investigation of this work. For perfect theory precedes perfect <term>practice</term> <note>original: "praxis"</note>, and not the other way around; but many errors precede perfect theory. For these errors are, as it were, the teachers and punishers in the art.

# Hieroglyphics, Book 2

<page-num>70</page-num>

<header>Hieroglyphics, Book 2</header>

...but errors are not recognized except through practice often tried and repeated; and thus it would appear that the instruction of **Chiron** <note>The centaur Chiron represents the preliminary, practical training in nature; in alchemy, this is the "labor" or manual work of the artist.</note> precedes the most perfect counsels of **Medea**; these counsels also should order and arrange the labors of the craftsman. This lineage comes from the genealogy of the Gods; for his paternal great-great-grandfather is **Jupiter**; **Polymeda** <note>original: "Polymeda" – from the Greek for "many-counselled."</note> is assigned as his mother, as if she were a woman of much counsel, daughter of **Autolycus**, also descending from **Sisyphus**, **Aeolus**, and **Jupiter**. Thus, if **Aeolus** or **Jupiter** were removed, the lineage of **Jason** begins from no one; likewise, if **Chiron** never existed, Jason had no teacher. Indeed, Chiron did not exist in the nature of things if **Saturn** had not coupled with the nymph **Philyra** while turned into a brute beast—a horse—or if he never lived at all.

<margin>Medea's grandfather is the Sun.</margin>
**Medea** similarly, the wife of **Jason**, is the granddaughter of the **Sun** and **Ocean**; she had **Aeëtes** as her father—named from "brightness" <note>original: "à fulgore dictum," a reference to the Greek 'aithô' (to burn/shine).</note>—whose sisters were **Pasiphaë**, the wife of **Minos** (who gave birth to the **Minotaur**), and **Circe**, who through sorcery <note>original: "veneficio"</note> transformed men into beasts; her mother was **Idyia**, named from "knowing" <note>original: "à cognoſcendo nominatam," from the Greek 'idreia' meaning knowledge or skill.</note>; for knowledge is the mother of counsel.

<margin>Jason the physician; the golden medicine; the craftsman; the Argonauts are sons of the Gods.</margin>
Such parents, teacher, and wife were fitting for **Jason**, the future physician and keenest investigator of natural things. Now we come to weigh his achievements; those fifty companions of the journey are chosen, almost all descended from the Gods. But why this? Perhaps because that age produced Gods? I do not think so: but because it pleased the poet **Orpheus** to assign such great parents to his **Argonauts**, lest they seem born from a humble place, but rather to be of the <term>golden family</term> <note>In an alchemical context, "golden family" refers to substances of "noble" or solar origin, essential for the Great Work.</note>. For since the ancestors of all of them are either **Aeolus**, or **Jupiter**, or **Mercury**, or other Gods, Goddesses, or Nymphs, who would not recognize them as true? Among the pagans it would have been a sin to deny the Gods themselves; among us it is permitted, and we add that neither Gods nor men were the ancestors of the Argonauts—such as **Jason, Hercules, Hylas, Aethalides, Amphion, Augeas, Calais, Castor, Cepheus, Iphiclus, Aeson, Lynceus, Meleager, Mopsus, Peleus, Pollux, Telamon, Zetes**, and the rest.

<margin>What the ship Argo is.</margin>
The ship **Argo** is built, which is called the first, from the **Oak of Dodona** <note>A famous oracle of Zeus where the rustling leaves of oak trees were said to deliver prophecies.</note>, from which oracles were given; from this it had a talking and prophetic mast. This is the first thing worthy of consideration, because it was constructed by the poetic and prophetic pen of **Orpheus**; the second...

And then the **Harpies** will be put to flight; that is, the volatile parts will cease to fly <note>In alchemy, "volatile" substances evaporate easily. The "flight of Harpies" symbolizes the fixation of these substances into a stable, solid form.</note>. For without seeing these rocks, the prefixed goal cannot be reached; they are one in essence, but two in reason. Their danger had to be explored by a released dove because they gushed with flames and fire. So it also suits the <term>Philosophical work</term> <note>The *Magnum Opus* or Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>; for a white dove is sent out, which teaches how to avoid every danger. For the *Albedo* <note>The "whitening" stage of the alchemical process, signifying purification and the successful union of spirit and body.</note> of the spirit does not allow it to flee and foretells the happy outcome of the work. 

But what goal was finally to be sought? The **Phasis**, the gold-bearing river, named from the Hebrew *Paz* <note>original: "Paz" – a Hebrew term for refined or pure gold.</note>, which means gold; and Scythia, a colony of the Egyptians, in which **Aeëtes**, King of the Colchians, reigned. They are said to have been kindly received by the sons of **Phrixus** and led to **Aeëtes**. He, born of the **Sun**, had taken a daughter of **Ocean** as his wife, and from her had fathered **Medea**. Thus the son of the Sun possessed this Treasure; no wonder, because the places closest to the Sun shine with our minerals suitable for Medicine. Indeed, the <term>Golden Fleece</term> is promised, but only after the dangers are overcome; however, because those dangers were great, very many had succumbed to them. A <term>Dragon</term> the size of a ship driven by fifty oars, ever-watchful, had to be killed. This is the task, this is the labor <note>A reference to Virgil’s Aeneid: "Hoc opus, hic labor est," implying the difficulty of the final stages of the work.</note>. 

Who would attack such a beast unless relying on the divine art of **Pallas** <note>Athena, representing wisdom.</note> and the counsel of **Medea** <note>The sorceress-princess who represents the transformative knowledge or "secret" of the process.</note>? I do not think there is a need to cite the passages of authors where they emphasize our great dragon, for they are innumerable. For an example, however, see **Lull** <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major philosopher and reputed alchemist whose "Testament" was a foundational text for later practitioners.</note>, who says in *Theory of the Testament*, Chapter 6: "From these three things, my son, you shall extract the great dragon, which is the radical beginning and the principal of firm alteration." The same, in Chapter 10: "And by this reasoning, it is necessary to say allegorically that the great dragon is from the four Elements, etc." And Chapter 9: "In that liquor the great dragon is rectified." Also Chapter 52: "And in all things dwells the Dragon, namely **Fire**, in which our <term>Stone</term> is more sharp; this property is in all the compounds of the World."

<margin>What do the remedies given to Jason by Medea signify?</margin>
Truly **Jason**, the Physician-Philosopher, received the most immediate aid from **Medea**, or Reason; images of the Moon and Sun to be worn on the neck, a <term>fire-resistant ointment</term> <note>original: "Apyrum" — a substance that resists the action of fire.</note> with which he might anoint himself, and a sleep-inducing cake with the clearest water, or <term>virgin's milk</term> <note>original: "lacte virginis" — a common alchemical term for a white liquid or precipitate, often a mercurial water.</note>, warding off and extinguishing every flame. Something of this sort truly happens in this medicine: for in order to have the seed-stock of our future harvest, it is necessary that what is to be sown will afterwards give fruit in its own proper earth. Moreover, this seed must be extracted by art from the Dragon, like teeth.

The seed previously prepared is entrusted to these Bulls in their own earth, and the earth is turned over until it is sufficient; then it is fit and disposed to bear fruit. Moreover, **Jason** used the same aids in subduing the oxen as he did in overcoming the Dragon. Indeed, just as this allegory is very pleasant to hear, it was not devised for idle ears, but has been passed down from the most ancient times to our own age; it affects the minds of the ingenious rather than providing mere pleasure to the senses. For what is more pleasing than gold? What is more lovely than apples? What is more beautiful than gardens? If anyone, therefore, were to hear that golden apples grow on trees, they would desire to enjoy them by a certain innate appetite. Thus, the novelty of the thing drew the listeners into no small amount of admiration, and so provided an opportunity for many people to probe and inquire what "kernel" <note>meaning the hidden essence or truth</note> was covered under such a beautiful "rind" <note>meaning the outer story or myth</note>. ### Book 2: Egyptian-Greeks

<margin>Interpretation of others.</margin>
...is narrated; they have interpreted it not literally, but in a far different way. Aretas, in his writings on Libyan matters, felt that these were sheep which were called "golden," and since they had a cruel and wild shepherd, they were said to be guarded by a dragon. However, he seems to have been misled by the word <term>mēla</term> <note>The Greek word μῆλα (*mēla*) is a homonym: it can mean "apples" or "sheep/small livestock."</note>, which signifies both apples and sheep. Pherecydes referred it to apples of a golden color, a view which Lucian also supports. This is also the point of Virgil's verse in his *Eclogues*:

> I have sent ten golden apples; tomorrow I will send another ten.
<note>original: "Aurea mala decem miſi, cras altera mittam" — Virgil, *Eclogues* 3.71.</note>

Among more recent writers, some have sensed a historical reality underlying these things—namely, that there were sheep of a yellow or golden color belonging to the two brothers, Hesperus and Atlas. Others apply it to astronomical matters, transferring the "golden apples" to the golden stars, and the "dragon" to the sun <note>In ancient astronomy, the "dragon" often refers to the constellation Draco or the ecliptic path of the sun.</note>. Some accommodate the story to ethics and the teaching of morals, as if the greedy, in guarding their own riches, are like serpents watching over golden apples.

<margin>Response to the interpretations of others.</margin>
To these, we will first give our response, and then we shall provide our own interpretation. Since subjects ought to be understood according to their own proper predicates, it is a wonder that Aretas turns apples into sheep. For although the latter and the former are both called <term>mēla</term> by the Greeks, they differ greatly in their nature and attributes. The sheep carry wool that is perhaps golden, but the apples are carried by trees. Nor is there any reason why all authors would have put "apples" for "sheep," or would have wanted "sheep" to be understood as "apples." Is there perhaps only a single author who used that ambiguous word so simply that the meaning is not clear whether he intended apples or sheep? Or have not many more mentioned this allegory? I believe very many have. Therefore, it is a play on words and a violent distortion from the fruit of a tree to a beast of the field—even if the latter is found to have provided golden wool, as was narrated before <note>A reference to the Golden Fleece of Jason, discussed on the previous pages.</note>. But it is altogether frivolous what he adds: that they had a cruel shepherd, and for that reason he was called a dragon. O miserable sheep, who, having golden wool, experienced such a wild shepherd! Truly they were worthy to be snatched away by Hercules once the shepherd was slain. Both ideas are childish: to believe that such a shepherd was called a dragon, and that sheep truly carried golden wool. Those who admit they were apples, but merely of a golden color, perhaps...

# Book 2 of the Hieroglyphics

...they look toward orange or citron apples; but since this fruit is good in itself, yet not so admirable or rare—but always, as even now, propagated its own species in its native places—it does not seem worth the effort for such a great guard to have been applied to these trees by nymphs and a dragon. Furthermore, the account refers to **golden apples**, and not to those merely **imitating the color of gold**. Those who make astronomical matters out of these do an injury to heaven, because they imagine the stars as apples and the sun as a dragon. For in this way, they picture the tree from heaven which the dragon called *Ladon* (as Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the *Argonautica*.</note> asserts in Book 4) embraces. But they say Hercules is the sun, whose twelve labors are just as many celestial signs; for when the sun arrives, the stars disappear. These ideas fit together very well indeed; but those who think so seem to me to babble and talk nonsense about things not understood as if they were understood—concerning which I shall speak elsewhere. In a similar way, those who believe these things were fashioned primarily for the sake of morals confess that they see nothing in physical secrets. In these matters, even if we do not imitate Lynceus <note>A hero of Greek myth said to have such keen sight that he could see through the earth.</note>, who is narrated to have penetrated the interior of the earth with his sharp vision, observing riches hidden in subterranean enclosures as if they were right before him, nevertheless, <margin>The truest explanation: Hercules is the industrious Artist.</margin> unless the daughter of Saturn <note>Likely a reference to Truth, traditionally called the "daughter of Time" (Saturn).</note> deceives us, we shall give a more evident and more genuine explanation of this allegory than those mentioned before. 

That by Hercules, the victor most patient of so many labors, is understood primarily the Craftsman of the <term>Golden Medicine</term> <note>original: "Medicinae aureae" — the alchemical Elixir or Philosopher's Stone.</note> shall be demonstrated below as his labors are unfolded. That being presupposed—although we do not deny that Hercules' example may also be used quite aptly to instill morals and virtues—we truly assert that **Atlas**, the most famous mountain of Mauritania <note>A region in Northwest Africa, home to the Atlas Mountains.</note>, was at that time (as it is still today) fertile in every kind of mineral whose use is for **Philosophical Medicine**, and that it surrounded the garden of the Hesperian Nymphs. <margin>Who ATLAS is.</margin> For Atlas is the brother of Hesperus, because he is situated toward the sunset <note>The word *Hesperus* refers to the evening or the west.</note> with respect to Egypt and Greece. Hence Mercury is also called *Atlantiades* <note>Descendant of Atlas; in myth, Mercury's mother Maia was a daughter of Atlas.</note>, because he is thought by some to have been born on Mount Atlas. Regarding Atlas the astronomer, who discovered the sphere and taught those nations of Mauritania...

# Book 2: Of the Egyptian-Greeks

...what some tell in fables does not agree with the truth; much less what others say, that he was a King of **Mauritania** <note>A region in ancient Northwest Africa, covering parts of modern Morocco and Algeria.</note> changed by **Perseus** into a mountain of such great size by the showing of the **Medusa’s** head. For these are the fictions and emblems of poets, with which they have sketched and depicted other more secret things <note>The author refers to "arcaniora," implying hermetic or alchemical secrets hidden beneath the literal myths.</note> lying hidden beneath them. They call **Atlas** an astronomer because the stars
<margin>Why Atlas is imagined as an astronomer.</margin>
can be observed most clearly on his peak, especially since, like Africa and Egypt, he enjoys a clear sky not clouded by rains. Second, because he is of such height that his peak seems hidden among the clouds and stars, as it appears. And third, because he is thought to hold up the sky, as if on his shoulders; for he is said to represent the figure of a statue of a man, with the peak rising up like a head. This **Atlas**, whose daughters are said to be the **Pleiades** (from one of whom, called **Maia**, **Mercury** was born to **Jupiter**, as will be handed down later under the genealogy of the gods),
<margin>Note.</margin>
had a brother **Hesperus** and from him three granddaughters, the **Hesperides**: **Aegle**, **Arethusa**, and **Hespertusa**. By **Hesperus** and his daughters, we understand those same mountainous regions of Atlas. For although **Atlas** is taken as if it were one mountain, yet by the same name and continuity it embraces all the other adjacent mountains. For Atlas pervades almost all of coastal Africa, and thus includes not one mountain, but many thousands. Just as it is similarly established regarding the **Taurus** of Asia, the **Alps**, **Apennines**, and **Pyrenees** of Europe, that countless mountains and hills are contained under each: so we understand concerning the **Pleiades** and **Hesperides**, that they are parts and, as it were, daughters propagated from those great mountains of abrupt height, **Atlas** and **Hesperus**. Therefore, **Mercury** is not unworthily born from **Maia**, so that he may be called the **Descendant of Atlas** <note>original: "Atlantiades"</note>, and from **Aegle**, **Arethusa**, and **Hespertusa** are kept the trees bearing **golden apples**, which for that reason are called those of the **Hesperides**. The **Dragon**, who was set in charge of their guarding,
<margin>Who the dragon is.</margin>
born from **Echidna** <note>A half-woman, half-snake "mother of monsters" in Greek myth.</note> and **Typhon** <note>A monstrous giant and the most deadly creature in Greek mythology.</note>, is said to have a hundred heads. A numerous offspring of those same parents is read to exist, and that offspring is always poisonous and monstrous: such as the dragon at the spring of **Cadmus** <note>The dragon of Ares killed by Cadmus, the founder of Thebes.</note>, lethal to his companions; another at the **Golden Fleece**; and this third one here at the apples...

## Hieroglyphics, Book 2

...of the Hesperides, the fourth [labor] concerned the cattle of **Geryon**; likewise *Cerberus*, *Sphinx*, *Chimæra*, and other such horrifying and many-formed monsters, which we will discuss in their proper places: *Typhon* signifies a sulfurous and burning spirit, while *Echidna* denotes a watery, cold, and flowing substance;

<margin>Minerals concealed under the names of monsters.</margin>

For from these two, various species of minerals sprout forth, which have always been named and described by the ancients using the names of monsters because of their natural variety. Regarding the Dragon, as a general category, as well as the birthplace of the golden apples, enough is established from these points; now we shall see to the appearance of such great trees and their fruits. Some natural philosophers <term>Physicis<gloss>Early scientists who studied the natural world</gloss></term> are pleased to think of a tree as an "inverted animal" for this reason: because its roots are toward the center of the earth, or the lower parts, which correspond to the mouth of an animal oriented toward the upper parts. If, however, we consider the stomach and its <term>mesenteric veins<gloss>the vessels that carry nutrients from the gut to the liver</gloss></term> or the liver <term>Epar<gloss>Greek: Hepar</gloss></term> in an animal as the starting point for the distribution of nourishment through the veins of the body, it is a different matter.

<margin>The mineral tree.</margin>

In the same way, the minerals from which metals are extracted and medicines are made—useful for the healing of human bodies—represent a certain kind of vegetable tree. For their "roots," which are a double smoke of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <term>argenti vivi<gloss>literally "living silver," or mercury</gloss></term>, are closer to the center, and from there, tending toward the upper regions, they extend their veins through the rocks and stretches of earth in a marvelous way. Indeed, they represent the form of some large tree spreading its branches far and wide, if they could be seen with the eyes, as is evident from the experience of those who investigate those veins <note>A reference to miners and prospectors who tracked "veins" of ore through mountain ranges.</note>. If these things are so, it is clear what was understood by those trees bearing golden apples. For truly, these are trees—not growing in the air, but beneath the earth—which bear golden apples, provided they are distinguished from the "wild" ones by being of a better nature. For the entire difficulty lies in this: namely, to choose those which are suitable for the art <note>The "Art" refers to the Alchemical Work or "Great Work."</note>. Therefore, **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist said to have taught the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> adds these noteworthy words near the end of his treatise:

> Likewise, you should know that the greatest root of this work is in the seeking out of the species that are best for this mastery <term>magisterium<gloss>The alchemical process of transformation</gloss></term>: for every mineral is of many types.

Concerning these mineral trees growing beneath the earth...

### Book 2: Of the Egyptian-Greeks

...almost all authors have mentioned [these] growing things under various words, yet hinting at the same thing: namely, that the **golden fruits** must be taken along with their tree and transplanted. 

*Thus **Flamel** <note>original: "Fla."; likely referring to the famous alchemist Nicolas Flamel</note> says: "The fixed grain is like the fruit, and **Mercury** <note>The Roman messenger god, here representing the alchemical principle of fluidity and transformation</note> is the tree; the fruit, therefore, must not be separated from the tree, because it cannot receive nourishment from elsewhere." And shortly after: "So that it may be planted again without removing the fruit, into a more fertile and noble soil, which will give more nourishment in one day than the previous field would have provided in a hundred years, because of the constant stirring of the winds." The other earth, because it is closest to the **Sun** <note>In alchemy, the Sun represents the perfection of Gold or the masculine principle</note>, makes the tree grow and flourish with continuous dew and the constant Sun in the **Philosophic Garden** <term>Hortus Philosophicus<gloss>A symbolic laboratory or state of matter in alchemical work</gloss></term>, shining morning and evening, day and night, and every single hour without interruption; and the tree is sprinkled and nourished by a most sweet dew more in one year than in ten thousand in the previous earth.*

<margin>What the golden apples are.</margin>

**Greverus** <note>Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century author on the "Palm Tree" of alchemy</note> also points out this mineral tree, whose roots, he says, are **Mercury**, while its branches are fourfold, made of the imperfect metals; and in these, silver and gold represent the flowers and fruits. Nothing clearer could have been said to declare the subject of the **art** <note>Alchemy was often called "The Art"</note> and to explain what the **golden apples of the Hesperides** are, and in what way they grow. 

Nor should this seem so wonderful, as if it were contrary to nature, since we daily see the improvement of fruits through the **grafting** <note>original: "insitionem"</note> of shoots from different kinds of trees into wild or base trunks; thus, it becomes manifest how much art can accomplish in plants, which consist of heterogeneous and dissimilar parts. From this, it is reasonable—and very well known from experience—that in the mineral kingdom, especially that which is purely uniform in substance <note>original: "homogeneum"</note>, this can be done much more quickly and easily. 

It has long been known that the same thing happens in the bodies of animals and even of man himself—namely, how the nose, ears, and similar parts can be repaired and restored from living human flesh. We were eyewitnesses to this fact, as we were personally acquainted with the most excellent **Gasparo Tagliacozzi** <note>A pioneer of plastic and reconstructive surgery (1545–1599) at the University of Bologna</note> in **Bologna** performing such things. Countless examples from the works of nature and art could be produced here testifying to the same, but they would be unnecessary...

## Book 2 of the Hieroglyphics

...we have thought it would be, since the senses of the craftsmen do not seek help or proof from reason, but on the contrary: Let this one thing suffice us in this place: <margin>1 **An example from plants**</margin> In certain places, where everything is stiff with cold and ice in winter time, if a shoot is cut from an apple tree around the beginning of December and placed in water for several days in warm places or **heated rooms** <note>original: "Hypocaustis"; these were rooms warmed by underfloor heating systems, often used in colder climates to keep plants or people warm</note>, it produces leaves and flowers striking in their beauty and novelty, which is a fact known even to common people. But from this, the Philosophers recognize the **prime matter** <note>original: "materiam primam"; the formless, fundamental substance that alchemists believed could be transformed into any material</note> lying hidden within the tree's shoots, and they judge similarly regarding the golden apples contained within their own branches and roots: To one who understands, enough has been said. Or, if it pleases you, we shall add a rarer example of the vegetable nature, which can illustrate this matter not a little: <margin>2 **A rarer example.**</margin> There are those who, around the 25th day of November, bury cabbage leaves in a trench a foot and a half deep under the earth, and leave them there in the open air through the winter snows and cold until the 25th of March; and then they take out from there not cabbage leaves, but the purest seed; as witnesses under oath have affirmed to me that they have done this every year. In this transformation, we see that through putrefaction alone, that plant is reduced to its **prime matter** (as they also assert regarding other plants) from which it began, or rather to its final state toward which it tends. This same process must also occur in the **alchemical** <term>Chymico<gloss>Referring to the "Art" of alchemy, which sought to mimic and accelerate natural processes in the laboratory</gloss></term> craft, but in its own specific way. Therefore, our golden tree bearing fruit became well enough known to rational men, as did the explanation of this allegory. Now, so that **Hercules** might seek out this tree, <margin>**Who the Nymphs were.**</margin> he went to the Nymphs of **Jupiter** <note>The king of the gods</note> and **Themis** <note>The goddess of divine law and order</note>, who lived near the **Eridanus** <note>A river often identified by ancient writers and alchemists as the Po in Italy, famous for being "gold-bearing"</note>, the gold-bearing river of Italy, in caves or subterranean mines; and from them he sought counsel. But why that? Because the works of nature must be consulted first; that is, one must consider how nature proceeds in its operations. For this reason, in many places, the Philosophers send the investigator to natural works to discover the true matter, and invite them to consider these things deeply, as can be seen everywhere in the writings of **Geber** <note>original: "Gebrum"; referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and the most famous figure in early alchemy</note> and others. Those Nymphs living in the caves or gold mines send **Hercules** back to **Nereus**; who, as the truthful son of the **Sea** <note>original: "Ponti"</note> and the **Earth**...

### Book 2. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

<margin>Who Nereus is.</margin>
He was believed to be a seer; he predicted the Trojan calamities to Paris; he was called the most ancient of the Gods by Orpheus. Hercules, coming to him while he tried to escape by shifting into various forms, held him until he returned to his original shape and revealed the matter. He was the father of the 50 Nereids, raised and nourished by the waves, whose daughters especially run about the chariot of Triton <note>Triton was a herald of the sea, often depicted blowing a conch shell</note>. This is the **First Being** <note>original: "primum Ens"; in alchemy, this refers to the fundamental substance or "prime matter" before it is specialized into a specific form</note> which philosophers often command to be sought, without which the way or passage to the **golden apples** <note>The "golden apples of the Hesperides," a common alchemist's metaphor for the Goal of the work or the Philosopher's Stone</note> does not lie open. Prometheus, indeed—called *from foresight* <note>original: "apo tēs promētheias"</note>, that is, named after providence—to whom one is sent by Nereus for counsel, brought fire down to men and is considered a fire-bearing Titan, a friend of Oceanus, a contemplator of divine things, who shared a common altar with Vulcan <note>God of fire and smithing</note> and Pallas <note>Athena, Goddess of wisdom</note>. 
<margin>Who Prometheus is.</margin>
By his advice, Saturn was cast down into Tartarus by Jupiter. From there, Saturn escaped to Italy to Janus, who was then reigning there; received kindly with hospitality, he taught Janus the way of living and the cultivation of fields. For the instruction he received, Janus is said to have rewarded him with half of his kingdom, and on the coins—which were first struck from his genius—there was a ship on one side and a two-faced image on the other, because the kingdom was governed by the joint counsel of Janus and Saturn, as Ovid records in Book 1 of the *Fasti*. 

Truly, we do not doubt that through Prometheus, the preliminary mental speculation regarding this work is expressed, which is why he had an altar in common with Pallas and Vulcan; nor is it undeservedly said that he gave counsel to Jupiter about imprisoning his father and thrusting him down to the underworld. For from the speculation of the mind, all this is foreseen—namely, that after the **dark blackness** <note>original: "nigredinem fuscam"; this refers to the *Nigredo* stage of alchemy, representing decay and the stripping away of old forms</note>, **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem"; the *Albedo* stage, representing purification and the first light of the Stone</note> will follow. Ancient histories do indeed mention the reign of Janus and Saturn, but from the fables of the poets: for the pagans were so persuaded that the god Saturn, son of Heaven and Earth, was expelled from his kingdom by the god Jupiter, and suffered many other things. But these are all **Hieroglyphics** <note>The author uses "Hieroglyphics" here to mean sacred, symbolic riddles rather than just Egyptian script</note>, and by the Egyptians M<unclear>an</unclear>

# Hieroglyphics, Book 2.

<margin>Secrets.</margin>
...or fashioned by the Greeks for those matters which they wished to wrap in such coverings. By **Janus the Two-Faced** <note>original: "Ianum Bifrontem"; Janus was the Roman god of beginnings and transitions, usually depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions</note>, we understand one matter or thing, called **Rebis** <note>from the Latin "res bina," meaning "double thing"; in alchemy, it represents the union of opposites, such as spirit and matter or male and female</note>, which contains two things, or if you prefer, a double mercurial substance. That Saturn is joined to him as a partner in the kingdom has a far different reasoning, which anyone could guess who is not ignorant of the reason why, in ancient Rome, a **Triton** <note>a Greek sea god, the son of Poseidon and Amphitrite</note> was seen atop the temple of Saturn. For these things are enigmatic and somewhat obscure. But as to why money was first minted under the auspices of Saturn, the reason is evident: because he is the first of the planets who carries the keys to treasures, if you consider his color and order <note>Saturn is associated with lead, the "heaviest" and "first" metal in the alchemical hierarchy of descent from the heavens</note>. 

<margin>*From where money was first named.*</margin>Money <note>original: "Pecunia"</note> is named from livestock <note>original: "pecude"</note>, not, as is commonly said, because a sheep could be bought with it, but because it had a sheep stamped on it together with a ship, that is, the *Argo* <note>the ship of Jason and the Argonauts</note>. For there is no doubt that this was the emblem of that voyage, containing both the ship and the beast whose fleece was golden. Besides many others, *Greverus* <note>Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century author of alchemical treatises</note> mentions these golden apples among the more recent authors, who can be read for themselves. 

<margin>*3. The golden apple of Eris.*</margin>From the same Garden of the Hesperides, the *Golden Apple* of *Eris* <note>the Goddess of Discord</note>—the primary cause of the Trojan War—was also sought, about which we shall speak in the following Book 6. 

<margin>*4. The golden apples thrown to Atalanta.*</margin>Especially those three golden apples which are fabled to have been handed by Venus to Hippomenes, to be thrown before Atalanta. Since this royal maiden was not only most excellent in the gift of beauty, but also most celebrated in the art of hunting and throwing the javelin, she attracted many suitors to her. But her father, Schæneus, wished to give her in marriage to no one unless she, otherwise most swift of foot, were defeated by him in a race; to the victor the maiden would be granted, but to the vanquished, death. And so, while many attempted this in vain and met their death, Hippomenes, by the counsel and gift of Venus, threw three golden apples, one after another, to the maiden as she ran. Thereupon she, delayed by the desire of picking them up, was defeated and given as a wife to Hippomenes. Who, when because of love he was impatient of delay and coupled with his bride in the temple of the Mother of the Gods <note>Cybele</note>, stirred up the anger of that goddess against himself, whence both, marked by lion skins and ferocity, roamed the woods. It is said, moreover, that Atalanta competed with men in hunting and of victory...

# Book 2. Of the Egyptian [secrets] of the Greeks.
<meta>catchword: golden</meta>

...was rewarded with a prize because of the boar of remarkable size killed by **Meleager** <note>In Greek myth, Meleager led the hunt for the Calydonian Boar and gave the skin to the heroine Atalanta</note>. and when, during the hunt near the shrine of **Stethaeus** (of **Aesculapius** <note>The god of medicine and healing</note>), she suffered from thirst, it is said that she struck a rock with her spear-point and drew forth a spring of coldest water bursting out from the stone. <margin>Note</margin> No one fails to see that these things are <term>Chemical</term> <note>original: "Chymica"; referring here to the laboratory art of alchemy</note>, unless they are perhaps blinder than a mole. Nevertheless, some people apply these things to the marking of morals and greed, or to the arranging of marriages by gold—which we do not begrudge them, provided they are not angry with us for restoring the story to a more hidden physics <note>i.e., natural philosophy or the study of matter</note> as if by its own rightful return. That the **Virgin** is our "royal matter" has become known by the testimonies of many; but she is fleeting and has wings on her feet, namely the winged sandals of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurij talaria"; Mercury's wings represent the volatility of the substance (mercury/quicksilver) which "flies" or evaporates easily</note>. Therefore she outruns anyone in a race, unless she is managed by cunning and strategy. 

How this ought to be done, however, this allegory of the wise implies: Therefore, let the **golden apples** be taken and thrown to her one after another, and you will emerge as the winner. Nothing is clearer, nothing more fitting. Afterwards, in the shrine of the Mother of the Gods, they lie together in the bond of love; that is, in the well-known vessel or in the "glass house," and they are turned into **lions**. Because they begin to turn tawny-gold and to dominate other "animals" <note>In alchemical symbolism, a lion often represents the fixed, "kingly" state of matter or the sulfuric principle that "devours" or fixes the volatile mercurial parts</note>. For they easily capture whatever things are fleeting as prey and convert them into nourishment for themselves. But why do those who are conquered by the virgin meet their death? Because, as <term>Bacasser</term> <note>A name often appearing in early alchemical compilations</note> says in the <term>Turba</term> <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: *“Nothing generates more pain in the heart than an error in this art; for while someone thinks they have succeeded and possess the world, they will find nothing in their hands.”* 

She kills the boar because she is another <term>Diana</term> <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, associated with the Moon and silver</note>; she draws the spring from the rock near the shrine of <term>Aesculapius</term>, because the hardest philosophical stones yield water. Thus <term>Ripley</term> <note>George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note> in his figures says: *He produced water from the earth and oil from the hardest rock.* 

Among the golden allegories let us also count that **Hind**, remarkable for her golden horns and bronze feet, captured by <term>Hercules</term>. <margin>5. Concerning the hind with golden horns captured by Hercules.</margin> But what skill is there, you will ask, in catching a deer? And you will think it entirely childish that such a task was commanded of or performed by so great a hero as **Hercules** is believed to have been. I admit, the matter would be too trivial to be handed down in writing, unless great secrets were hidden beneath the hunting of this hind. Now, the hind then...

# Hieroglyphics, Book 2.

...she had **golden horns** and **bronze feet**, and she was sacred to **Diana** <note>The goddess of the hunt; in alchemy, she often represents a pure, lunar state of matter</note> and inviolable. Therefore, she was not to be caught with arrows or spears, nor with dogs, but by running. For it was not fitting that blood should flow from wounds there; for in that way she would have been either weakened in strength or entirely destroyed. She had to be captured alive and in perfect health, and thus worn out by running alone. She used to dwell on **Mount Maenalus**, where both the boar and the lion, and other beasts of that kind, lived. **Hercules**, sent to her by **Eurystheus** <note>The king who assigned Hercules his twelve labors</note> to bring her back, is said to have spent a whole year running before he could weary her. But finally, exhausted, she fled to **Mount Artemisius** and was captured just as she was about to swim across the **river Ladon**, and was carried back to **Mycenae** on his shoulders. Then they say **Eurystheus** was so struck by Hercules' courage that he prepared a bronze jar for himself as a hiding place and would not admit Hercules into the city.

Now, the hind is a fugitive animal of black blood and melancholic flesh <note>In ancient medicine, "melancholic" referred to the humor of black bile, associated with coldness and dryness</note>, and therefore of innate fear. She seeks safety in flight if pursued, and is extremely swift in it. But since she has bronze feet and small golden horns, contrary to the common nature of hinds, she is somewhat hindered and slowed down by these in her flight, so that she can be worn out. For unless that very **solar light**, or golden ray, were in the fugitive and volatile <term>Philosophical matter</term> <note>The substance the alchemist works upon in the lab, often symbolized as a "fleeing" animal like a deer or bird</note>, it would almost never be noticed to stop or be "fixed" <note>In alchemy, "fixing" means making a volatile substance, like mercury, withstand fire without evaporating</note>. This is clear from countless testimonies of the Philosophers. For thus says the <term>Rosarius</term> <note>Referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum" (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note>: 

> *Quicksilver,* <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> *he says, is worth nothing by itself; but when it is "killed" <note>i.e., chemically altered or solidified</note> with its hidden body, then it is worth something and lives an incorruptible life, and this body is of the nature of the **Sun**.* <note>original: "Solis"; in alchemy, the Sun represents Gold</note> 

And <term>Arnoldus</term> <note>Arnold of Villanova, a celebrated 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>: 

> *In our stone are the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>Gold and Silver</note> in virtue and power, and also in nature. If this were not so, neither Sun nor Moon would be made from it; because the Sun and Moon in our stone are better than common ones in their own nature, because the Sun and Moon in our stone are living, and common ones are dead compared to the Sun and Moon in our stone. Therefore, the Philosophers have named the stone itself the Sun and Moon interchangeably, because they are in it potentially, not visibly, but in virtue and essence.*

More recent authors also mention this hind, but they join a **Unicorn** to it, when they say: *The philosophers say vigorously, that there are two animals in this forest, one praiseworthy, beautiful and swift: a great and robust stag; the other is a unicorn, as the Philosopher demonstrates.* And **Basilius Valentinus** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, likely a pseudonym for Johann Thölde</note> relates that an ass, having rotted underground, was changed into a stag with golden horns. It also has bronze feet, shining and white. For the matter whose head is red, eyes black, and feet white, is our **mastery** <note>original: "magisterium" — the completed alchemical process</note>. And it is well known how often the **philosophical bronze** <note>original: "æs philosophicum" — a term for a specific stage of purified metal in the work</note> is refined; for this is the foundation and basis of the work, so that it is not without merit that it refers to the feet in the animal. 

It is sacred to **Diana** because, according to custom, a hind was sacrificed to her, as is evident in the allegory of **Iphigenia** <note>In Greek myth, Artemis/Diana replaced Iphigenia with a deer at the altar to save her from sacrifice</note>. Now, **Diana** is the **lunar nature**; for the Sun and Moon constitute the entire composition. The hind is exhausted by the chase—that is, it is blocked by ascending and descending in its vessel <note>This refers to "reflux" or circulation, where a liquid is boiled, turns to vapor, and then condenses and falls back down</note>, so that it cannot escape, until the matter remains at the bottom as if weary, and no longer ascends, and this is done with a **lighter fire**. 

Truly, if the force of the fire were present, violence would be done to the fleeting animal. It fled, exhausted, to **Mount Artemisius**, and was captured at the **river Ladon**; for it was necessary for the virgin to remain inviolate, as she was sacred to Diana, who is called **Artemis**, as if <term>aerotomis</term> <note>original: "ἀεροτόμις", meaning "air-cutting"</note>, that is, "cutting the air," as some wish, or as others say, because she "makes whole" <note>relating the name Artemis to the Greek "artemes" (safe/sound)</note>, as **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note> testifies in Book 14. 

Now, **Ladon** is a river of **Arcadia**, from whose daughter **Metope** and the **Asopus** (a Theban river), the nymph **Thebe** is imagined to have been born, who gave her name to the city. **Ladon** is also the name of the serpent guarding the golden apples, as has been said. Whichever way it is referred to, the sense of the matter agrees. She used to dwell on **Maenalus**, a mountain of Arcadia abundant in minerals (whence the Maenalian verses); for that place was most celebrated by the poets. She is carried back to **Mycenae** on the shoulders of **Hercules** so that she is not harmed. 

But why did such great fear seize **Eurystheus** because of the capture of the hind by Hercules, when he had more often laid low other more monstrous beasts—namely the lion, the boar, the hydra, and those like them? Thus it appears that it is a greater thing to conquer by **Art** than by **Mars** <note>By skill and science rather than by brute force or war</note>, by delay than by haste, and by gentleness than by violence. Hence, for a whole year...

## Hieroglyphics, Book 2.

...[it] consumed itself by constantly running and chasing the beast; for thus the logic of the work <note>original: "operis ratio" — referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy</note> demands: 
> *For we take a year, says **Ripley** <note>Sir George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), an influential English alchemist and author of "The Compound of Alchymy"</note>, in the first gate: before we prepare our **lime** <note>original: "calcem" — the powdered residue left after a metal or mineral has been heated or "calcined"</note>:* 
For in a shorter span of time, our lime cannot be made, which must be capable of fusion with a color that does not vanish. To explain these fables according to their own understanding, mythologists make the sun of heaven out of **Hercules**, who runs through an entire year and chases I don't know what hind with golden horns; but since these interpretations are easily recognized as being twisted from their genuine nature to a foreign one, they do not stand firm. Nor do they offer any usefulness to the minds of readers or listeners, except for clouds and darkness which we have discussed to some extent.

<margin>6. Concerning Midas, a participant in the golden vow.</margin>
**Midas**, moreover, holds the symbol of gold, as well as the vow. He obtained this from **Bacchus** because he had humanely received **Silenus** <note>The tutor and companion of Bacchus, usually depicted as a wise but drunken old man</note>; namely, that whatever he touched should turn into gold. The wretched man was almost killed by hunger, until, led by repentance for his vow, he obtained a cessation of this "gold-making" <note>original: "aurificationis"</note> by this remedy: he was to wash himself in the river **Pactolus**. The river transferred this **golden-sickness** <note>original: "auriginem" — a play on "aurum" (gold) and "aerugo" (rust/sickness) or "icterus" (jaundice)</note> to itself, so that from then on it cast forth golden sands. This is a very beautiful little story, not unpleasing to the ears nor to the eyes, since it displays nothing but gold (which is burned for and thirsted for by everyone). It is most fit for declaring and restraining the insatiable appetite of the greedy. For it is certain that very many are like Midas in their *vow*, but very few in the *effect*: because to desire an immensity of riches is in everyone's will, but to obtain it is by the gift of God. But what god is it who granted such a harmful gift to the petitioner? A fictional and **hieroglyphic** god, not He who is truly God; for the true God gives good things that are more useful than pleasing, as a father to his little sons. For **Bacchus**, who is also **Dionysius** and **Osiris**, is the primary of the "golden gods," and therefore the granter of such a gift. But it is fitting to receive **Silenus**, his teacher or companion, kindly; though he is an old man mocked by boys as he sits upon a swaying donkey, he has more in reserve than he promises on the surface.

<margin>The Sileni of Alcibiades.</margin>
Hence that saying about the **Sileni of Alcibiades** <note>A famous reference from Plato’s *Symposium*, where Alcibiades compares Socrates to statues of Silenus that look ugly on the outside but contain golden images of gods within</note> became common; a taunt against **Socrates**, who was most deformed on the exterior, but most beautiful within.

### Book 2. The Egypt of the Greeks.

...tossed about; for a noble master sometimes resides in a lowly little house, just as a mind polished by literature may dwell in a body covered in rags and worn by years. By <term>Silenus</term> <note>The tutor of Bacchus, often depicted as an old, drunk, but wise man; here he represents the rough exterior of alchemical matter</note>, as well as by <term>Pan</term> and the <term>Satyrs</term>, the companions of <term>Bacchus</term> or <term>Osiris</term> on their journeys, nothing else is understood than the cheapness and wildness—or the crudeness—of the <term>philosophical matter</term> <note>The raw material used in the "Great Work" of alchemy, which appears worthless to the uninitiated</note>. If this matter is treated with human kindness and gentleness, the "gold-powerful" god who soon follows, <term>Bacchus</term>, repays multiple "grace for grace." This is what the vow of <term>Midas</term> denotes. Specifically, however, this refers to the gold-making power impressed upon its subject, which is immense and always capable of being multiplied, unless it is restrained and that fiery power is extinguished in its own water. The philosophers discuss this in many places, especially <term>Raymund Lull</term> <note>A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> in his *Practice of the Testament*, Chapter 23, where among other things he says:

> *And when,* he says, *he leaves it in the special form of sulfur—that is, a subtle powder—then he shows that it is of great ignition <note>original: "ignitionis" — referring to the energetic or "fiery" potency of the alchemical powder</note>; you should not value it less for this reason, but honor it more strongly, since it can be brought to the simple limits of ignition by the discretion of the operator who is wise in the doctrine which the Art provides regarding the multiplicative substance.*

To these we shall add other golden symbols and hieroglyphs of anti-

<margin>7. *Concerning admirable golden things.*</margin>
quity, which in truth never existed in the nature of things, but were invented by craftsmen and poets to declare other things through them. 

<margin>*The Golden Age*</margin>
Such things are the <term>Golden Age</term>, the golden rain, the golden harvest, and similar things. Regarding the <term>Golden Age</term>, it is generally accepted that it once occurred under the reign of <term>Saturn</term>, just as the Silver Age occurred under <term>Jupiter</term>, and afterwards the Bronze and Iron ages under others. But if <term>Saturn</term> was neither a god nor a man or king, then in truth no Golden Age ever existed. Even if we grant that he was a king, was the time under him truly more "golden" than under <term>Jupiter</term>? Perhaps because <term>Jupiter</term> was impious toward his father, whom he castrated, and was an adulterer and a murderer? But is <term>Saturn</term> not also depicted as such? He castrated his father <term>Caelus</term> <note>The personification of the Sky (Uranus)</note>, took his sister <term>Rhea</term> as his wife, and kept <term>Philyra</term> as a mistress among others, and even devoured his own children. However, instead of <term>Jupiter</term>, he swallowed a <term>STONE</term> <note>original: "LAPIS" — the Stone of Cronus, but here used to signify the Philosopher's Stone</note> in the form of a rock or stone; and when he could not digest it <gloss>on Mount Helicon</gloss>, he vomited it up. And that is the Stone, as <term>Hesiod</term> <note>An ancient Greek poet; the author refers to his "Theogony" which describes the origins of the gods</note> describes.

## Book 2 of the Hieroglyphics

...he mentions, was placed as a monument for mortals on <term>Mount Helicon</term> <note>A mountain in Greece famous in mythology as the home of the Muses and the site of the Hippocrene spring</note>. So that they might see and touch this stone, so many of the most ancient poets created fables about overcoming Helicon, on whose summit wisdom is to be drawn from the fountain of the <term>Muses</term> <note>The nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences</note>. It is clear from what was said before that <term>Saturn</term> never actually reigned with <term>Janus</term> <note>The Roman god of beginnings, often depicted with two faces; the author is arguing against taking these myths as literal historical kingship</note>, as the Pagans believed and imagined in order to prove to others that they derived their origin from the gods. However, it is likely that the first money was struck through his effort, as was told above. We know indeed that the **Golden Age** is said to have been spent under Saturn, because the beginning of all "golden gods" depends on Saturn as if on their forefather. Frequently, poets and other writers also make mention of a **golden rain**, and they do not accept it metaphorically, like the "Golden Age,"

<margin>Golden rain</margin>

but literally, as if it had actually occurred. For they tell that when the Sun lay with <term>Venus</term> on the island of **Rhodes**, a golden rain fell, and afterwards from that union <term>Rhodus</term> <note>The nymph or personification of the island of Rhodes</note> was born. This might have been forgiven of the poets because of their creative license, were it not for the fact that historians also affirm the same. For thus *Strabo in Book 14* <note>Strabo was a Greek geographer and historian living around the time of Christ</note> left it written: *On the island of the Rhodians it rained gold when Minerva was born from the head of Jupiter.* We read notes everywhere in histories of it having rained stones, grain, frogs, blood, small beasts, and insects, as well as many other monstrous things beyond the order of nature. They strive to provide physical causes for each of these—as if they were snatched into the air by living creatures or by solar rays, and there condensed and generated, either from their own "seed" or from the disposition of the matter, and later released. However, regarding gold and its generation in the air, even if we were to read of it, we would not give it any credit. Yet there is no doubt that miraculous rains have occurred at times by the will of God—as in the time of **Moses in Egypt**—or by magical power (as also happened there), and that they can still happen, since experience testifies to this in all ages and places. Indeed, that golden rains fell in Rhodes could be held as certain, if by divine fate and miracle...

### Book 2 of the Egypto-Greeks. 93

...might be clearly <note>The text begins mid-word: "manifestly" or "clearly," completing the thought from the previous page</note> demonstrated; but when it is added that it happened then, when the Sun had lain with Venus, and Pallas having been born from the Brain of Jove flowed forth, we rightly recognize the Allegory or fable. The Heathens did not turn such monstrous and incredible things into doubt or question, as being possible for their Gods, because they thought the Sun was a God and Venus a Goddess, and they judged that nothing but something Divine would be procreated from them. The same reasoning was given regarding the birth of Pallas. We know that an Allegory underlies all those Gods, and thus also this golden rain, having fallen at their intercourse or birth. Truly it is a rosy offspring, or Rhodes, who is brought into the light from such a great embrace. 

Thus Pallas, the Goddess of wisdom, is said to have arisen from the Brain of Jove, but with <term>Vulcan’s</term> <note>The god of fire and smithing; here representing the actual heat and manual labor of the alchemist</note> axe acting as midwife, not without cause, while gold fell through rain in Rhodes. For without Vulcan, as the primary instrument of the work, the wisdom of the <term>mastery</term> <note>The "Magisterium" or the successful completion of the Philosopher's Stone</note> is not perfected; that is, a perfect knowledge of the hidden thing cannot be had without prior manual handling. For theoretical science is a perfect Virgin, and is born only from the Brain of Jove as if from its Seed-bed, nor is it mixed with Vulcanian or smithing arts. Wherefore the same Pallas manfully repelled Vulcan, when he attempted to force her, from whose strife <term>Erichthonius</term> <note>A legendary ruler of Athens born from the earth; alchemically, he represents a "terrestrial" byproduct or a stage that falls short of the "Virgin" theory</note> took his origin.

## BOOK THREE.

# ON THE GOLDEN

### Genealogy of the Gods and Goddesses, from which, as if from a Philosoph-

->ical tree, countless branches of Hiero-<-
->*glyphic Heroes are propagated.*<-

**T**o wish to undertake a refutation of the pagan <note>original: "gentilium"</note> Gods and Goddesses—who have been accepted for so many ancient centuries by Poets and Historians, as well as by the greater part of the world—in this our "final age" <note>A common early modern reference to the era preceding the expected end of the world or the fulfillment of Christian history</note>, in which the Christian religion shines most brightly by the grace of God, would be to unweave a web woven over many thousands of years, and perhaps even to labor in vain. This is partly because such a refutation is superfluous for Christians who are already sufficiently confirmed in their faith, and partly because it might seem impossible to the Heathen <note>original: "Ethnicis," referring to non-Christian, Greco-Roman authors</note> writers themselves, who filled nearly everything with the superstitious deeds of the Gods and the Heroes descended from them. Therefore, let no one suppose that we have compiled this treatise because the truth of doctrine must now be perceived for the first time, or because the falsehood of the impious Heathens must only now be discovered; for those things have long been made known through sacred history <note>i.e., the Bible</note>, which is beyond all exception. Nevertheless, since many things together may assist where single things do not, and since it is permitted to light a lamp in private houses even while the Sun occupies the center of the Heavens <note>original: "Sole medium tenente Cœli," meaning at high noon</note>, so that those places which are more obscure...

<header>Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics</header>

[...while things outsi]de are clear, they might be looked into more deeply; we also considered, not without merit, that we would do something worthwhile if we rendered the genealogies of the Gods and Goddesses—which are quite entangled in themselves and have not yet been reduced to their true origin from which they flowed—clearer by our own illustration, such as it is. <margin>*No knowledge arises from negative propositions.*</margin> For it does not seem that so much light reaches the human intellect if it only knows that the things or persons held as Gods and believed to be so for the longest time are *not* Gods, as it does if one investigates from the fountains of truth what was understood—and ought to be understood—by the wiser ones through those things or persons, since they are not actually gods. For anyone can imagine that they were not introduced in vain or by chance.

To achieve this, according to the talent granted to us by the highest Giver <note>A reference to God as the source of all intellectual gifts.</note>, in the first book we unfolded the principal **Egyptian** matters, called **Hieroglyphics**; in the second, we ran through the more conspicuous **Greek** **Allegories** marked with gold; <margin>*The golden genealogy of the Gods.*</margin> now we shall review the golden family of Gods and Goddesses, from which, as if from a numerous Chain, the progeny of Gods and Heroes depends, under which the World has labored until now. <margin>*The golden chain of Homer.*</margin> Homer, in the 8th book of the *Iliad*, relates that all the Gods, hanging from a **Golden Chain**, tried to drag **Jupiter** down from Heaven, yet their effort was in vain. For if Jupiter is removed, the greatest part of them is taken away, as he exists as their Progenitor. He therefore outweighs all others in authority and dominion because the empire of Heaven, as they tell in their fables, fell to him. 

All the Heathen <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> worshipped him as the greatest of the Gods; but since he is not said to have arisen from himself, but from parents prior in time to him, we shall begin from them. Since even they—namely **Saturn** and **Rhea**—are not acknowledged to be without any origin, but were born from others, we shall proceed to these: namely, **Heaven** <note>original: "Caelum"</note> and **Earth** <note>original: "Terra"</note>. 

The Heathen, without any tradition or knowledge of the sacred scriptures, and presupposing things from the thick darkness of the human mind, conceived various opinions about God and the parts of the world. Some contemplated a first eternal cause, but joined the world to it as a co-eternal effect, as did the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who famously argued that the universe had no beginning and no end, unlike the Christian doctrine of creation.</note>.

# Book 3. Of the Egypto-Greeks.

...with his **Aristotle**; others [held] that the <term>efficient cause<note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note></term>, the eternal God, did not establish the World from eternity, but voluntarily in time, like the **Platonists**, along with the divine **Plato**; whose opinion is more closely aligned with Christians than that of the other philosophers. Some imagined that the world flowed together by chance from atoms. Certain others feigned that some smaller parts were made, or <term>coagulated<note>The author uses a culinary metaphor here, comparing the formation of matter to the way solids separate from liquids.</note></term> one after another, like butter from milk; 
<margin>See **Censorinus** on these matters.</margin>
Thus the **Arcadians** boasted that they existed before the Moon <note>Ancient writers referred to the Arcadians as "Proselenes" (Before-the-Moon), a claim to extreme antiquity.</note>; and others, attempting to solve that question of whether the egg existed before the hen, or the hen before the egg, hand down wondrous origins of men and animals, just as we related concerning the **mice of Egypt** in the beginning of the first book <note>A reference to the once-common belief in "spontaneous generation," where the mud of the Nile was thought to sprout mice after a flood.</note>. And these people, since they did not recognize the Creator of heaven and earth, who made all things from nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note>, thought that all animals, as well as plants, sprang forth spontaneously from earth and water mixed together in various proportions, with air and fire added, and that heaven and earth had always been without origin. Therefore, if they considered them as works made or created, they would be forced to admit an efficient cause for them, and thus progress into infinity; so they received them as the first unbegotten gods; encompassing the air within **Heaven**, and water or the **Ocean** and seas within **Earth**. Besides these, they established rivers, springs, mountains, and winds as contemporaries of the earth and heaven, or as relatives or kinsmen; or what is more credible, born from the first sexual union. Thus, the origin of all the **Gods** is deduced from heaven and earth, as is the origin of all other things. But although it is not necessary to offer a response to such frivolous and most absurd opinions, nevertheless we will embrace many things in very few words, by which their intention is utterly destroyed:
<margin>Reasoning against the opinions of the Heathens concerning individuals propagated from eternity.</margin>
If man [is born] from man of double sex, as well as the remaining animals from their own seed, and likewise plants from their own kind, and these always arise in time, according to individual instances; then none of them were produced by chance, nor is anything eternal according to individuals, nor indeed according to species; and what is true of the parts, there is no reason why it should not also be most true of the whole...
