### Book 3 of Hieroglyphics.

...is made; But first, this is held to be certain by experience itself. The reason for this connection is well known: because whatever arises from the seed of its own species arises naturally and not by chance. Furthermore, that which has arisen in time across all individuals cannot be said to be eternal in the past. Therefore it follows, and according to the truth: Man, as well as the other animals, the plants, and all parts of the earth and water—their species and contents—the air, and the whole Heaven with its contents, were not from eternity, but began to be in time. They did not come from themselves; therefore, they came from another. Who is that other? The God of Gods, the Creator of all creatures.

Let us pass over other arguments here, since they are well known, and let us consider those believed to be the first and great Gods—Heaven and Earth—along with their offspring. We do not deny that some of the wiser <term>Heathens<note>original: "Ethnicorum." Referring to non-Christian, particularly Greek and Roman, philosophers.</note></term>, when they saw such a great crowd of Gods was being presented, which must finally be reduced to the unity of a first cause, reduced almost all the Gods to the Elements of the "greater world" <note>The "Macrocosm" or the physical universe.</note>, and thus silently renounced the plurality of deities. Among these, **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a Roman scholar who attempted to categorize and provide rational/physical explanations for the Roman pantheon.</note> is most occupied with this, lest the Gods appear entirely mythical. But since this opinion fosters many absurdities and is not in line with the intention of the authors who first brought this kinship of the Gods from Egypt into Greece, we reject it entirely.

<margin>The **Golden Chain** <note>A reference to the "Catena Aurea," a concept in Homer and later Neoplatonism symbolizing the hierarchy of being connecting heaven and earth.</note> of Gods, Goddesses, and Heroes, or their Genealogy.</margin>

From Heaven and Earth, therefore, Saturn and Rhea were brought forth. Then Titan, Iapetus, Thetis, Ceres, Themis, and others whom **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet whose *Theogony* describes the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note> enumerates. From Saturn and Rhea came Jupiter, Juno, Neptune, Glauca, and Pluto. From Saturn and Philyra, Chiron; from the <insert>severed</insert> genitals of Saturn <note>In classical myth, this usually refers to the genitals of Uranus (Heaven), which fell into the sea after he was castrated by Saturn (Cronus).</note> came Venus. From Juno alone, Hebe. From Jupiter alone, after he had devoured his wife Metis, Pallas <note>Athena</note> was born from his head. From Jupiter and Juno his wife, **Vulcan and Mars**; to Jupiter by his mistress Latona, Apollo and Diana; from Maia, Mercury; from Semele, Dionysus; from Danae, Perseus; from Alcmena, Hercules; from Leda, Pollux and Helen, Castor and Clytemnestra, born from two eggs. From Europa, Minos and Rhadamanthus; from Antiope, Amphion and Zethus; from Thalia, the Palici brothers; from Ceres, Proserpina. And these are the chief among the many sons of Jupiter, of whom alone, omitting the others, we shall treat.

## Book 2 of the Egypto-Greeks.

Then we shall touch upon a few of the more distinguished among his grandsons and great-grandsons, though many of the eighty sons of Neptune (as they are numbered) were born from various Nymphs, 

<margin>Heaven & Earth.</margin>
and others are neglected for the sake of brevity. That **Heaven and Earth** coupled—if understood naturally, insofar as Heaven is the active principle and Earth the passive, the former being form and the latter matter—we do not object, as this applies to things created and to be created, and whatever arises from its own seed. But if it is understood supernaturally, or according to the literal sound of the words as an act of generation or coitus, we judge it a delusion to be uprooted with <term>hellebore<note>A plant used in antiquity as a treatment for madness and gout.</note></term>, not requiring reason or argument. It is a wonder that the "Wise Heathens" dreamed this dream, that they attributed testicles to Heaven, the father of Saturn, and that they were cut off by Saturn so that no more children would be born to him. No one in the <term>workhouses<note>original: "ergastulis." Often referring to prisons or places for the mentally ill.</note></term> ever raved more than these so-called wise men; none embraced a true opinion of God less than these so-called <note>The author uses "si dijs placet" (if it pleases the gods) sarcastically here.</note> Theologians. Truly, they will respond that this was done rationally—that is, that Heaven was castrated so that it would not generate another heaven or another earth. But if every like generates its like, then Saturn and Rhea, and the other children of Saturn, would be new heavens and new earths, which is not accepted by them; instead, they mostly make **Time** from Saturn, certain progenitors from Titan and Iapetus, a sea goddess from Thetis, a goddess of grain from Ceres, and a goddess of justice from Themis. Let us first see Saturn, and consider the father from the son, or the following sons from this father: 

<margin>
Saturn & Rhea.
Hieroglyphics of Saturn.
</margin>

He was depicted by the ancients as a pale, bent old man, carrying a scythe in one hand and a dragon biting its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, a symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of time.</note>, while with the other hand he placed a small son to his mouth and devoured him. His head was covered by a helmet, and over that was a veil. Beside him he had four sons, from whom Jupiter cut off the genitals, out of which Venus was born <note>The author is recounting a specific, perhaps syncretic, version of the myth where Jupiter castrates Saturn, though in Hesiod's more famous version, Saturn (Cronus) castrates his father Heaven (Uranus).</note>. They say that although Saturn was younger than **Titan**, he nevertheless transferred the kingdom to himself; therefore a war arose between the Titans (his sons were also called Titans) and Saturn. It was settled by this law: that if any male children were born to Saturn from **Rhea**, they should be put out of the way <note>i.e., killed or disposed of.</note>. And so Saturn...

He [Saturn] ordered the newborn Jupiter to be brought to him, but being tricked by Rhea, he received a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes, which he immediately devoured instead of Jupiter. And Jupiter was raised elsewhere in Crete by the Corybantes <note>A group of armed dancers who worshipped the goddess Rhea/Cybele and were said to have drummed their shields to drown out the cries of the infant Jupiter so Saturn would not hear him.</note> until he reached the proper age. In the same way, **Neptune** and **Pluto** are said to have been saved from the voracity of **Saturn** after their birth by **Rhea**, who was always offering something else in their place. Moreover, when he loved **Philyra**, the daughter of **Ocean**, and Ops <note>Another name for Rhea, Saturn's wife.</note> came upon them, he turned himself into a horse, and from her he fathered **Chiron**, the most just and wise of the centaurs (the teacher of so many disciples such as **Jason**, **Hercules**, and **Achilles**). 

Afterward, this same **Saturn** suffered from his son what he had inflicted upon his own father: namely, castration and expulsion from his kingdom; according to the rule, *A man is punished by the same things through which he sins* <note>original: "Per quæ quis peccat, per eadem punitur." A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 11:16.</note>. Then the fugitive son of Heaven is said to have come to **Italy**. It is a wonder that such a small portion of the earth could support the son of so great a father, and that it received him as an exile hiding there (from which they would have the name **Latium** derived) <note>Roman tradition often derived the name "Latium" from the Latin verb "latere" (to hide), because Saturn hid there from his son Jupiter.</note>. But it pleased the Pagans to trifle in this way, so that they might at least trace the names, foundations, and governments of their regions and cities back to some of the most ancient gods, lest they be believed to have sprung from men, but rather born and descended from the gods. 

In ancient times, the precinct of Saturn was honored with lit wax candles, and candles were sent to one another by the wealthier citizens; because Saturn seemed to be, or to signify, the light of human life, and was considered the inventor of many useful things. In honor of this god, when the **Saturnalia** was celebrated among the **Romans**, masters served their slaves.

But more memorable than the rest is that, as Natalis <note>Natalis Comes (1520–1582), an influential Italian mythographer whose works were standard textbooks for interpreting classical myths in the Renaissance.</note> cites from Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the Hermetic Corpus is attributed.</note>, three wise men in all flourished in the time of Trismegistus: namely, **Heaven**, **Saturn**, and **Mercury**. Most people, as mentioned, have explained **Saturn** as Time, as if this arose from the motion of the heavens, and that it is at least one [unique thing]; for this reason, Saturn, like the heavens, was deprived of his virility. They say this same Time is all-devouring, and consumes and as it were devours all its children, generated in time and from time, sparing no one, except perhaps the hardest stones; and thus the stone [was ejected] by Saturn through vomit—

### Book 3. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

...that he was cast out by castration. These things are indeed similar, but as they say, they do not walk on four feet <note>A Latin idiom meaning the analogy is "limping" or imperfect.</note>. For if <term>Cœlus</term> <note>Heaven, or Uranus</note> be the father of time, <term>Saturn</term>, why is <term>Terra</term> <note>Earth</note> the mother? Did <term>Earth</term> conceive time? What does the earth contribute to the production of time? What does heaven contribute, unless you consider the motion of the <term>Planets</term>? What if heaven stood still and only the <term>Planets</term> moved; would there not still be time? Why is it not rather the <term>Sun</term>—which causes the year, day and night, summer and winter, and the other changes of time—who is held to be Time or the father of time, rather than <term>Saturn</term> or <term>Cœlus</term>? Why is <term>Saturn</term> portrayed as lame, when time is most swift and possesses wings faster than the winds? Why is the same figure established as an old man, when time does not grow old, but rather represents a youth? For just as the flame of a fire is always brand new, and does not remain the same for even the smallest space of time but always succeeds itself with newness, so also Time, and its very moment—which they call the *Now*—is always growing young, possessing nothing of old age. Does not the <term>Dragon</term> <note>The Ouroboros, or serpent biting its tail.</note> which *Saturn* carries reflect youth rather than the circle of the year, since it sheds its skin? Is it not the same in appearance as those assigned to *Mercury*, *Aesculapius*, the gardens of the *Hesperides*, and other places previously assigned? Or does it denote the roundness of the year here, the concord of two most opposing things elsewhere, and elsewhere still the prudence of the mind or the highest vigilance? However, the true reason for this Hieroglyphic is that which <term>Basilius Valentinus</term> <note>A legendary alchemist; his works are foundational to early modern chemistry and hermeticism.</note> explains in these words:

> "I, Saturn," he says, "the highest of the Planets in the Firmament, testify before all you Lords, that I am among you the most useless and vile, of a weak and corruptible body, of a black color, subject to the injuries of many afflictions in this valley of miseries, yet I am the tester of you all; for I have no permanent dwelling, and I carry with me one like myself, the cause of whose misery is to be blamed on no one but inconstant Mercury, who by his carelessness and negligence inflicted this evil upon me."

The same is found in *Occult Philosophy*, Chapter 12: On Generation.

# Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics.

...of Saturn; he relates that he was exposed to many vices through the fault of his nurse, and made lame in one foot, yet in intellect he was rendered no less teachable, wise, shrewd, and cautious, so that he conquered everyone in war, except for two who were superior in wealth and power. Hence he is seen as pale and stooped, namely on account of poor digestion; he carries a sickle because he is the tester <note>The "prover" or "tester" of all things; often an allusion to Time or the chemical "trial" of metals.</note> of all things; he carries the *Dragon* <note>original: "Draconem"; likely the Ouroboros or tail-eater mentioned in the previous page.</note> because it as it were renews them, or itself. But why the *Dragon* devouring its own head and tail is so often repeated among authors, there is another reason than what anyone might see there; and if one considers the difference with this case, he will notice how far apart bronze coins are from *lupines* <note>original: "Lupinis"; lupine seeds were used as play-money or worthless stage props in Roman theaters.</note>, and golden things from leaden ones. 

He devours his sons, born from himself, for whom if anyone takes the four Elements or other bodies, it is just the same. His head is covered by a helmet because he is strong in war, but a cheaper cloak is added on top; hence he is esteemed to be of a lower fortune. But what does the war with the *Titans* mean? Namely, that from others of his kind *Saturn* must be chosen for the kingdom; he who, if not in age, nevertheless excels *Titan* in wisdom and authority. 

When *Jupiter* was born to him by *Juno*, a stone is offered and swallowed: a fine story <note>original: "Probum commentum"; the author is being ironic, suggesting the literal myth is absurd.</note> about such a great God, unless some secret meaning lay beneath it. But let this stone be seen on *Mount Helicon*, where it was left as a monument. Was the cast-out lust of Saturn the cause of all lust in nature, since *Venus* is said to have risen from it—she who is present in all things that propagate themselves? Did so much good come to the world from the entrails of Saturn? O human madness, to be met with the laughter of *Democritus* <note>A Greek philosopher known for laughing at the follies of mankind.</note>; O blindness of minds, to be deplored with the weeping of *Heraclitus* <note>A Greek philosopher known for his melancholy view of the human condition.</note>, if the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> truly thought such a thing was done to their Gods by Gods, or to a father by a son. But we will hardly presume this of those who have left enough testimony for us in their writings as to how great and what sort of men they were.

<margin>By *Saturn*, authors commonly understand the <term>blackness</term> <note>original: "nigredinem"; refers to "Nigredo," the first stage of the alchemical Great Work, characterized by decomposition.</note> coming upon the work at its beginning, as they have reminded us in many places where they observe the sequence of the Planets. And then, by the castration of *Saturn* performed by *Jupiter*, they not improperly understand the removal of the blackness, followed by a dark or ashen-gray <term>whiteness</term> <note>original: "albedine"; refers to "Albedo," the second major stage of alchemy, where the matter is purified.</note>...</margin>

# Book 3 of the Egypto-Greeks

...they receive it as completed by the following Jovian <note>Pertaining to the planet or metal associated with Jupiter (tin), or a specific phase of the alchemical work.</note> action. Natalis Comes <note>Noël Conti (1520–1582), a famous mythographer whose "Mythologiae" was widely read and often critical of alchemical interpretations.</note>, when discussing Saturn, takes a dim view of the chemical practitioners' judgments regarding this planet: <margin>He fights like a blindfolded gladiator <note>original: "Andabata pugnat"; an Andabata was a gladiator who fought without sight, suggesting Comes attacks what he does not understand.</note></margin> *Furthermore,* he says, *since individual metals have been attributed to individual planets due to a certain resemblance, the tormentors of metals, or chymical craftsmen, have twisted almost this whole fable to their own art, since they profess to want to imitate Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century chemist.</note>, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note>, and Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (1232–1315), a philosopher often credited with alchemical works by later followers.</note> as Platonists. This is because Saturn is a certain salt, the father of Jupiter—that is, of a prepared salt which is made from him. But because, when Jupiter exists in a glass vessel, he is dissolved into a very sharp and thin water due to the force of fire (which is also taken from Jupiter himself), bringing the virile parts with him, cutting into and separating the innermost sulfur <term>sulfur</term> <note>The active, combustible principle in alchemy, believed to be hidden within salts and ores.</note> lying hidden in the salt, which remains in the vessel placed to receive them. For this reason, they say Saturn’s virile parts were cut off; and since the salt falls into water as if into a sea, Venus is born from that salt and sulfur.*

For these "tormentors of metals" strive to devise these and other similar arts by which they might transform metals into other forms, terrified by the hideous specter of poverty, and always keeping in mind that sentiment of the most witty poet Timocles <note>A Greek comic poet of the 4th century BC.</note>, who says: *Money is the blood and spirit for mortals; he who has no supply of it wanders like a ghost among the living.* <margin>A very fair response to the slanders.</margin> But hold your tongue, I beg you, Comes! Does a Saturnine star <note>Referring to Saturn’s association with melancholy, gloom, and harsh judgment.</note> so disturb you that you thus attack the whole chymical art and think it a dream, simply because of one or two interpretations of fables that do not suit your palate? Let us grant that he who wrote thus about Saturn (perhaps you mean the Italian Bracesco <note>Giovanni Bracesco, an Italian alchemist who wrote the "Exposition of Geber."</note>) applied those things poorly; is there therefore no truth in chymistry? Meanwhile, he understood that those things which you twist toward moral lessons rather look toward the secrets of chymistry and nature. What if chymistry is true even against your prejudice and above your comprehension? Will you make it false just because you judge differently or do not understand it? You will not, I pray. I am not speaking of the "tormentors of metals," but of the chymical art itself.

### Hieroglyphics, Book 3

...the chymical art, which may perfect the **Golden Medicine** <note>The "Golden Medicine" or Universal Medicine was the ultimate goal of alchemical healing, intended to restore health and prolong life, often equated with the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, even if it does not manufacture physical gold, nor devise anything contrary to nature. How Jupiter obtained the love of Juno, as well as their marriage, is a most absurd matter if taken literally; but if one looks to the secret meaning, it perhaps represents a correspondence with the nature of a bird. The Cuckoo <note>original: "Cuculus"</note> lays its eggs in the nest of another small bird, and once the chick hatches, it devours its foster-mother as a "reward" for her nursing—a detestable mark of ingratitude. Juno was considered the Goddess of Riches because a golden chain was placed upon her hands, and the Goddess herself was suspended high by her feet by Jupiter. Since the active and passive parts—the fixed and the volatile—are represented by Jupiter and Juno, she is sometimes suspended in the air because of her volatility, while she ascends and adheres to the upper part of the vessel. The Nymphs attributed to her are portions of water; and the peacock refers to the various colors which occur by reason of the volatile matter; for while the whole remains fixed, there is only one unchangeable color.

Because his father had disguised himself as a horse when he sought *Philyra*—so that he might not be recognized <note>Saturn took the form of a stallion to hide his adultery from his wife, Rhea/Ops.</note>—for this reason, **Chiron** had the upper body of a man from the navel up, and the lower parts of a horse. To revere **Mars** as a God and to bestow honor upon him seemed somewhat contrary to human nature, because he was believed to rejoice in the shedding of blood and in death; on the contrary, to acknowledge the Goddess **Venus** and to show her reverence through pleasures was judged something lovely and pleasant to every kind of person.

<margin>Venus accepted as a goddess as a friend to nature.</margin>

<margin>The Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> are insane in divine matters when they seem to themselves to be wise.</margin>
...they might understand the underlying things; hence it happened that a god, goddess, hero, or heroine is said to be descended from these or those parents, places, times, and circumstances, as is evident in almost all cases. And therefore, lest a fable or falsehood seem to be present in the accepted religion, a distinction was invented as a remedy, by which even the most diverse things could be reconciled. In this way, I say, Cicero in the mentioned passage <note>Refers to Cicero's *De Natura Deorum* (On the Nature of the Gods), Book 3, where he lists multiple origins for gods to show the confusion of pagan theology.</note> affirms that there were **three Venuses**, differing in their origin: The first born from **Heaven** and **Day**, whose shrine exists at Elis; the second from the foam, from whom and **Mercury** the second **Cupid** was born; the third procreated from **Jupiter** and **Dione**, who married **Vulcan**.

We know that Venus was neither a goddess nor a human, but a persona introduced among the Egyptians, as if on a stage, to declare things hidden under those names. Therefore, the ancients related that she was born from **Jupiter** and **Juno**, together with **Osiris**, **Isis**, **Typhon**, and **Apollo**. Whether, therefore, Venus is said to be begotten from **Saturn**, or **Jupiter**, or **Heaven**, or elsewhere, the thing itself is one, and not many, as the wiser among the Pagans [foolishly] raved. If there is agreement among authors about the *thing* <note>The physical or alchemical reality.</note>, they do not care about the *names*; for they say names exist for the sake of things, and not things for the sake of names. These [names] are in the place of garments; those [realities] are the things of living bodies. "Lovers love the stitching of the garments," says the Comedian <note>A reference to a lost or common proverb in Roman comedy; it suggests getting distracted by the outward decoration rather than the person inside.</note>, "not the garment itself." So too, philosophers admire and look upon the stitching of names—not the names themselves—that is, the things alone.

Nor will whatever is said about the gods cease to be a fable just because Cicero distinguishes well among personas, things, and times. He is cautious enough, certainly, but not truthful: for his distinctions are about non-existent and manifestly false things. Is Venus born from Heaven and Day? Did Heaven lie with Day, as with Earth as previously mentioned? **O Physicians, puncture the middle vein** <note>original: "O Medici mediã pertundite venam"</note>; Cicero is insane from too much wisdom! <note>The "middle vein" (median vein) was commonly bled in ancient and medieval medicine to treat madness or frenzy.</note> Thus he creates **three Jupiters**, of whom the first and second were born in Arcadia—this one with **Heaven** as his father, that one with **Aether**. He says the third, the Cretan, had **Saturn** as his father. From the first, **Proserpina** and **Liber** <note>The Roman name for Dionysus.</note> were born; from the most ancient Jupiter, king of Athens, and Proserpina, the **Dioscuri** <note>The twins Castor and Pollux.</note> were born. Likewise, he names **five Mercurys**, several **Apollos**, **Cupids**...

By the command of Jupiter, he fashioned Pandora to be offered to men in exchange for the fire stolen by Prometheus. He forged weapons for Jupiter against the giants, for which he sought **Minerva** in marriage; but she resisted his lust. Lions were consecrated to him, because they are fiery animals. His servants were the Cyclopes: Brontes, Steropes, and **Pyracmon**, whom Virgil mentions in the 8th book of the *Aeneid*. <margin>Ardalus.</margin> <margin>Brotheus.</margin> His son Ardalus built a shrine for the Muses among the Troezenians; and Brotheus, who, being mocked by everyone because of the deformity of his face, threw himself into the fire. Besides Venus, his wife is said to be Aglaia, that is, "Splendor." Vulcan, by no means forgetting the injury received from his mother Juno (who is imagined as the goddess of riches), sent her a golden chair with certain hidden bonds as a gift, which immediately entangled the goddess when she sat down. Natalis <note>referring to Natalis Comes (Noël Conti), a famous 16th-century mythographer.</note> records under the heading of **Vulcan** that the Chemists <note>the term "Chymicos" here refers to Alchemists.</note> also claim a **Vulcan** of their own, and by him they understand sulfur or "running silver" <note>original: "argentum cursitans," usually a term for quicksilver/mercury, but here used to describe a volatile alchemical principle.</note>, which receives nothing into itself except its own nature, but is separated from all things. And what he [Gargittius] then scatters out of mental impotence—whether I should call it ignorance or envy, I do not know; <margin>Gargittius, envious of Hercules.</margin> but let him keep his taunts to himself. Having "the eyes of a dog" <note>original Greek: "κύνα ὄμμᾰτ’ ἔχων," a Homeric insult for a shameless or insolent person.</note>, he "pokes the fire with a sword" <note>An ancient proverb meaning to provoke an angry person or to act foolishly in a volatile situation.</note> while he treats **Vulcan** so insultingly. Indeed, he shows that he knows no use for Fire other than for warming hands, cooking food, or for the convenience of blacksmiths' workshops; thinking that the best medicines can be prepared without the service of fire, in which he is mistaken. For the best medicines require the best element, which is fire, being closest to spirituality and simplicity, without which neither nature nor art operates.

### Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics

...revered. Vulcan, therefore, is not to be separated from Medicine, but is to be closely joined to it, like a cook to a kitchen. We have already mentioned before that Vulcan has something in common with Pallas <note>Pallas is another name for Athena or Minerva, the goddess of wisdom.</note>—if not a marriage bed, then at least the worship of a single altar. Pallas should therefore govern Vulcan; that is, foresight and Wisdom should guide the **Philosophical** fire. We find it discussed in many places that this fire is manifold. Yet, there is no doubt among the same witnesses that all fires mentioned by authors can be reduced to four types: namely, natural, unnatural, fire against nature, and <term>occasioned</term> <note>original: "occasionatum"; this refers to heat applied externally or through a specific setup, like a furnace.</note> or Elemental fire. 

Thus **Ripley** <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist known for his "Twelve Gates."</note> writes in his 3rd Gate: *There are four kinds of fire which you must know: natural, unnatural, and fire against nature, and the Elemental fire which lights wood; these fires we use and no more. Fire against nature must torment the bodies; it is the Dragon itself, as I tell you, burning violently like the fire of hell. The fire of nature is the third menstruum <note>original: "tertium menstruum"; in alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent or "water" capable of dissolving metals.</note>; that fire is naturally present in every thing. We call the occasioned fire "unnatural," such as the heat of ashes and baths used for putrefaction. Without these fires, you will bring nothing to putrefaction, so that its matter may be separated and simultaneously proportioned for a new conjunction. Therefore, make a fire inside your glass which burns the bodies more effectively than Elemental fire.* 

These are his words, with which Lully, Flamel, the *Ladder of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Scala Philosophorum"; a famous 16th-century alchemical text.</note>, and others agree. By Vulcan, therefore, we properly understand the "occasioned" or unnatural and Elemental fire, rather than the natural fire; but we add that the "fire against nature" must be prepared by Vulcan himself. If you recognize this fire, you have obtained half of the **Philosophical** work. 

He is said to have lived in Lemnos, because it is well known that this island possesses a warm and primarily medicinal earth. The smith-work he performed is partly **Philosophical**, and partly of another intent, if considered more closely. He made the shields and weapons of the Gods and Heroes, and distributed their insignia; because all their movement and power proceeds from fire; hence they are or are held to be such. He gave the scepter and thunderbolts to Jupiter, the shield to Mars, the trident to Neptune, and to others other monuments of his art...

...he leaves monuments. <margin>*Apollo or the Sun. 5th Son of Jupiter.*</margin>
Latona <note>Leto</note>, as most believe. But Herodotus writes in his book *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus’s *Histories*.</note> that they say Apollo and Diana are the children of Dionysus and Isis, and that Latona was their nurse who kept them safe. For Latona, being one of the eight original gods of the Egyptians, saved Apollo after he was entrusted to her by Ceres <note>In this context, Ceres/Demeter is equated with Isis.</note>; she protected him on the island of Plote (or the "Floating Island") <note>Usually identified as Delos.</note> from the attack of Typhon, who was searching for the sons of Osiris. 
<margin>*Four Apollos according to Cicero.*</margin>
Tullius [Cicero] lists four Apollos in the third book of *On the Nature of the Gods*. The oldest was born of Vulcan and was the protector of Athens; another was the son of Corybas in Crete; the third was from Jupiter and Latona; the fourth was named Nomion in Arcadia. To the third, because he is the most famous, are ascribed all the great deeds and the many children fathered by various concubines.

However, if we consider the matter as it truly happened, or according to its nature, neither Herodotus nor Cicero would have needed such distinctions. It makes no difference from whom Apollo is said to be born, since he is at least a <term>Hieroglyphical person</term> <note>original: "Hieroglyphica persona"; a symbolic figure used to represent a natural principle or an alchemical process rather than a literal historical or divine individual.</note>, who finds no place in actual substance, but only in quality or relation—unless we prefer to create "secondary notions." <note>A philosophical term for concepts that exist in the mind to help categorize reality.</note> The meaning is the same, whether Apollo is said to be born of Latona, of Isis, of Osiris, or of Jupiter; for Osiris and Jupiter, and Isis and Juno, are in fact one and the same. Nor does it matter whether Latona is established as the nurse or the mother of Apollo; the office is the same. But if we look at the logic of the matter, the opinion of her being the nurse is more approved. Yet because it has been so widely accepted, we state that Latona is both the mother and the nurse of Apollo and Diana.

The pagans determined nothing certain regarding Apollo and the Sun, or Diana and the Moon: whether they are the same persons, or others, or different; whether they were on earth or in heaven; whether they are those lights of the sky, or were truly heroes of the earth. Cicero, in his usual manner in the 3rd book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, brings forth five Suns. 
<margin>*Five Suns according to Cicero.*</margin>
One of them, he says, among those who are called "Suns," was born of Jupiter...

...is said to have been the son of the **Ether** <note>The upper atmosphere or "pure air" of the gods.</note>; the second was the son of **Hyperion**; the third of **Vulcan**, son of the Nile—whose city the Egyptians claim to be the one called **Heliopolis** <note>Literally "City of the Sun" in Greek; an ancient Egyptian religious center.</note>; the fourth is the one said to have been born to **Achanthas** at Rhodes in heroic times, the grandfather of **Ialysus**, **Camirus**, and **Lindus**; the fifth is he who is said to have fathered **Aeetes** and **Circe** at Colchis. Anyone, unless they are blind, can see that all these names are fictions, attributed by different poets to various things, persons, and places. Yet the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnici*</note> were pleased to seek a remedy for their superstition in this way, so they would not have to attribute many different parents and homelands to a single God. But if they say all these were Gods, where then did so many Sun-gods reside? If they were the lights of Heaven and the same as the celestial Sun, perhaps when they grew old, they were gathered into one place once their light was spent? If they were Kings and men, why are they called Gods, or said to have performed the deeds of Gods? For the name of "the Sun" could not make them Gods, nor could the many adulteries ascribed to them, nor the other crimes or wicked deeds which—if taken literally or historically—prove they were not even men, but barely half-men; far from it that they deserved the name of Gods. 

Therefore, although **Apollo** is established as fourfold and the **Sun** as fivefold, born of different parents and places, there is nevertheless a single **Hieroglyphic persona** <note>A symbolic figure used in the "sacred alphabet" of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>, known not to the Pagan writers, but to **Christian artists and Physicians** <note>Here, "Physicians" likely refers to alchemists or iatrochemists who sought the "Sun" of the philosophers.</note>. This figure is born from **Osiris** and **Isis**, or even **Jupiter** and **Juno**, or **Jupiter** and **Latona**. Meanwhile, through both Apollo and the Sun, 

<margin>Who can be called the Sun of Heaven.</margin>

the **Sun of Heaven** is commonly understood. And that Sun can indeed be called the eye of the world, the **Heart of Heaven**, the **King of the Planets**, the lamp of the earth, the chaser of shadows, the fountain of life, the smith of the day, the father of light, and the runner of Almighty God; but by no means is it God himself. To the Pagans, it seemed irreligious and a crime punishable by death to deny that the Sun and Moon were Gods. 

<margin>Anaxagoras said the Sun was a burning stone.</margin>

**Anaxagoras** was the first who, despising the threats of false religions, said the Sun was not a God but an ignited and burning stone. He demonstrated that the causes of **eclipses** of the Sun and Moon happen through nature, and not—as the Pagans thought—as the sufferings and illnesses of the Sun or Moon, which they would try to cure by clashing auxiliary brass <note>A reference to the ancient practice of clashing cymbals or pots during an eclipse to "rescue" the moon or sun from being swallowed or falling ill.</note>.

Hence Ovid writes in the 4th book of his *Metamorphoses*: *When the auxiliary bronzes of the moon ring out in vain* <note>original: "Cum frustrà resonant æra auxiliaria lunæ." This refers to the ancient custom of clashing bronze vessels during an eclipse to "help" the moon recover its light.</note>. Whether Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher famous for being the first to suggest the sun was a physical object rather than a god.</note> understood the Sun analogically, as some wish (referring to a glowing red stone, the <term>Philosophical Sun</term> <note>A term in alchemy referring to the perfected state of matter or the "Red Lion."</note>), or whether he did it for the sake of mockery and to elude the superstition of the common people, his opinion should be embraced: for it strips away all divinity from created things and from the lights of the world.

<margin>Sons of Apollo.</margin>
Many sons are ascribed to Apollo: **Orpheus**, **Hymenaeus**, and **Ialemus** from the Muse **Calliope**; **Delphus** from **Acachallis**; **Coronus** from **Chrysorthe**; **Linus** from the Muse **Terpsichore**; and **Aesculapius** <note>The god of medicine.</note> from the nymph **Coronis**. They say that Apollo came to Delphi from the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical people who lived in the far north "beyond the North Wind."</note>, and the place was named after his son Delphus. Regarding this location, the ancients told a story: when Jupiter wished to find the middle and the **navel of the earth**, he released two eagles—one from the East and one from the West—at equal speed. He commanded them to fly straight toward one another, and when they finally met at Delphi, a golden Eagle was dedicated there to the eternal memory of the event.

<margin>Delphi believed to be in the middle of the earth.</margin>
While this story is fabulous and contains no truth in itself—except perhaps to demonstrate that Delphi and the Delphic temple of Apollo are at the "navel" of the earth—it betrays a meager knowledge of Geography. For every place is in the middle of the world relative to its own position, because the earth is a spherical body, not square or any other shape. Yet that most famous Temple at Delphi, where Apollo gave oracles in ancient times and possessed an altar made of solid golden bricks (a thousand of which **Croesus**, the wealthiest king of Lydia, had sent), raised this place so high in honor and worship that it seemed to be the apex of the world, or the center of the earth.

<margin>A golden altar established for Apollo.</margin>
But if those fictions are intended as an Allegory, the Author of the "Advice" from the *Letters of Aristotle* <note>Referring to the "Secretum Secretorum," a text falsely attributed to Aristotle that was highly influential in medieval science and alchemy.</note> explains it quite elegantly, where he says:

> *That there are two principal stones of this art, the white and the red, of a wonderful nature: The white begins to appear above the face of the waters at the setting of the Sun, hiding itself until midnight, and afterward it sinks into the depths. But the red stone works in the opposite way, for it begins to rise above the waters at the rising of the Sun until noon, and afterward it descends into the depths.*

These, therefore, are the two eagles that meet in the middle of the earth, and there the golden eagle is established as a monument.

Truly, there are evident reasons why all these things are attributed to Apollo: because **Apollo** is a golden God, hot, and unchanging, who shoots arrows at Typhon and excels in the art of healing. This is because he himself is **Horus** <note>original: Orus</note>, the last of the Gods who are imagined to have reigned in Egypt, and the sought-after Medicine of human bodies. He is the leader of the **Muses**, the light and pillar of Poets, whose Laurel is said to be melodious and ever-green. His image shares traits with the Moon (or Diana, his sister), who offers the Graces with her right hand because it is a gracious gift of God, and arrows with her left; for he can multiply himself anew and extend his powers against Typhon. 

The Ox is sacred to him because the bull-god **Apis** corresponds to Horus. The Golden Tripod is his because the triple bond—consisting of body, soul, and spirit—is perfect; and from the circle of the Sun a triangle is made, which is again reduced to a circle through the middle of a square <note>This is a famous alchemical formula known as the "Squaring of the Circle," symbolizing the creation of the Philosopher's Stone from the elements of body, soul, and spirit</note>. He dwells on the three-peaked mountain of Parnassus, because a twin labor of preparation and operation must be overcome before reaching him. 

Among his sons, <margin>Orpheus.</margin> **Orpheus** is imagined to have been one, as well as **Linus**, rather due to their poetic power and knowledge of singing than for other reasons. For the poets who came after Orpheus and Linus offered this honor to them out of gratitude, as if to their masters. Thus they ascribed certain incredible things to Orpheus, such as that by playing his Lyre...

->To pass over other things, of which I might say many and great things:<-
->*If by chance he desires to know, he will know whatever mortals*<-

->*Chirp among themselves as they fly through the heights of Heaven,*<-

Although others may interpret these words as referring to Magic or the art of **augury** <note>The practice of interpreting omens from the flight and cries of birds</note>—as perhaps they might—nevertheless, since Orpheus was not truly a magician, and even if he had been such a man or an augur, he could only claim to know these things **Allegorically**. 

So they tell of **Democritus** <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 460–370 BC) famous for his atomic theory, who traveled extensively in the East</note> that he understood auguries and the voices of birds, just as is said of **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>. They say that Democritus (who drew his doctrine from Egypt) was accustomed to name certain birds by a specific name, from whose mingled blood a snake would be born; if anyone ate of this snake, he would understand the language of all birds. 

And they recall that certain snakes were seen by **Melampus** <note>A legendary healer in Greek myth said to have been given the gift of animal speech by snakes that licked his ears</note>, from which encounter he is later said to have understood the speeches of birds. Any person endowed with reason can discern that such things are utterly false if taken at face value. Thus **Cicero**, looking at the literal meaning of the Democritean doctrine, said: *No man has brought forth greater lies with greater authority.* 

But lest Democritus be held as such a liar—whose wisdom and golden sayings **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine"</note> admired and whom **Plato** held in high delight—we shall save his honor, as well as the honor of Orpheus, Apollonius, and Melampus, through Allegory. We shall say that by "birds" and "flying things," and by "serpents," we are to understand **volatile philosophical subjects**. For from the snake born from the putrefied blood of certain birds, once consumed, it is believable that the voices of birds do not remain unknown to a person. 

For from volatile substances, a firm and fixed thing is made through the "putrefaction of solution" <note>An alchemical term for the decomposition and breakdown of matter</note>, called the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quinta essentia: The purest, most refined substance in alchemy, thought to be the material of the heavens</term>. Since this essence is penetrating and liquefying, it is called a "snake," which then causes those same "birds" (from which it was composed) to be perceived through a likeness of nature. Such is the nature of these Allegories.

# Book 3. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

The books of modern writers are full of these matters, which may be examined by the curious. This same Orpheus feigned that he, led by the love of his wife, approached the underworld seats of Pluto and the gates of Taenarus <note>Taenarus was considered a traditional entrance to the underworld in Greek mythology, located at the tip of the Peloponnese.</note>; as he says in the *Argonautica*:

> *I have told the rest, what I saw when I approached Taenarus,*
> *And the shadowy homes of Dis <note>Dis is another name for Pluto, the god of the underworld.</note> and the sorrowful kingdoms,*
> *Trusting in my lyre, and compelled by the love of my wife.*

<margin>Aesculapius.</margin>
We have already previously explained what the kingdoms of Pluto truly are: namely, those subterranean places around the Pyrenees mountains, from which minerals for medicine and metals for the wealth of men were obtained. But leaving aside the remaining stories of Orpheus to be told elsewhere, we shall add a few things here concerning Aesculapius, who is recognized by all as the natural son of Apollo. His mother is said to be Coronis, who, after she had conceived by Apollo and later had relations with another, was put to death by Diana. When she had been placed upon the funeral pyre, Mercury extracted Aesculapius from the womb of the dead woman—or Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> himself did so, as Ovid says in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *Phoebus did not allow his own seed to fall into those same*
> *Ashes, but snatched his son from the flames and the womb*
> *Of his parent, and carried him to the cave of the double-formed Chiron.*

They maintain that his nurse was Trigone and that he was raised by Chiron the Centaur, and educated by the same, from whom he learned the art of healing. He was first called Apius (the Greek word *ἤπιος* <note>original: ἤπιος (epios)</note> signifies "mild" or "gentle") because he soothed the pains of the sick with medicines. But it is handed down that when he had healed Ascles, he was named Aesculapius, who to the Greeks is Asclepius. They fable that *Hippolytus*, having been torn apart by horses, was restored to life by his art; for which reason it is said that Jupiter, angered by the discovery of an art by which men could be recalled to life, struck the discoverer of the art with a lightning bolt: as Virgil has it in the 7th book of the *Aeneid*. When his father <note>Apollo</note> had taken this heavily and mourned greatly (his tears are believed to have been turned into amber), he [killed] the Cyclopes with his arrows...

### Hieroglyphics, Book 3 ###

...he did; Hence he was banished from Heaven and wandered the earth; and when, captured by love for the boy Hyacinthus, he accidentally killed Hyacinthus while competing with him in the discus, as Ovid reports in the 15th book of the *Metamorphoses*, he is said to have fled as a fugitive from Sparta to Laomedon at Troy. Laomedon happened to be overseeing the construction of the city walls at that time, and Apollo offered him his labor for hire, as will be discussed under the section on Troy.

The wife of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note> was Epione, by whom he fathered Machaon and Podalirius, Iaso and Hygeia. Others establish Hygeia not as the daughter, but as the wife of Aesculapius. They wrote that serpents were under his protection, and the dragon was dedicated to him; for twin dragons encircled his very staff; a rooster and a goat were offered to him.

Now, Aesculapius, the author and patron of all medicine (as the pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> imagined), is derived from Apollo and the nymph Coronis <note>The name Coronis is related to the Greek word for "crow" or "raven," which in alchemy signifies the *nigredo* or black stage of the process.</note>, because our Apollo and Horus <note>The author equates the Greek Apollo with the Egyptian Horus, seen as symbols of the "Red Work" or perfected gold.</note> are to be seen in a purple garment at the bottom of the vessel, still embracing Coronis—that is, the black, damned, and reprehensible dregs. From these dregs, our Aesculapius is separated through combustion or calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to purify it.</note>. 

Hence the mother of Coronis is Phlegyas; (for to *phlegein* <note>original: "φλεγειν"</note> is to burn); for Coronis, the mother of Aesculapius, is burned, just as was Semele, the mother of Bacchus, in almost the same respect. If indeed it is said that Mercury extracted Aesculapius from the ashes of his mother, the matter returns to the same point; for this is the office of Mercury, and it is nothing but Mercury of whom it is said: 

This is the highest <term>Philosophical and Medical Secret (Arcanum Philosophicum)</term>, which lies hidden under the extraction of Aesculapius from his own dregs or ashes; and it is so evident that if this alone remained from the most ancient monuments, it would nevertheless provide sufficient testimony of this golden Medicine and the vanity of pagan theology. 

For first, when Jupiter couples with Latona (who, although she may be red, is nevertheless useless until she becomes white), after some space of time Luna or Diana is born, of whom we shall speak soon; and a little later Apollo, the brother of Diana—he to be seen in a purple garment or flesh, she in a white one. And although the sister and brother are twins, yet the sister comes forth into the light before the brother; that is, the <term>albedo<note>The "white" stage of alchemy, signifying purification.</note></term> before the <term>rubedo<note>The "red" stage, signifying the final perfection of the Philosopher's Stone.</note></term>, and thereafter it excels...

### Book 3 of the Egypto-Greeks ###

...the duty of a midwife toward the mother, which is a marvelous thing, occurs nonetheless in the Philosophical Art <note>The "Art" is a standard term for alchemy, specifically the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, where the redness <note>original: "rubedo," the final, perfected stage of the alchemical process</note> does not appear without the whiteness <note>original: "albidine," or albedo, the stage of purification and silver-making</note> preceding it. When the Redness, or Apollo, is born, he lies here in the very vessel with Coronis—that is, a black nymph in the likeness of a crow <note>Coronis's name is related to the Greek word for "crow," symbolizing the *nigredo* or "blacker than black" stage of the work.</note>—and generates Aesculapius, who is the author of all Philosophical medicine. This Aesculapius cannot be separated from his mother, or the black earth, except by combustion; and then the purest Aesculapius is born: the Golden Philosophical Medicine, perfect in every respect.

*The authors discuss that black dross, making mention of it everywhere. Let one author, Arnoldus <note>Likely Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous medieval physician and alchemist.</note>, suffice for us here; who says in "The New Light," chapter 7: "This Ash, however, which is most red and impalpable <note>original: "impalpabilis"; a powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers.</note> in itself, is also raised and grows in the manner of leaven; and in the aforementioned calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to purify it or reduce it to ash.</note>, a most subtle and transparent black earth is separated from it, which is found at the bottom of the vessel beneath the said red powder, etc."* This is our Aesculapius, of whom Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says in chapter 3: *"Our son now reigns and is clothed in a red ornament and flesh. Now our born son, the king, takes his tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent substance capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals into gold or healing the body.</note> from the fire; indeed, the sea and darkness flee from him, and the Dragon who guarded the openings flees from the sun's rays, and our dead son lives, and the King comes from the fire and will rejoice in marriage, and hidden things will appear, and our son, now quickened <note>Brought back to life.</note>, becomes a warrior by fire and excels in tinctures."* Trigone <note>A nurse figure in mythology, here interpreted as an alchemical process.</note> is called the nurse of Aesculapius because a twofold repetition <note>original: "bina iteratio"</note> suits his nourishment. He is called Apius, meaning "mild" or "soothing," because he denotes the medicine *Nepenthes* <note>A legendary herbal potion mentioned by Homer that banishes all sorrow and anger.</note> used by Helen. He restores the dead to life, because the dead earth, having received its soul, is quickened again, as is asserted in many places, and as Bonellus <note>An alchemical authority frequently cited in the "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers).</note> testifies in the *Assembly*: *"Therefore," he says, "that nature from which moisture has been taken away, when it is left through the nights, appears like a dead thing; and then that nature needs fire, until the body and its spirit are turned into earth, and then it becomes a powder like a dead man in his tomb."* When these things are performed, God returns the spirit and soul, and once every infirmity is taken away, our nature is strengthened and improved. Therefore, it is necessary to burn that substance without fear until it becomes ash; which ash is fit to receive the spirit, soul, and infused tincture.

# Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics

Aesculapius, therefore, by his art, restores dead bodies to life; for he transforms those things which are imperfect and, as it were, dead from infirmity, into health and eternal life <note>In alchemy, "health and eternal life" refers to the perfection of metals into gold or the creation of the Elixir of Life.</note>. The reasoning behind the names of his wife and children is clear: for Iaso <note>A daughter of Aesculapius; her name is derived from the Greek word *iasis*, meaning healing or recovery.</note> is named from healing, and Hygieia <note>Another daughter, from whose name we derive the word "hygiene."</note> from health.

As for why serpents are under his protection, the reason is quite apparent: because the double serpents—one of which is winged and the other without wings, or the double <term>mercurial substance</term> <note>The "mercurial substance" refers to Philosophical Mercury, the essential "spirit" alchemists sought to extract. Its "double" nature refers to it being both volatile (winged) and fixed (unwinged), or male and female.</note>, male and female—are the beginning and the end of the work. For this reason, the Dragon watches over him and is sacred to him, just as it is to Mercury and other gods and heroes of this same family for the same cause.

This was held as such a certainty among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note> that their ambassadors brought Aesculapius the God back to Rome in the form of a Serpent or Dragon when a great plague was raging there; this is narrated below in Book 4. <margin>From Epidaurus.</margin> Thus the Devil, who deceived our first parents in that same form, supports the superstition of the Pagans by shaping himself into a Dragon to be believed as Aesculapius.

What some add regarding the **eggs of the crow**, from which serpents were hatched by knowing priests, perhaps stands thus: although it is a Hieroglyphic <note>Meaning a symbolic or allegorical image rather than a literal historical event.</note> and not a historical matter, that <unclear>Aesculapius</unclear> was brought forth from a <unclear>crow's egg</unclear>; for this is the **philosophical egg**, blackish and abounding in many superfluities, from which our Aesculapius must be separated. For thus says Arnoldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> in the place cited shortly before:

> *Because the aforementioned black earth,* he says, *is separated from the mixture during calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to purify it.</note>, which otherwise was inseparable in the whole work because of its very strong union; and therefore it was necessary for it to be separated by the strongest artistry. And if it remained mixed in, because of its impurity, it would hinder the entrance of the pure matter.*

So he says. But Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, or more likely a later author writing under his name (Pseudo-Lull), famous in alchemical circles.</note> shows that our medicine, when elaborated to that point, moreover takes the form of an egg, in his book on the *Fifth Essence*, Distinction 3, part 2:

> *When it has cooled,* he says, *you will find our infant most skillfully rounded in the manner of an egg; let him extract and clean it, etc. And in the Tree of Philosophy, under the 11th principle: After the rising of that color, it begins to gather together in the middle in a round form, in the manner of a certain most round moon, contained in a circle.*

Aesculapius is extracted from the ashes by the operation of Chiron <note>Chiron the Centaur was the teacher of Aesculapius. In alchemy, "Chiron" often represents the "work of the hands" or the manual labor of the chemist, as his name is related to the Greek word for hand (*cheir*).</note>, or the work of the hands.

It further interprets the "crow's egg" as the philosophical egg from which the pure medicine must be separated from black, impure earth.</summary>

### Book 3: Of the Egyptian-Greeks

[He] is handed over to be educated by reason; because, as Bodillus testifies in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba" [Philosophorum], a famous early alchemical text where various sages discuss the Great Work.</note>: "The extracted fetus is nourished only by milk and fire, by itself and gradually, while it is small; and the more it is scorched, its bones having been strengthened, it is led into youth; reaching this stage, it is self-sufficient." This is what the education of **Chiron** <note>The centaur who mentored heroes; in alchemy, he represents the skillful management of the fire and the natural growth of the "stone."</note> signifies: that one must be led, as if by the hand, to tolerate the fire. **Hermes**, the most ancient, also mentions **Aesculapius**, having addressed Dialogues to him which are cited elsewhere.

<margin>
Sons of the Sun: Aeëtes, Augias, Phaëton.
</margin>

We here pass over the sons of the **Sun** (who is the same as **Apollo**), among whom are **Aeëtes** (mentioned previously), **Augias** (to be mentioned later), and **Phaëton**. This Phaëton, the son of the nymph **Clymene**, once came to his father and obtained the right to mount the chariot of the **Sun**—a wish that proved harmful to him. For while he was being carried through the Heavens by the four horses of the **Sun**, he was cast down into the **Eridanus** <note>The river Eridanus, often identified with the Po in Italy; here it represents the alchemical "river" or solvent.</note>, not far from the **Pyrenees** mountains. By this graceful fiction, the **Poets** provided lessons in both physical and moral philosophy. 

Namely, how the **Philosophical Phaëton** falls headlong into the gold-bearing **Eridanus**; and that one should not seek things too high, nor attempt anything beyond one's grasp or own strength. And if the matter is properly considered, **Phaëton** is the same as **Aesculapius**, except that the latter looks toward the use of medicine, while the former looks toward other things which many judge to be incredible. For then **Phaëton**, by his heat conceived from the **Sun**, scorched and dried up the **Eridanus**—indeed, he made it gold-bearing, as others fabulate. Regarding this, **Augurellus** <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, an Italian poet who wrote on alchemy.</note>, following **Lully** <note>Ramon Llull, a medieval philosopher to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note>, considers that if he were to fall into the sea, the entire sea would be scorched and dried up, and would become gold-bearing—not to mention, as those others chatter, that it would be turned into gold. 

But let us return to the sister of the **Sun** or **Apollo**, who is the **Moon** or **Diana**. She was brought forth in the same birth as him, but was prior in time. 

<margin>
Diana or the Moon, 6th daughter of Jove.
</margin>

Most people consider **Delos** to be the birthplace of **Apollo** and **Diana**. And some babble that the **Arcadians** were called **Proselenos** <note>Greek: "before the moon."</note> (as if they were "pre-lunar") because they lived near the **Apidanus** and arose before the Moon existed. Among these writers are **Apollonius** in the 4th book of the *Argonautica*, his commentator **Mnaseas**, and **Aristotle**. Likewise, **Theodorus** in his 29th book, **Aristo of Chios**, and **Dionysius of Chalcis** in the first book of his *Foundations* most impudently affirmed that shortly before the war, which...

...was carried out by **Hercules** against the giants, that the **Moon** first appeared, at which time they tell stories that **Proselenus** <note>A name meaning "Before the Moon" (from the Greek *pro*—before—and *selene*—moon).</note>, the son of **Orchomenus**, ruled over the **Arcadians**, as **Duris of Samos** relates in book 15 of his *Macedonian Affairs*. In these most lying accounts, it was a pleasure for the Pagans to have demonstrated the antiquity of their race, taken from the name of a person who never existed; or if he did exist, it was a meaningless name. Even if someone called "Proselenus" had lived, would he for that reason have existed before the **Moon** had risen? 

But if someone wished to respond to these people, would they not rightfully ask whether **Proselenus** and his **Arcadians** had lived for so long in darkness? This is especially pertinent since these same authors testify that the **Moon** (or **Diana**) and the **Sun** (or **Apollo**) were brought forth on the same day and from the same birth—not into the light, because there had been no light before them, but into the world along with the light. Truly, "the **Arcadian donkey** thrives on such lettuce." <note>original: "Arcadicus asinus his lactucis luxuriat." A Latin proverb referring to a fool who is pleased by foolish or worthless things.</note> 

And not only the **Arcadians**, but other nations as well, have claimed for themselves the monuments of the **Gods** and the **Heroes** descended from them, with the **Poets** leading the way. Hence **Jupiter** is said to have been born in so many places; as **Natalis** <note>Natalis Comes, an influential 16th-century mythographer who interpreted myths as allegories for natural philosophy and alchemy.</note> wonders in book 2, chapter 1: *now in Crete, now at **Thebes**, now in **Arcadia**, now among the **Messenians**.* And lest I say anything 

<margin>See book 6, below.</margin>
about the other gods or heroes, how many cities have boasted that they were the homeland

or kinsfolk of **Homer**, and how many have shown his tomb? As **Cicero** testifies in his speech *In Defense of Archias*; we recognize the same signs of vanity and false little glory in our **Thessalus**, the son of **Hippocrates** <note>Thessalus was a famous physician and son of the legendary Hippocrates; he was often criticized for his arrogance.</note>, who impudently boasts before the **Athenians** that his lineage—and his art <note>The "art" refers to medicine, traditionally said to be founded by Apollo and Aesculapius.</note>—descends from **Apollo**. 

What if **Aesculapius** and **Apollo** had never lived? Would **Thessalus** therefore have been without ancestors? But these things were common at that time: were not **Aeneas** born from **Venus**, and **Romulus** and **Remus** from **Mars** and the Vestal **Rhea Silvia**, who was herself descended from **Aeneas**? How many cities, regions, and nations are there that had writers—while they were still under **Paganism**—who did not derive themselves from gods or heroes, **Trojans** or others? Thus truth was suppressed through flattery, and the reputation of dignity and antiquity was impressed upon the minds of men through lies. Concerning the **Moon**, insofar as [she is] a light of the Heaven...

# Book 3: Egyptian-Greek Affairs

...to illuminate, here we say nothing; but insofar as she is the daughter of **Latona** and sister of **Apollo**, otherwise known as **Diana**, we consider her: That the sister brought aid to her brother as he was being born, and acted as a midwife to her mother **Latona**, we have already touched upon; and the reason for this matter is clear enough: For the **Redness** <note>original: *Rubedo*, the final stage of the alchemical Great Work.</note> ought to follow the **Whiteness** <note>original: *Albedo*, the purifying stage of the alchemical process.</note>, and not the other way around, as all *Philosophers* <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to the alchemists.</note> testify. Indeed, **Diana** vowed perpetual virginity and obtained it from her father **Jupiter**, namely because she was terrified by the danger of childbirth, which she had witnessed: For the **Whiteness** which appears must not be removed, but must be cooked until it reaches **Redness**; and for this reason, she is said to remain a virgin.

She was also invoked by the Pagans as **Lucina** <note>A Roman title for a goddess of childbirth, meaning "she who brings to light."</note>, who, like **Juno** (who herself was brought forth by **Rhea** in the same birth as **Jupiter**), was believed to preside over and bring aid to those in labor, as well as to call all things being born into the light. She was always depicted as a **Huntress** using a bow and arrows, with which she pierced **Orion**, the greatest hunter, while he was swimming in the waters—acting out of envy and at the prompting of **Apollo**, though she herself was unaware of what her target was. 

They also called her **Cynthia** after the highest mountain of **Delos**, where she was born, and they considered her to be both male and female at once, as **Orpheus** says in a hymn: *Increasing and decreasing, the same is both female and male.* <note>original: "Aucta & deficiens, eadem quoque fœmina masq;." This refers to the waxing and waning of the moon, which alchemists often viewed as having an androgynous nature.</note> **Alcman the Lyric Poet** <note>original: "Alcman Melicus"</note> considers her the wife of the **Air**, from whom she conceived and gave birth to a son, **Dew**. **Marcus Manilius** imagines her being carried in a two-horse chariot <note>term: <term>Bigis</term> — a chariot drawn by two horses, contrasted with the solar *quadriga* (four horses).</note> and not a four-horse chariot like the **Sun**. And the hymn-writer **Homer** writes that she puts on and takes off splendid garments when she wishes, and bathes in the ocean, appearing now bright, now dark according to the splendor of her robes; they say her chariot is pulled by white does. 

<margin>*Cicero's three Dianas.*</margin> **Cicero**, in book 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, established that there are three **Dianas**: the first, the daughter of **Jupiter** and **Proserpina**, who is said to have mothered the winged **Cupid**; the second, more well-known, whom we accept as born from the third **Jupiter** and **Latona**; the father of the third is said to be **Upis**, and her mother **Glauce**; the Greeks often call her **Upis** after her father's name. 

**Latona** is the mother of her and **Apollo**; and this is most true: For what is called **Lato** or **Latona** denotes one and the same subject; and **Morienes** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary early alchemist reputed to have taught the secrets of the stone to King Khalid.</note> emphasizes this very frequently when he says: *Our **Lato**, although it is red at first, is nevertheless useless, etc.* <note>In alchemy, "Lato" or "Latten" often refers to a base metal or an impure alloy that must be cleansed to reach the white stage (Diana).</note>

And: *If however Laton is burned with sulfur, etc. Likewise; when however pure Laton is decocted for so long, etc.* <note>original: "Laton," an alchemical term for an impure metallic body or the "mother" of the stone, associated with the goddess Latona.</note> And countless similar things are to be seen in their proper places: Diana killed Orion with her darts—Orion the great hunter, that "Thrice-Fathered" <note>original: "Tripator." According to myth, Orion was born from the hides of an ox buried in the earth by Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury.</note> one, the son of Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury. Having been blinded by Oenopion and traveling to Lemnos, he was most kindly received by Vulcan. Vulcan, pitying him, wished for him to be led to the rising sun by his servant, where, restored to health, he recovered his sight. What help, I ask, did Vulcan provide to Orion, if not from his own art <note>Vulcan's "art" is metallurgy and fire-working, the mythological foundation of alchemy.</note>? And for that reason, he sent him to the rising sun; which is easy to understand and requires no explanation. Diana pierced this Orion with arrows while he was swimming in the sea, thinking she was aiming at a piece of wood. However, Diana is both male and female; because she is of a <term>Hermaphrodytic</term> <note>Representing the union of opposites—the "Rebis"—which combines masculine (hot/dry) and feminine (cold/moist) qualities.</note> nature, since redness exists beneath the whiteness, and the female becomes male in the <term>Philosophical Mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterio Philosophico," the process of the Great Work.</note>. For thus says Senior <note>Referring to Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabian alchemist.</note>:

> *This is the virtue of the woman, whom he had made female in 9 days; it signifies the soul, which is the virtue of the woman, which they made male when it is coagulated and fixed in the fire, and it becomes a hot and dry male through that which it acquired from the fire's part; and it is then named "male," and they call this coagulated water by the name of any male: then they betrothed her, and he is from her, and he is her root and her coagulation.*

Diana, or the Moon, has a son called Dew <note>original: "Ros." In alchemy, dew was often collected as a "pure" form of celestial water.</note>, even though she is established as a virgin: because it is necessary for the dew to fall before her rising. <margin>Flamel’s Hieroglyphic <note>original: *Flamelli Hieroglyphicum*; a reference to the famous alchemist Nicolas Flamel and his symbolic "hieroglyphic" figures.</note></margin>
This is that double connection of serpents, where one is depicted with wings and the other without wings; this is the double face of Janus, which looks back at the past and forward to the future; or rather, it is the means by which the unfixed nature enters the fixed, as if through an open door. <margin>Mercury instructed by Vulcan.</margin>
Regarding the thievishness of Mercury, there is a wonderful agreement among authors: that while he was still a tiny infant taken in by Vulcan <note>The god of fire and the forge.</note> to be taught, he stole the tools of the forge from the workshop. He stole the girdle of Venus, the scepter of Jupiter, the quiver and the cattle of King Admetus being grazed by Apollo—all on the very day he was born! And shortly after coming into the light, he defeated Cupid in a wrestling match.

<margin>The Duties of Mercury.</margin>
Later, as an adult, he obtained various duties: namely, to sweep the dining hall of the gods, to prepare the court, to carry the commands of Jupiter throughout the day, and to scurry here and there through the night to lead the souls of the dead to the underworld. He presides over wrestling grounds and public assemblies, and rests at no time. He invented the lyre; he was the first to stretch nine strings over a tortoise shell found by the Nile; he first discovered the three musical tones: high, low, and middle. He turned the shepherd Battus into a touchstone <term>touchstone</term> <note>original: *saxum Indicem*; a dark stone used to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak it leaves.</note>, as Ovid records in Book 2 of the *Metamorphoses*. He killed Argus of the hundred eyes, who was guarding Io (who had been turned into a cow).

<margin>Mercury. [In] Stone. He gave laws and letters to the Egyptians. Author of Astronomy and Philosophy.</margin>
He ruled over Egypt and handed down laws and letters to the Egyptians, by whom it was considered a sacrilege to even speak his name. Some also called him Trophonius <note>A Greek hero associated with an underground oracle, here identified with the chthonic or "underground" aspect of Mercury.</note> while he dwelled beneath the earth. The fourth day of the moon of every month was dedicated to Mercury, just as the first and seventh were to *Apollo*, who is the Sun. He had many sons (among whom was *Aethalides the Argonaut*) and daughters, of whom *Angelia* is mentioned by *Pindar*. A *calf* was sacrificed to him. His image was carried among the other sacred symbols of the Eleusinian Mysteries, which we shall discuss under the heading *Eleusinian Rites*. These things, beyond what was previously set forth, explain clearly enough the nature of Mercury, and why he was employed in sacred rites and believed to be a God: namely, that he is among the primary Hieroglyphics <note>In this context, a "Hieroglyphic" refers to a symbolic or alchemical principle rather than a literal deity</note> of the Egyptians and Greeks. For this reason, his solemnities were celebrated in silence by initiates and sworn persons, so that they might not reveal anything to another. Hence, *Lactantius*, in his book on *False Religion*, wrongly considers Mercury to have been a man of singular talent and wisdom. And *Cicero*, in his book *On the Nature of the Gods*, produces several Mercuries, asserting that one was born of Heaven as father and Day as mother; a second the son of *Valens* and *Phoronis*; a third born of *Jove* and *Maia*; a fourth from the *Nile* as father; and a fifth whom the *Pheneatae* worship. For in truth, there is at least only one Mercury, and he is a Hieroglyphic—neither God nor man; although I would not deny that there have been...

<margin>
Hermes, according to the testimony of Junius, is to the Hebrews a "wayfarer treading the paths." Mercury is a "seller and merchant."
</margin>

...that there were certain men of supreme wisdom called Hermes or Mercuries in Egypt, yet nothing of the aforementioned things can be attributed to them. Thus, Hermes Trismegistus <note>a legendary Hellenistic figure conflating the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth</note> himself counts Mercury among the wisest, not meaning himself, but the Hieroglyphic <note>the symbolic or divine principle of Mercury</note>. Just as this figure was numbered among the Egyptian and Eleusinian gods, so he was among those of the Samothracians <note>initiates of the Great Gods on the island of Samothrace</note>; their solemn rites had the same purpose as the others. Mercury was present among these most secret matters just as he was among the others. The priests and the initiates had a "golden key upon the tongue" <note>original: "clavis aurea in lingua"; a metaphor for the vow of silence regarding sacred secrets</note>. Both groups made offerings to Angerona, the goddess of silence, or to the god Harpocrates <note>the god of silence, often depicted with a finger to his lips</note>.

Therefore, it was a divine crime to scatter the names of the gods among the common people; not because it was evil in itself to name those believed to be gods, but so that the secrets hidden beneath the names of those gods and their sacred rites would not become known. This was the sole and proper reason why the initiates were chosen and sworn—those who celebrated those rites and saw the sacred images—and why it was forbidden to publish anything about the gods or the rites, or to name the gods themselves.

Hence, certain common and general names were attributed to those gods to designate their supreme dignity, such as Axioerus, Axiocersa, and Axiocersus <note>epithets used in the Samothracian mysteries to avoid speaking the gods' true names</note>; these correspond to Ceres, Proserpina, and Pluto. Ceres is the same goddess for whom the Eleusinian mysteries were instituted (concerning which we will speak below in the following book), and Pluto is the subterranean god of riches (of whom we spoke above). Mercury is added to these as a minister, who is "All in all."

They tell the fable that Ulysses was initiated into these rites; for so it pleased Homer. However, purple bands, not white, were used in those rites; and since Ulysses wandered while wearing them, he was the cause of the many errors and storms sent against him on his return—though he was nonetheless saved by them.

Why Mercury is "three-headed" is known to him who reads among our own authors from Hermes: *I saw three faces in one father.* So says the *Rosarius* <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical text</note>: *The matter of the Philosophers' Stone,* he says, *is water, and it is understood as the water of those three, as Hortulanus <note>a medieval alchemical commentator</note> proves; there should be neither more nor fewer. And he says that the Sun is the male, the Moon the female, and Mercury the sperm.* Mercury is called *Nonacrites* <note>The Nonacrian</note> because Nonacris is a mountain in Arcadia...

### Book 3: Egyptian-Greeks

A very famous mountain has, upon its ridges, very cold fluids dripping from the rock; moreover, this is called **Stygian water**, in which neither silver, nor bronze, nor iron vessels can endure without being consumed and eroded. It was believed that nothing could preserve it except the hoof of a mule. <note>Historical legend claimed that the water of the Styx, being incredibly corrosive, could only be transported in a vessel made from the hoof of a horse or mule; some ancient sources claim this was used to poison Alexander the Great.</note>

Mercury is called "Marine," as others have thought, because he fulfilled the commands of the Gods through the sea; "Celestial" through the Sky; and "Terrestrial" through the Earth. But we know that in him there is a "superior" and "inferior" <note>original: "superius & inferius," likely referring to the Hermetic maxim "As above, so below"</note>, the **Heaven and Earth of the Philosophers**, and that the Earth is a participant in the water; therefore he is said to be of "three natures," or because he consists of water and earth—as his own visible elements—and furthermore of a <term>quintessence</term> <note>the "fifth essence," a pure, celestial element beyond the four physical elements</note> or hidden celestial power. By Hecate's <note>the goddess of magic and the crossroads</note> union with this triform matter, he generated sons.

*Mystical matters.*
