A mystical cause is also noticed to underlie the days of the month dedicated to Mercury; and from this it seems the custom of numbering the seven planetary days began among the Romans. Since among them—even as it is still done now—the first and seventh days are assigned to Apollo <note>associated with the Sun</note>, and the fourth day <note>Wednesday, or "Mercurii dies"</note> to Mercury, yet without respect to the age or movement of the Moon, as in the past. 

That Mercury, having borrowed laws from Jupiter and Pluto, the God of riches, explained them to men, has now been declared quite often. The **tongue** is sacred to him, not as has been thought until now—as if he were the God of Eloquence—but as the God of **Silence**; and because his sacred matters must be kept quiet, with the tongue suppressed within the "wall of the teeth" <note>original: "dentium vallum," a Homeric metaphor for the lips and teeth that restrain speech</note>. 

<margin>
The tongue is sacred to *Mercury*, the herald of *silence*.

### Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics
->*The Secret Cave of Mercury*<-

Through a most secret art known to them at that time, he nonetheless ruled, ordained, fixed and un-fixed <note>original: "fixit & refixit"; a phrase likely referring to both the making of laws and the alchemical process of making substances solid (fixed) or volatile.</note> all worldly things as an <term>earthly God</term>. From <term>Egypt</term> he penetrated into <term>Phoenicia</term> and to the <term>Greeks</term> with his mystical religion; from these, he reached the <term>Romans</term>, who offered <term>Mercury</term> and his kindred Gods to almost the entire world over which they ruled, commanding them to be observed. For this reason, the <term>Spanish</term>, <term>Gauls</term>, <term>Germans</term>, <term>Britons</term>, and other peoples offered sacrifices to <term>Mercury</term>, as well as to <term>Mars</term>, as is evident from ancient histories.

However, I would rather judge that the <term>Germans</term> drew the worship of <term>Mercury</term> from the <term>Egyptians</term> themselves—since they hardly cared much for Roman names or deities, given that the Roman Empire was scarcely confirmed there for many centuries. My reasoning is that the <term>Egyptians</term> called <term>Mercury</term> "**Theut**" in their own language <note>The author is connecting the Egyptian god Thoth (Theut) with the Germanic roots of the word "Deutsch."</note>, and the <term>Germans</term>, who perhaps called themselves <term>Teutons</term> or <term>Teutschen</term> after the cult of Mercury, worshiped <term>Mercury</term> in the forests along with <term>Mars</term> long before the arrival of the Romans in <term>Germany</term>. I am not ignorant of what others may bring forward regarding different origins of that name, nor do I strongly refute them, unless they are mere presumptions rather than proofs. <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and natural philosopher.</note> in Book 4, Chapter 14, thinks the <term>Teutons</term> of <term>Germany</term> were so named after the <term>God Teutonus</term>, whom they believed was born from the earth. Indeed, <term>Mercury</term> is truly said to be born from the earth. So too was he once called <term>Teutates</term> in the Gallic tongue—the <term>Mercury</term> who was also worshiped by the <term>Gauls</term> and appeased with human blood. Whence <term>Lucan</term> <note>A Roman poet; the quote is from his epic "Pharsalia."</note> writes:

> *And those by whom pitiless Teutates is appeased with dreadful blood.* <note>original: "Et quibus immitis placatur sanguine diro Teutates"</note>

<term>Aventinus</term> <note>Johannes Aventinus, a 16th-century Bavarian historian.</note> in Book 1 makes <term>Tuisco</term> a son of Noah, whom Noah had fathered in Armenia and sent into Europe, assigning to him everything contained between the Rhine and the Don rivers. Others claim <term>Tuisco</term> is <term>Ashkenaz</term>, the firstborn son of <term>Gomer</term>, from whom the <term>Germans</term> are called *the Teutschen*. But since those matters regarding the origins of nations are highly uncertain and not very truly recorded in literature, we believe as we have received, or we receive them, though we do not believe everything.

Therefore, let us not worry about the names attributed to this matter and subject by modern writers, since they are innumerable. We say that among the most ancient people, this one and the same thing called Mercury was known, and through it one should understand <term>Apis</term> <note>The sacred bull of Egypt.</note>, all the bulls sacred to the gods, the other tamed dragons mentioned before, and almost all the hieroglyphic animals and deities; likewise so many monsters, the offspring of <term>Typhon</term> and <term>Echidna</term>: <term>Cerberus</term>, the <term>Chimera</term>, the <term>Sphinx</term>, the <term>Hydra</term>, <term>Hecate</term>, <term>Geryon</term>, and so many lions, horses, birds, and beasts, some of which have been mentioned, and others will be in their proper places.

He is said to have killed an **amphisbaena** <note>original: "amphisbænam" — a mythical serpent with a head at each end.</note> (that is the name for a viper having a head on both ends) which had bitten his shin, using a vine shoot that happened to lie nearby. He is imagined to have been carried to heaven by **Jupiter** but nearly cast down by **Juno**. **Ovid** (in Book 4 of the *Metamorphoses*) said he was always young; others have painted him bearded, and others beardless. **Isacius** <note>Isacius Tzetzes, a Byzantine scholar.</note> testifies that **Dionysus** was thought by the ancients to be both young and old at once, and **Orpheus** records that he was both male and female.

<margin>Poetry is compared to the head of an octopus.</margin>
What some have claimed regarding the head of an **Octopus**—that it is pleasant to eat, but produces many fantastic dreams—others explain regarding **Poetry**: they say it seems pleasant for its fictions, but scatters many vanities and things similar to ravings. If this is true, it applies especially to this allegory of **Dionysus**, **Osiris**, or **Bacchus**, which encompasses his birth, life, and deeds. Truly, although some commonplace things were attached to **Dionysus’s** deeds by poets of a later age, there remains no doubt that many things concerning most secret matters of great importance have been transmitted and propagated down to us from antiquity within the "wrappings" of fables. For if the ancient writers attributed only the making of wine and the invention of the vine to **Dionysus**, and thus offered such great things to be considered by the world as are ascribed to him, they would be worthy of **Hellebore** <note>A plant used in antiquity as a treatment for madness; the author implies the writers would be considered insane.</note> rather than praise; indeed, they would seem the most wicked and foolish of all men. Certain **Egyptians** among them have handed down things far different from what has been said so far regarding the birth of **Dionysus**:

<margin>A not unpleasant allegory, embracing the whole matter.</margin>

### Book 3: Of the Egyptian-Greeks

<margin>The expedition of Dionysus.</margin>
<margin>Pallas, leader of the Amazons.</margin>
...he stirred up the hatred of his subjects against himself, and not long after, having gathered great forces, he campaigned against **Nysa** and **Dionysus**. **Dionysus**, having heard of his father’s flight, gathered many soldiers from **Nysa**, and among these were two hundred infantrymen outstanding in strength, goodwill toward him, and dutiful service. To these were added gathered forces from **Libya** and a great band of **Amazons**, who joined all the more willingly because they understood they would have **Pallas** <note>Also known as Athena or Minerva, here depicted as a warrior leader.</note>—who was eager for military affairs—as an ally in the war. Thus, **Dionysus** held the supreme command of the men, while **Pallas** led the army of the women. 

Once the battle had begun and many on both sides had fallen, **Saturn** <note>The Roman name for Cronus, the father of the Olympian gods, here cast as Dionysus's rival.</note> was wounded, and the victory belonged to **Dionysus**, whose remarkable valor shone forth especially on that day. The **Titans** <note>A race of powerful deities who preceded the Olympians.</note> saved themselves by fleeing to the regions of **Ammon**, and after they were later captured through surrender, **Dionysus** restored them to liberty. He gave them the choice of whether they wished to serve in the military with him or depart; they all chose to serve with him and honored **Dionysus** as a health-bringing God. 

They say the expedition against **Saturn** was undertaken with the most noble **Nysaeans** serving alongside him, who were called **Sileni** <note>Usually depicted as rustic spirits or companions of Dionysus, often elderly and drunken.</note>, since the first man who reigned at **Nysa** was named **Silenus**. On the journey, he tamed many monsters and filled deserted regions with colonists. **Saturn**, having heard of **Dionysus’s** forces, set the city on fire, and taking **Rhea** <note>The mother of the gods, often associated with the earth.</note> and certain friends with him, he fled from the city under the cover of night. However, when they fell into the guards distributed everywhere and came into the power of **Dionysus**, they not only suffered nothing inhuman, but were even voluntarily invited to live together with him from then on out of fatherly affection, and were to receive all due reverence on account of their blood relation. But when the **Titans** again secretly prepared weapons, they were defeated by him in battle and slaughtered to a man. 

This narrative concerning the birth, war, and victory of **Dionysus** graphically depicts the entire **Philosophical Work** <note>original: "artificium Philosophicum" — a term referring to the alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> with all its circumstances, as we shall soon hear. ### Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics

<margin>Mercury, Hercules, and Prometheus appointed governors of Egypt.</margin>

...and he is said to have left **Hercules** as the governor of **Egypt**, and to have given **Prometheus** the highest rank after **Hercules**. In the mountains of **India**, not far from the River **Ganges**, he erected two columns in the East, just as **Hercules** did in the West. He subdued all of **India** and conquered the cities of the East; his army was composed of farmers and women. After three years, he returned from **India**, and soon traveled through **Libya** and the **Spanish territories**. He kept many women in his camp who indulged in dances and rhythmic movements. Once he had founded **Nysa**, a most flourishing city in **India** near the **Indus** River, he married **Ariadne**. Stricken, however, by a madness cast upon him by **Juno** <note>In mythology, Juno (Hera) often persecuted the illegitimate children of Jupiter (Zeus), such as Dionysus.</note>, he wandered the whole world. It was said that the *Kobali* <note>original: "Cobali"; mischievous or cruel spirits from Greek folklore.</note>, certain cruel and inhuman demons, as well as Satyrs, Bacchae (from which he himself was called **Bacchus**), and Sileni accompanied him with cymbals and a great noise wherever he went; he traveled in a chariot drawn by **Lynxes**. *Ovid: Metamorphoses, Book 4:* lynxes, tigers, and panthers were usually around him. He always wore a leopard skin, for which reason he was called **Bryseus**. **Lusus** <note>The personification of Play or Sporting.</note> was his companion. Instead of a scepter, he carried a *thyrsus* <note>A staff topped with a pine cone and wrapped in vine leaves or ivy.</note>. Sacred to him were the fir branch, the fir tree, ivy, bindweed, and oak. The magpie among birds, and the leaves of the fig tree, and a crown of **Narcissus** were not unpleasing to him; and among reptiles, the **Dragon** <note>In this context, a large serpent.</note>. His priestesses were women called **Maenads**, **Thyades**, **Bacchae**, and **Mimallones**. Having turned into a lion while being carried on a ship, he put all the pirate sailors to flight except for the pilot himself, so that they immediately jumped into the sea and were turned into dolphins. He slept for three years in the realm of **Proserpina** <note>Persephone, the Queen of the Underworld.</note>, then having been awakened, he indulged in dances with the Nymphs. He returned to his fatherland from the **Indian** expedition after three years and crushed his enemies. And since he is the same as **Osiris**, as has been said, when he had been buried, he is reported to have come back to life whole. He was imagined by the ancients not only as horned, but even with a bull’s head. 

<margin>Dionysus was the first to be worshiped as a God among the Greeks.</margin>

This god is said to have been the first of all mortals to raise the minds of men—sunken toward every base thing—to the worship of the gods, as **Ovid** has it in the *Fasti, Book 3*: *Before your birth,* etc. <note>original: "Ante tuos ortus"; a reference to Ovid's description of the origins of religious altars.</note> This is to be understood primarily concerning the *Trieteric* festivals <note>original: "Trietericis"; festivals celebrated every three years (by inclusive counting, meaning every two years) which Orpheus is said to have brought from Egypt to Greece.</note> of **Orpheus** which were transferred to the **Greeks**, concerning which

...which we will deal with later. When he was torn apart in the war of **Jupiter** against the **Titans**, **Pallas** <note>Athena</note> brought his throbbing heart to **Jupiter**. He was the first of all to lead a triumph, and because he wore a mitre <note>A ritual headdress</note> around his head, the custom remained for kings afterward to use a diadem in imitation of him. If we wished to examine all these things "to the nail" <note>original: "ad vnguem"; a Latin idiom meaning to examine something with extreme precision, as a sculptor checks the smoothness of a joint with a fingernail.</note> and apply them worthily to the subject for which they were fashioned, we would perhaps exceed the limits of our intended brevity. Regarding the burning of **Semele**, the mother of **Bacchus**, we spoke during the account of the birth of **Aesculapius**, because the manner is similar in both. The former is said to have been snatched and nourished from the ashes of **Coronis**, the latter from the ashes of his mother **Semele**; the former by **Chiron**, the latter by **Mercury**, or both were raised by nymphs, the **Hyades**, which represent the "watery parts." He is "twice-mothered" <note>original: "bimater"</note> because he was twice begotten from **Mercury**, as all <term>philosophers</term> <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers to alchemists or "philosophers of nature."</note> hand down.

<margin>Lull: *Theory of the Testament*, ch. 46.</margin>
*For our son, they say, has two fathers and two mothers, and because he was dearly nourished in fire, he will therefore never die.* He is imagined as being sewn into **Jupiter's** thigh so that he might mature; for thus it is appropriate in the <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" is a standard term for Alchemy.</note>; for the fixed fixes the volatile. And in this place, **Jupiter** approaching the mortal **Semele** with his lightning—she being endowed with very long hair—is our <term>Fire</term> kindled in the glass, which burns more than the fire of hell, as we cited from **Ripley** <note>Sir George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist.</note> under the section on **Vulcan**. This **Jupiter** helps and matures our "fetus," who, having been torn apart from the earth-born or earthly parts by Mother **Ceres** <note>Demeter, representing the earth or grain.</note>, the watery substance, lived again whole with joined limbs. 

Regarding his birthplace and parents, we have said enough. The miracles he performed point to the same thing: that he himself has the power of uniting and reviving things that are divided and dead. He killed the **Amphisbaena**, a serpent with a double head; this is because the serpent to be killed in the <term>Art</term> is twofold: with wings and without wings. The liquids produced by him occur because the whole compound consists of water and earth; if therefore **Dionysus** has grown into a substance reduced to earth, he is not said to produce liquids without cause. He is young, bearded, beardless, old, male, and female; for so says **Agmon** in the <term>Assembly</term> <note>original: "Agmon in turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: 

*"He is beardless,"* he says, *"and he is also most heavily bearded; featherless and not flying, he is also endowed with feathers and flying; and if you call him water, you speak the truth; if you deny he is water, you have not denied falsely."*

# Book 3. of the Hieroglyphics

<meta>Catchword: liquor</meta>

Regarding the Egyptian tradition, which makes **Ammon**—who took **Rhea**, the sister of **Saturn**, as his wife—the father of **Dionysus**, and the Nymph **Amalthea** the mother, we say that they looked toward the things themselves rather than the names. This is evident because they assign different parents to **Dionysus** and others to **Osiris**, whom they nevertheless establish as one and the same as **Dionysus**. Clearly, therefore, they deny that this is literal history, but rather a "hieroglyphic" fiction invented to signify certain realities. They look simultaneously toward the horn of **Amalthea** <note>the cornucopia</note>, the source of all abundance, and the gardens of the **Hesperides**. Yet by that topical description of so many circumstances, the first inventors wished to suggest nothing other 

<margin>A most complete explanation of the allegory.</margin>

than to place before the eyes of those who understand a universal allegory of the entire work <note>The "Great Work" of alchemy, or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note> with all its variations and parts. Indeed, I hardly think a more evident likeness exists among more recent writers by which the operation of the entire art is better foreshadowed than by this one: By the "boy," the subject <note>the base material or "prime matter"</note> is understood. By the city of **Nysa**, the vessel is meant; where the narrow "Nysaean Gates" represent the sealing and closing of the vessel. The pleasant region with various trees, vines, winds, flowers, and the songs of birds denotes that everything necessary for life and pleasure is present for the matter there. **Aristaeus**, the most prudent and excellent craftsman, is put in charge of the work. **Pallas** <note>Athena</note>, representing singular wisdom and subtlety of mind, is also required to be present. 

What is then added concerning **Saturn**—who, at the instigation of his sister **Rhea** (who had left **Ammon**), waged war against **Dionysus**—we understand as the **Saturnine** blackness <note>the *nigredo* stage, the first phase of alchemy involving decay and darkening</note> appearing at the beginning of the work. The **Amazons**, virgin female warriors, are present for **Dionysus**; for "virgin’s milk" <note>original: "Lac virginis"; a symbolic name for a potent alchemical solvent or purified mercury</note> performs much, as does the "virgin power"; for his mother is a virgin, and the father did not lie with her. **Dionysus** conquers **Saturn** because the blackness ceases, and he takes the **Titans** by surrender; that is, he halts the smoky exhalations of the matter. And **Dionysus** is a god of health-giving worship because he was born for the health of men, just as **Aesculapius** was. He tamed many monsters, since the matter itself bears the name and omen of monsters (as we have shown before), which he tames, and he fills deserted regions with settlers. For as **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull, a famous medieval philosopher and purported alchemist</note> testifies in the *Theory of the Testament*, chapter 9: In that liquor...

<margin>Anius.</margin>
When Apollo had known <note>original: "compressisset"; to have sexual intercourse with</note> Rho, and Staphylus realized she was pregnant, he shut her in a chest and cast her into the sea. This Anius later fathered Spermo, Oeno, and Elais by the Nymph Dorippe; Apollo granted to these daughters that as often as they wished, they might receive either wine, seeds, or oil, according to the meaning of their names <note>Their names are Greek for the staples of life: Spermo (Seed/Grain), Oeno (Wine), and Elais (Oil). ### Hieroglyphics, Book 3

[With the gods'] help, he approached Medusa; looking at her only through the reflection of a mirror <note>Athena’s polished shield</note> so that he would not be turned to stone, and covered by the helmet of Pluto <note>the Cap of Invisibility</note> so that he could not be seen, he decapitated her with a single blow while Pallas <note>the goddess Athena</note> guided his hand. On his return journey, he rescued Andromeda, the daughter of the Ethiopian King Cepheus and Cassiopeia, who had been offered up to be torn apart by a sea monster. He freed her by showing the monster Medusa’s head and then took her as his wife. He also turned Atlas into a mountain. From this wound, Acrisius died, just as the oracle had predicted. Furthermore, from the spilled blood of Medusa, the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor were born.

### Book 3 of the Egyptian-Greeks
<note>Egyptian-Greeks likely refers to the "Hermetic" or "Hieroglyphic" interpretation of Greek myths through an Egyptian/alchemical lens</note>

...are imagined; Pegasus, a winged horse led to Pallas <note>the goddess Athena</note>, by whom he was given to Bellerophon, the son of Glaucus (grandson of Sisyphus, great-grandson of Aeolus, and great-great-grandson of Jupiter), in order to slay the Chimaera. This was a triple-formed monster born of Typhon and Echidna. As Theopompus writes in the seventh book of his *Philippics* based on legendary tradition, this Bellerophon, while seated upon Pegasus, did not pierce the Chimaera with arrows, but instead attacked it with a certain spear that had lead attached to its tip. When Bellerophon thrust this part of the spear into the Chimaera's mouth, the lead was melted by the fire (which the beast breathed from its mouth) and flowed down into the Chimaera’s belly, burning all its intestines, from which it died. This was a clever stratagem devised by Bellerophon; but if anyone accepts this as a literal historical event, or fails to perceive the reason and purpose for which it was invented, he might be judged as having a "leaden" wit. <note>original: "plumbeus ingenio"</note>

<margin>The origin of the fountain of Helicon.</margin>
It is said that the fountain Hippocrene <note>literally "Horse-spring"</note> was struck out on the two-peaked Parnassus by the hoof of this same Pegasus. From this spring the Muses, Apollo, poets, and all learned men drink and emerge more enlightened. Thus, the erudition of poets depends, like a golden chain, from the fountain of Parnassus; this from the hoof of Pegasus; Pegasus from the blood of Medusa; Medusa from a sea monster; she was slain by Perseus; Perseus was born of Jupiter; Jupiter from Saturn; and Saturn from the Sky <note>Uranus</note>. The same must be said of Chrysaor, who is the father of the three-bodied Geryon, the owner of the purple cattle. 

But who does not recognize this allegory of Perseus from what has already been said? Nevertheless, we shall add a few points: The golden rain and Jupiter descending into the lap of Danae denotes neither greed nor pleasure bought with gold—except in a secondary sense—but rather it is so described because it fits the philosophical artifice <note>The "Great Work" of alchemy</note>. For there, gold is mixed with gold, and from both, "our son" <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is born in the air, as Ripley <note>George Ripley, a 15th-century English alchemist</note> has it in his sixth Gate, so that you do not labor too much in blowing the coals. And as the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous alchemical treatise</note> says:

> The conception and the betrothal take place in the putrefaction at the bottom of the vessel, and the generation of the offspring takes place in the air, namely in the head of the vessel, that is, the alembic. <note>A distillation apparatus</note>

And Senior <note>Senior Zadith, an influential Arab alchemist known as Ibn Umail</note> says:

> Just as we see the sun having two rays raining down upon the dead ash, and that which had been given over to death is revived, just as one is restored after great poverty: This is the sister and this is the brother.

### Book 3 of Hieroglyphics

<margin>Riddle:</margin> [The bones] were found, because an oracle had predicted that they were to be sought out and would be found in that place where the winds, the striker, the struck-back, and the ruin of men were found together. When Lychas <note>A Spartan official who, according to Herodotus, discovered the giant bones of Orestes by solving this blacksmith's riddle</note> interpreted this as a blacksmith's workshop—understanding the "winds" as the bellows, the "striker" as the hammer, the "struck-back" as the anvil, and the "ruin of men" as iron—the bones of Orestes were found there, near the shrine of the Fates in the tomb of Agamemnon, and were buried as the oracle commanded.

<margin>Note.</margin> To the ignorant, nothing seems more absurd than this fiction; to those who understand, hardly anything seems more elegant. We have already considered who Agamemnon represents at Troy; here it is clear that Clytemnestra is the daughter of Jupiter, although others assert that the egg from which Castor and Clytemnestra were produced belonged to Tyndarus <note>The mortal King of Sparta and husband of Leda</note>. For the same truth appears regarding both: You might say it is something new for women to give birth to eggs and imitate birds. This did not seem strange to the Pagans because Jupiter had copulated with Leda in the form of a swan. But we, outside of allegory, know this to be monstrous and a total lie. Nor is it enough to think that some sort of moral fiction lies beneath it, because one can invent moralizing tales about anything, for good or for ill; but the genuine natural truths contained and hidden within these stories are not so flexible.

Among the practitioners of alchemy <term>alchemy: the source uses 'chymia,' referring to the early modern art of transforming matter</term>, it is very frequently repeated that "the mother is devoured by the son, killed, and buried in his belly." For it is truly necessary that it be so. Flamel <note>Nicolas Flamel (c. 1330–1418), a French scrivener whose name became synonymous with the discovery of the Philosopher's Stone</note> says: *This whole work consists in two things: namely, that you make your fiery sulfur penetrative and attractive, so that it can devour its mother, and then you will have completed the work. Fix the mother in the belly of the offspring she previously bore, and then finally he will be a father to himself, and a perfect spirit <note>original: "spiritus perfectus"; in alchemy, a "spirit" is a refined, volatile substance</note> [formed] from the two.* And in the same place: *Then the offspring devours the mother and suffocates his father in a single lake, in which flowers, milk, fruit, and blood are found at once.*

And in Riddle 6: *Place a red servant equally upon the pregnant mother; mortify the mother, cutting off her hands and feet.* And Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan polymath to whom many later alchemical texts were attributed</note> in his *Codicil*: *It is necessary that the mother who first generates the son be buried in the belly of the son, and be generated by him.* Not only does the son enter and kill the mother, but he also slays his own father under an allegory; just as Oedipus <note>The tragic hero who unknowingly fulfilled a prophecy to kill his father and marry his mother</note> killed his father Laius when they met on the road and Laius would not yield, and [married] Jocasta...

# Hieroglyphics, Book 3.

[Minos] married the sister of King Aeëtes <note>This refers to Pasiphae, daughter of the Sun (Helios)</note>, so that like might rejoice in like—namely, a son of Jupiter with a daughter of the Sun. From her he fathered Ariadne and the Minotaur; the latter, enclosed in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus, was slaughtered by Theseus through the help of Ariadne. It is possible that some history underlies these figures, as people still tell of the remaining traces of the Cretan Labyrinth, although Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> says that the Cretan one had perished by his time, while the Egyptian Labyrinth, much older than it, had endured. Regarding the rest of the stories concerning Minos and Rhadamanthus and their incorruptible judgment in the underworld, we shall not speak of them here, since most were invented by the poets of the following age.

<margin>Amphion and Zethus, sons of Jupiter.</margin>

From Antiope, the daughter of Nycteus (or as others believe, of Asopus), Jupiter fathered Amphion and Zethus. Amphion learned to play the lyre from his master Mercury; with his song he moved wild beasts and stones, just as Orpheus, the son of Calliope, did. These two brothers are said to have founded Thebes and fortified it with walls and towers. Thus, it was fabled that the stones flocked together of their own accord and the wall was built while Amphion sweetly struck the lyre, as Horace says in his *Art of Poetry*:

> *Amphion also, the founder of the city of Thebes,*
> *Was said to move stones by the sound of his lyre <note>original: "testudinis," literally "tortoise shell," referring to the instrument's frame</note>, and with persuasive prayer*
> *To lead them wherever he wished.*

They report the same regarding the walls of Troy built by Apollo, and the music of the prophet Orpheus, with which he steered the ship *Argo* and attracted beasts and stones. But anyone can see that these accounts are hyperbolic <note>exaggerated for effect</note>, however one interprets them—whether as a reference to common poetry and its sweetness and power, or to the [philosophical] matters contained within it. Amphion was the first to dedicate an altar to Mercury, because he had received the lyre from him. Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century CE Greek traveler and geographer</note> in the later books of his *Description of Elis* thinks that Amphion and Orpheus were Egyptians and excelled in the knowledge of the magi <note>original: "magorum scientia," meaning ancient priestly or scientific wisdom</note>; however, this is not believable. It is proven by all authors and circumstances that these men were Greeks, and that they transferred the knowledge of the Egyptians to the Greeks. Regarding the miraculous things enumerated thus far...

<margin>The Festival of creation every seventh day.</margin>
SINCE the memory of men is so fleeting and the mind so weak, that unless it is often moved by some object striking the senses, it is easily led into forgetfulness of things past or invisible; for this reason, in difficult and great matters that should never be set aside from the mind, the wisest men—both among the **Heathens** and the **Israelites**, the people chosen by God—established certain perceptible solemnities. By the consideration of these, any diligent person might be stirred to the recollection of those things which were previously performed and celebrated, or which are otherwise held as secrets not to be revealed <note>The author suggests that public religious festivals often hide deeper, "philosophical" or alchemical secrets known only to the initiated.</note>, so that he may give everlasting thanks for His gifts to **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Deo Opt: Max:" (Deo Optimo Maximo), a title originally for Jupiter but adopted by Christian scholars for the Judeo-Christian God.</note>, from whom alone all good and perfect things descend. ### Book 4 of the Egyptian-Greeks.
<sig>Y 3</sig>

contained within them, completed in the space of six days; because on the seventh day the Creator rested and ceased from His work of Creation. 
<margin>Passover.</margin> Furthermore, the **Passover** <note>original: "Pascha"</note> was established in memory of the angel of God striking the firstborn of the Egyptians and sparing those whose doorposts were marked with the blood of the spotless lamb. **Pentecost** 
<margin>Pentecost.</margin> was established in remembrance of the divine law proclaimed on Mount Sinai by God Himself; and the **Festival of Tabernacles** 
<margin>Tabernacles.</margin> was a recollection of the forty years of wandering through the desert. 

With the same intention (though those religious rites are accepted piously, as is fitting, and these civil ones are accepted politically), in well-ordered republics, statues and images were placed and always preserved of those who had provided great utility to their people, or liberation from enemies, or other benefits. For this is, as it were, an **artificial memory** <note>original: "memoria artificialis," a classical system of memory enhancement (the Method of Loci) where information is mentally "placed" in specific locations or images.</note> consisting of images and places, representing to any informed person the memorable deeds of things or people, just as monuments of this kind were formerly in use among the **Greeks**, **Romans**, and other nations, and are still found everywhere. 

So it was among the **Egyptians**: since the greatest of earthly goods—by the indulgence of **God**, the most kind giver—had been granted to certain most acute geniuses, such as **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure perceived as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, a series of sacred texts on philosophy, magic, and alchemy.</note> and others, certain ceremonies and solemnities were established with singular pomp, most suited to the matter in whose memory they were made, so that forgetfulness of it might not flow down to posterity, but that thanks might be rendered to God in whatever way possible. 
<margin>Egyptian festivals for memory.</margin> Of this kind were the selection, consecration, nourishment, and worship performed in the **Temple of Vulcan** <note>The author uses the Roman name Vulcan for the Egyptian god Ptah, the patron of craftsmen and smiths.</note> for **Apis** <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, seen as an embodiment of Ptah and later Osiris.</note> (the Egyptian bull distinguished by certain colors), as well as his submersion in water, his burial, and the selection of a new bull once again. Likewise, there were the festivals of **Osiris**, **Ceres**, **Adonis**, and others similar to these, of which we have already partly made mention, and will partly speak of in the future. 

There is no doubt that these were originally established by the priests for a good purpose, since it was not permitted to deal with those **secrets** <note>original: "arcanis"</note> in any other way. But how they were then dragged into abuse by the ignorant common people and changed into horrendous **idolatry** is evident from experience itself. Besides these festivals, the Egyptians had two other ways of secretly handing down their mysteries, about which [now]...

### Hieroglyphics, Book 4.

<margin>Allegories serve the mind, Hieroglyphics serve the eyes, for the purpose of remembering the concepts understood within them.</margin>
...as [mentioned] before: namely, one method which serves the mind, and another which serves the eyes. The one for the mind consists of the **Allegories** of gods, goddesses, and heroes, containing their deeds and wonders; of these we have treated extensively enough so far, especially in the second and third books of this treatise. The one for the eyes consists of the **Hieroglyphics** <note>original: "Hieroglyphicis"; here referring to the visual symbols used by Egyptian priests to encode knowledge.</note> of animals and other figures of things, painted or sculpted, used in place of letters and writing; these we also discussed in the first book. And these three things—namely, the celebration of deeds, the narration of allegories, and the sketching of hieroglyphics—were kept so strictly among the secret archives by the initiated priests that they were never known to any of the common people or the uninitiated, but remained unknown to all others except for the philosophers who were the "sons of the priests." The reasons for hiding these matters have already been set forth by us, and more extensively by others, so there is no need to repeat them. Therefore, since these three things were least understood by the common people, while being regarded everywhere by the priests as sacred and enveloped in silence, they began to be worshipped more and more every day as divine matters, concerning which it would be a sin to inquire into their meaning, or why and by whom they were introduced. This is the single and triple-headed source of the many abuses, errors, and superstitions that were later transferred from the Egyptians to the other nations of the world. Just as we have until now discussed the gods and goddesses, as well as the heroes, and their origin and worship, according to the plan of our undertaking, so now in this book we shall briefly treat the festivals, games, solemnities, and contests established for the sake of those same things.

# Book 4. Egyptian-Greek [Matters].

Since indeed all things are allegorical which are said to have been undertaken concerning the wandering of **Osiris** into **India** and other parts of the world—where he supposedly taught men the method of cultivating fields, the sowing of the vine, and many other useful inventions—so too must that festival be judged as nothing if not allegorical, which takes its origin from those events or is handed down as a tradition instituted in memory of that wandering. 

For if in the true state of God <term>polytia</term> <note>original: "polytia," from the Greek "politeia," referring here to the divine administration or governance of a religious community</note>, among the **Israelites**, sacred rites were celebrated which proceeded from the truest causes (as said before), calling past deeds to memory and allegorically foreshadowing things to be done or future events concerning **Christ**, the same could happen in its own way among the **Gentiles** <note>original: "Ethnicos," referring to non-Jewish/non-Christian nations</note>, so that they might understand the allegory inherent in their own festivals.

<margin>The difference between the festivals of the Church and of the nations.</margin>

But the difference between these and those is "as wide as the whole heaven," as they say. Those [of the Israelites] were ordained by the true, eternal, and one God in His honor, both to represent things that had truly happened in the past and things that would follow in the future as figures. These [of the pagans] seem to have been forged by the sagacity of human genius alone, so that monuments and mute symbols might exist for a thing as if it had happened that way, or were believed under the veil of allegory. 

And just as **Moses** received those laws from God Himself, the fountain of Truth, and promulgated them by His command to be observed by the **Israelite** people, so **Orpheus** <note>In the Renaissance, Orpheus was often viewed as a "theologian" who brought Egyptian mysteries to the Greeks.</note> transferred these rites from the **Egyptian** priests—the authors of every superstitious vanity—to the **Greeks**. The former aim toward the end of eternal salvation; the latter, toward the temporal. Both, however, are directed toward the glory of God the Creator and the giver of all good things: the former were received by the true Church of God under both the Old and New Covenants; the latter by the crowd of unbelievers and the rest of the world.

<margin>The Gentiles wished to imitate the Israelites in many things, just as the devil imitates God.</margin>

But having dismissed those matters for now, or at least having mentioned them (since it is believable to many that this rite of instituting festivals and sacred ceremonies was taken from the **Israelites** through a certain perverse imitation <term>cacozylia</term> <note>original: "cacozylia," a rhetorical term for "distorted imitation" or "bad affectation," used here to suggest pagans mimicked holy rites incorrectly.</note> and transferred to the pagans), we shall speak of these as worldly inventions of men. 

What was understood by the wandering of **Dionysus** or **Osiris**, we have sufficiently declared in the first book under **Osiris**, and in the third under **Dionysus**. However, for exactly as much time as he is said to have consumed in his Indian wandering, for that same amount of time **Apis**, the **Egyptian** bull, was permitted to live, and was afterwards drowned in a spring; so they fabricated stories to express the same...

# Hieroglyphics. Book 4

<margin>Although Dionysus is the Sun, he is called terrestrial.</margin>

> *We sing of terrestrial **Dionysus** and the divinity of **Bacchus**,*

<margin>The Orgia. Those who prohibited the Orgia.</margin>
These sacred rites instituted by **Orpheus** were also commonly called the **Orgia** <note>original: "Orgias." While the modern word "orgy" implies debauchery, it specifically referred to the secret, ecstatic rites of the Dionysian cult.</note>. In these rites, such great abuse was eventually introduced during the nocturnal gatherings of the **Bacchants** <note>ecstatic followers of Bacchus/Dionysus</note> that **Lycurgus**, king of Thrace, **Diagondas** of Thebes, and many others abolished all nocturnal sacrifices by perpetual law because of their shameful nature.

<margin>False Gods are known by false miracles; the true God is known by true ones.</margin>
Miracles were said to occur during the days when these festivals were celebrated. For when empty jars were left in the temple throughout the night, they were found the following day to be full of the finest wine. This was the result of trickery by the priests, intended to deceive the gullible and superstitious commoners—just as is well known regarding the followers of **Baal** <note>original: "Baalitis." This refers to the biblical story of the priests of Baal (or Bel) who used secret trapdoors to consume food offerings, making it appear the idol had eaten them.</note>. The fact that the priests entered through secret passages and filled the jars is too notorious to even require proof.

Furthermore, those sacred rites were performed by women because **Dionysus** had them as companions during his expedition to **India**. These same women would carry the <term>Phallus</term> <note>a representation of the male reproductive organ</note>—that is, a visible image of the male member of significant size—in their processions. This was done in memory of **Osiris**, who, having been cut limb from limb by the **Titans** and his genitals thrown into the river, is said to have had his limbs collected and reassembled by **Osiris** <note>The text credits Osiris with collecting his own limbs, though standard mythology usually attributes this to his wife, Isis.</note> once the **Titans** were captured—except for the male member, which could not be found. 

As for what others add—that it was commanded that this member, in the form of a <term>Phallus</term>, be worshiped as a god—this is utterly absurd to reason. However, we shall see that these rites, sharing the same intent as the **Eleusinian** <note>festivals of Demeter and Persephone at Eleusis</note> mysteries, existed among the **Egyptians**, where the solemn carrying of the <term>Phalli</term> was also common. And this is because, as the **Comic poet** <note>Likely Terence in his play *Andria*.</note> says, *it is the nature of all men to be inclined from labor toward desire or luxury.* 

The same must be concluded regarding the later festivals and sacred rites of the **Egyptians**, who for the most part were ignorant of the causes of antiquity and their original institution, and worshiped signs instead of the things signified—animals, images of men, and beasts—until they eventually brought garlic, onions, and almost everything, both useless and harmful as well as useful, into the ranks of the gods. -># Hieroglyphics. Book 4.<-
<page-num>172</page-num>

Just as those [the Greeks] took from the **Egyptians**, so these [the **Romans**] received from both the **Greeks** and the **Egyptians** whatever deities existed among both: Hence **Lucan**, in Book 7, says this regarding **Egypt**:

> *We have welcomed your **Isis** into our Roman temples,* <note>original: "Nos in Templa tuam Romana accepimus Isim,"</note>
> *And the semi-divine dogs, and the sistrums commanding mourning,* <note>The "semi-divine dogs" refers to Anubis; "sistrums" were musical rattles used in Egyptian rituals.</note>
> *And **Osiris**, whom you testify is a man by your wailing:*

And **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who wrote the *Divine Institutes*.</note> says in Book 1 of his *Institutes*: *The Romans,* he says, *held their own evils as gods, namely rust, paleness, and fever:* Whence, as is clear from **Ovid’s** *Fasti* <note>Ovid's poetic explanation of the Roman calendar.</note>, the festival of **Rust** <note>Known as the Robigalia.</note> was held near the end of **April**, specifically the 6th day before the Kalends of May [April 25th]; they worshipped her then, as Ovid says, so that she would not harm the crops or the farming tools; and in the same way they worshipped **Fever**, so that she would not trouble them: For as **Valerius** <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman historian/moralist.</note> says in Book 2: *And they indeed venerated the others for doing good, but Fever for doing less harm:* And the same author describes the locations where there were three temples to Fever. Furthermore, the **Romans** worshipped a god of their own, **Romulus**, whom they called **Quirinus**; whom, along with **Fever**, **Rust**, and others of that kind, they did not receive from others, but had discovered for themselves by their own industry; but **Mars**, **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, **Mercury**, **Apollo**, and **Aesculapius** <note>The god of medicine.</note> they had borrowed from either the **Greeks** or the **Egyptians**: Concerning the occasion and the manner of bringing Aesculapius to **Rome** from **Epidaurus**, there stands a famous example which we shall bring forward here, so that from it the propagation of the remaining pagan gods may be estimated: **Saint Augustine** mentions this Aesculapius being brought to Rome in Book 3 of *The City of God*, chapter 12.

<margin>All gods are imagined to be born from Rhea as a mother. The Dog-headed one is imagined as the grandson of Rhea, insofar as he is Mercury.</margin>

Who does not see, even at first glance, that these are the most secret **Chemical** <note>In this 17th-century context, "Chemical" (Chymica) refers to Alchemy.</note> matters?

<margin>Hieroglyphic sign. Note.</margin>

For who has ever found it written, either historically or allegorically, that men—and those mere infants—were usually hidden under live coals?

### Book 4. The Egyptian-Greeks.

Who has ever seen a salamander—that animal that lives in fire—or a true fire-fly <note>original: *pyrausta*, a mythical insect supposed to live in fire.</note>, except in chemical works? Let the **Palici brothers** <note>Twin Sicilian deities who were said to have emerged from the earth.</note> come forth from the earth, **Venus** from the sea, and other monstrous offspring from the other elements; yet scarcely anything living can emerge from fire, except for the **philosophical salamander** and the **Phoenix** rising from the ashes left behind by the flames. Two things are unconquered by fire: gold and glass. Everything else eventually succumbs to it. To these, a third may be added: namely, the Phoenix and its nest, the seed from which is reborn he who is the ash brought back to life from the dead. However, I think it would be superfluous to demonstrate with further arguments that in Chemistry, the "infant" is nourished and grows by fire, as it were, since this concept occurs almost everywhere in the art.

<margin>*Only the philosophical offspring is nourished by fire.*</margin>

Truly, we shall be content here with citing just a very few authors. **Arnold of Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, in the *Rosary of the Philosophers*, book 2, chapter 25, says: *“When indeed she has given birth, nourish the son until he is able to tolerate every fire.”* And **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull, to whom many alchemical treatises were attributed.</note>, in the *Theory of the Testament*, chapter 29: *“Son, therefore, impregnate the body by fire, and multiply its combustion, and you shall have a strong tincture.”* And in the same place: *“Therefore, make your earth white, and nourish it if you wish that the son of the father should assist you in your needs.”* Likewise, in chapter 57: *“The humidity of metals is fixed and permanent in fire. Therefore, with such water we fix the little birds flying in the air by the power of our Stone, which is created from their own substance.”* In chapter 41: *“And therefore, when our Stone is created, make it be born from its mother’s womb; nor should you place anything else there from now on, because it carries with it the virtue of its mother’s womb—namely, that sulfurous nature which congeals all quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*.</note>.”*

That this **Triptolemus**, cooked and ripened under fire, is our salamander, our fire, our earth and lime, our ash, and our seed which is cast into its natural earth, could be proven by six hundred testimonies. We will set down at least two or three here. **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath.</note>, in his treatise, chapter 5, says: *“One must not harvest the seeds until the time of the harvest has arrived.”* The philosophers have called this Stone of ours a "salamander" because, just as the salamander is nourished and lives—that is, is perfected—by fire alone, so too is our Stone. Concerning fire, Lull says in the *Practice of the Testament*, chapter 22: *“Our sulfur has the power of sealing and forming something similar to itself, and everything that is sought, and of not retaining it within itself; and therefore we say that...”*

### Book 4 of the Egyptian-Greeks
<page-num>179</page-num>

<margin>*Mysteries.*</margin>
<margin>*Threefold cause of the concealment of the mysteries.*</margin>
<margin>*1st Cause.*</margin>
<margin>*2nd Cause.*</margin>
<margin>*3rd Cause.*</margin>
Many hold various opinions, of which we will first bring forward theirs, and then our own: *Mysteries*, says **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar and writer.</note>, are closed off by silence and by walls; by silence indeed, so that it was not permitted to speak of them; by walls, so that their inspection was not open except in certain places and to certain persons. Regarding the silence, as **Thomas Valois** <note>Thomas Waleys (c. 1287–1350), a Dominican theologian known for his commentaries on Augustine.</note> commented on **Augustine’s** *City of God*, book 4, chapter 31, it should be known that there seem to have been three causes why they wanted the demons and priests to hide the <term>theletae</term> <note>original: *theletæ* (from the Greek τελεταί), meaning sacred rites, initiations, or religious ceremonies.</note> and mysteries:

One cause was because their errors could easily be refuted if it had been permitted to speak and dispute about them publicly.

Another was that within those mysteries were contained the origins of the gods and the true conditions of those who were worshipped: for example, what kind of being Jupiter was, and who first began to worship him and how—and likewise for the other gods. If such things had been made known among the people, they would have despised the gods, and thus all fear of the gods would have been removed. This would have greatly harmed the republic and the common social life of men. For this reason, as **Livy** <note>Titus Livius (59 BC–17 AD), the great Roman historian.</note> says in the first book of *The Origins of the City*, **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing its religious rites.</note> believed it was supremely necessary to instill the fear of the gods into the people.

The third cause was because they performed certain purifications in secret and certain altogether abominable sacrifices which the people would have shuddered at if they had come to their knowledge. For they very often sacrificed infants and pregnant women in secret, and did many other horrific things to appease demons in hiding, as is clear in the case of **Julian the Caesar** <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan emperor who attempted to roll back Christianity.</note>. As **Socrates** <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD), a historian of the early Church.</note> relates in the *Tripartite History*, in the city of **Carrhae** <note>An ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia, famous for the Roman defeat by the Parthians.</note>—where that most wicked idolater had sacrificed secretly in a temple before going out on that war expedition—a woman was found hanging by her hair with her arms stretched out and her womb cut open; he had looked into her liver to see if he was owed a victory. Also, in his palace at **Antioch**, many chests were found full of the heads of the dead. And **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note> relates concerning the emperor **Maxentius**, that he sought out noble pregnant women for this purpose, and cut them in half to seek divinations in the entrails of the infants. And therefore, says **Valois**, the priests took the greatest care lest their mysteries and <term>theletae</term> were betrayed—

# Book 4 of the Hieroglyphics
<page-num>180</page-num>

[si]-lence: <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "silentio" from the previous page's catchword.</note> For this reason, there was a certain statue in almost every temple where **Isis** and **Serapis** <note>Isis and Serapis were major deities in the Graeco-Roman period of Egypt; Serapis combined traits of Osiris and Apis with Greek attributes.</note> were worshipped, which seemed to warn that silence should be kept by pressing a finger to its lips. This was done so that the fact that they had been human beings would remain unspoken, as is recorded in **Augustine's** *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 5. There, it is stated (regarding **Apis**, the King of the **Argives**, who was believed to be a god) that it was even decreed that whoever said he had been a man should suffer the death penalty. And since there was indeed a statue in all the temples where **Isis** and **Serapis** were worshipped that appeared to advise silence with a finger pressed to the lips, **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), an influential Roman scholar.</note> considers this to mean the same thing: that their human origins should be kept quiet. These are the words of **Augustine**, who in the same book, Chapter 5, reports that among the **Egyptians**, anyone who said **Isis**, the daughter of **Inachus**, had been a human, was made guilty of a capital crime.

And these causes, which the aforementioned **Valois** <note>Thomas Waleys (c. 1287–1350), a Dominican theologian and commentator.</note> brings forward, seem entirely probable to me—especially since a horrific <term>idolatry</term> <note>The worship of physical images or created beings as gods.</note> had already occupied all parts of the earth. However, our discourse concerns the first origin of the concealment of the mysteries, particularly the **Eleusinian** <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries were the most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece, held annually for the cult of Demeter and Persephone.</note> ones. If we consider these from all circumstances, the first and second causes narrated before will find a place here, but the third will hardly do so.

<margin>
The third reason for the concealment of the Eleusinian mysteries.
</margin>

It cannot be denied that such <term>mactations</term> <note>original: *mactationes*; the ritual slaughter of victims, often implying human sacrifice here.</note> of men and the inspections of their entrails were practiced by certain **Pagans** through the most foul abuse and kept hidden under secrecy; yet it is not reasonable to believe that such things were committed in these specific rites, which were held as the most sacred. **Saturn**, who was fabled through allegory to devour his own children, was perhaps appeased with this sacrifice by superstitious and idol-worshipping **Pagans**—as were **Baal** and other idols of that sort, or **Mars**, who was believed to delight in human blood. But regarding **Ceres**, **Dionysus**, or **Venus**, it is scarcely believable. For besides the fact that the rites of **Ceres**, or the **Eleusinia**, were celebrated by chaste and immaculate persons (as we shall hear later) and not by others, it finally became known what was actually contained in them. The nature of those rites is not such that it would be abhorrent to human reason or good morals, as we will explain below. We think, therefore, not without merit, that the first and second causes of concealment are found in the **Eleusinia**, but the third in no way applies. To this we add our own view: that there was a third reason for wrapping things in mystery and under si-[lence]...

<summary>This page discusses how the ancient "silence" of the mysteries was used to hide the human origins of gods like Isis and Serapis under threat of death. The author argues that while some pagan cults involved horrific sacrifices, the Eleusinian Mysteries were likely kept secret for more noble, philosophical reasons rather than to hide immoral acts.</summary>

### Book 4 of the Egyptians and Greeks
<page-num>181</page-num>
->A a 3<-

[si]-lence <note>The text completes the word "silentio" from the previous page.</note> of retaining those sacred rites, lest the artifice by which all those things were introduced become known to the common people. As we have often warned above, led by evident arguments which we omit here, this threefold cause was hinted at by that image of **Harpocrates** <note>Harpocrates was the Greek adaptation of the Egyptian god Horus the Child, often depicted with a finger to his lips, which the Greeks interpreted as a gesture of silence.</note> with his fingers pressed to his mouth. The commentator on **Theocritus**, following the opinion of **Thelytus of Methymna**, writes thus concerning this festival and its chosen participants: *It was a law for the Athenians that these **Thesmophoria** <note>The Thesmophoria was a festival held in honor of Demeter and her daughter Persephone, celebrated primarily by adult women.</note> should be celebrated annually by virgins and women of honest life, who, on the day of the solemnity, carrying the lawful and sacred books upon their heads, would proceed to **Eleusis** like suppliants.*

Access to these sacred rites was not open except to the initiated, and the herald ordered the "profane" <note>In this context, "profane" refers to the uninitiated or those not ritually purified.</note> to stay away. From this, **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> claims that **Virgil** took that famous verse: *Stay far, oh stay far away, you profane ones!* <note>original: "Procul ô procul este prophani"</note>. And they write that so much trouble was caused for **Alcibiades** <note>A prominent and controversial Athenian statesman and general.</note> because he, being uninitiated, was said to have been present at the sacred rites of **Ceres** <note>Ceres is the Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter.</note>. Indeed, no one was allowed to take part in them who was conscious of a crime he had committed, as the herald would proclaim. The Emperor **Nero** did not even dare to attend these rites because he was impious, whereas Prince **Antony** <note>This likely refers to a Roman Emperor (Princeps) such as Antoninus Pius or Marcus Aurelius, who sought initiation to demonstrate their virtue.</note> wished to be initiated to prove his innocence.

Moreover, it is said that in those later times there were two types of Eleusinian rites at Athens: the **Lesser**, into which guests and foreigners were received, and the **Greater**. <margin>Two types of Eleusinian rites.</margin> Regarding the latter, there was an old law that no foreigner should be admitted to them, as the commentator on **Aristophanes** mentions. For when many great foreign men came to Athens and sought to be initiated into those rites, they were rejected for no other reason than that the Athenians did not want those secrets of nature to become known to others. Therefore, they added certain "Lesser" rites for them, as if they were superficial, into which the newcomers were initiated; even Prince **Antony** himself is believed to have been received into these, rather than the Greater ones. For this reason, they would cite the old law, claiming that even **Hercules** himself—as great a hero as he was—was not admitted because he was a stranger, as if **Hercules** had ever truly been in Athens or had sought these things. They called the Greater rites those of **Ceres** and the Lesser those of **Proserpina** <note>The Roman name for Persephone.</note> to distinguish between them. From these facts, it appears clearly enough that in these rites, no lusts, murders, or other horrific acts were carried out, but rather there were most hidden reasons why they were kept under silence. Indeed, as I must admit, for many among the Christians, a suspicion...

<page-num>183</page-num>

Regarding this dream—told within a commentary on another dream—it is surprising that **Socrates** is said to have argued in this way (as **Juan Luis Vives** <note>A 16th-century Spanish humanist whose commentaries on St. Augustine were standard for the era.</note> records in his notes on Book 7, chapter 20 of **Augustine's** *City of God*), that this is surely a judgment that shameful things are contained within those rites. For if they were honorable and holy, they would never have been ashamed to be made public. Socrates touches upon these things indirectly, as he does many other things, when he commands that the shameful and foul deeds committed by the gods be hidden in the most secret rites; and whoever threatens to publish the hidden rites of **Isis** (who is the same as Ceres)—by which saying he forces Isis herself to do what he commands—sufficiently declares that those things are nefarious and shameful.

This is surely a line of reasoning established against all reason; not to mention that the speech and treatment on both sides is **allegorical**, and further, conceived within dreams.

We, who are very far removed from them in both place and time, shall judge them from those things which we have truly known as best we can; we shall "estimate the lion by its claw," as the saying goes—that is, the whole from the part, the signified from the sign, and the effect from its causes. 

When these sacrifices were first celebrated at Eleusis, **Eumolpus**, the son of **Deiopes** <note>Also known as Deiope; in some traditions, she is a daughter of Triptolemus.</note> and **Triptolemus**, first brought them to the Athenians; or, as others say, it was a fifth Eumolpus descended from him. These are his words. 

Indeed, that this was the custom—that for this reason the Eumolpidae were initiated into the rites of **Ceres** <note>The Roman name for Demeter, goddess of the harvest.</note> and were the priests of those ceremonies—is testified by **Sophocles** in *Oedipus at Colonus*, with these words:

### Book 4 of the Egyptian-Greeks.
<page-num>185</page-num>

...there was a place called **Callichorus** <note>The "Well of Fair Dances" at Eleusis, where the goddess Demeter was said to have rested during her search for her daughter.</note>. But the common people of **Eleusis**, lest the story seem like a mere fable and so they themselves might be more certain of such a memorable deed by **Pluto** <note>The god of the Underworld, also known as Hades.</note>, said that it happened in their own land, and they even dared to point out stone monuments as proof. However, many poets, such as **Ovid** in the fourth book of his *Fasti* and others, contradict them, saying that it happened in **Sicily** while **Proserpina** <note>The daughter of Ceres (Demeter), whose abduction to the underworld triggered the change of seasons.</note> was gathering flowers. Yet, while both the **Eleusinians** and the **Sicilians** accepted it as history, we recognize as a fable whatever has been sung to the whole world concerning the abduction of **Proserpina**; we do so, however, in such a way that it demonstrates the reality of what happened under a symbolic figure. 

For **Pluto**, who abducted **Proserpina**, is explained by mythologists as the earth, and **Proserpina** as the seed or the roots of the crops. Since the seed is hidden under the earth for nearly six months, she is said to be with **Pluto** for that much time, and for just as many months she is above the earth in the air with **Ceres** <note>The goddess of agriculture and mother of Proserpina.</note>. These things indeed suit the explanation, but are these secrets not well known to everyone? Do these festivals really require so many and such great concealments? We accept this explanation regarding the seed; but regarding our most secret **Philosophical** mystery <note>The author uses "Philosophical" here in the alchemical sense, referring to the "Great Work" or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, which the common peasants are ignorant of and only the **Philosophers** know, there are true reasons for hiding it. 

From this came that institution of sacred rites, the priestly order restricted to a single family, and the "golden key" on the tongue of the priests. Nor should anyone be so mad as to believe that the **Eleusinians** were the first to receive grain from **Ceres** and taught the rest how they ought to knead and eat bread, or that the **Thebans** received wine from **Dionysus** <note>Also known as Bacchus, the god of wine.</note>. No, no; bread and wine were in use among mortals long before those times, as is established from Sacred Scripture as well as the most ancient secular writings.

...[the high] priest is the Hierophant <note>A title meaning "one who shows sacred things," the chief priest at Eleusis.</note>; of the **SUN**, he is the torch-bearer; of the **MOON**, he is the attendant at the altar; of **MERCURY**, he is the herald of the sacred rites. And just as in the rites of Dionysus a Priapus <note>A representation of the phallus, used as a fertility symbol.</note> was carried around, so also in the rites of Isis the "female nature" <note>Theodoret is referring to the display of a representation of the female genitalia (the *kteis*), which Christian apologists frequently cited as proof of pagan indecency.</note> was displayed, as Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), a Christian theologian who wrote "Cure for Pagan Maladies."</note> testifies; he also affirms that Jupiter lay with his mother Ceres and with his daughter Proserpina. Thus far Ludovicus <note>Likely Ludovicus Vives, a 16th-century humanist whose commentaries on St. Augustine's "City of God" were widely read.</note> writes.

These matters are certainly not so obscure as to require a "Delian diver" <note>original: Delio natatore; a proverbial expression referring to a diver who could reach the bottom of the deepest waters, used to describe someone who can solve deep mysteries.</note>; but <margin>*Note.*</margin> more is expressed by those four images than by many volumes written on the same subject. Whether it is imagined by those ignorant of the sacred rites that obscene and most foul things were performed and therefore hidden, or whether it is said that Jupiter lay with his mother and Proserpina, and that the bull was the father of the Dragon, and the Dragon in turn the father of the bull, or other such things—none of this detracts from the truth of the matter. For these images, which are like silent poetry and hieroglyphic writing, <margin>*Hieroglyphic writing.*</margin> speak something other than what is commonly thought. 

But what shall I say? Are these things fabricated? Not at all; they are brought forward by authors worthy of trust and beyond all exception, even by those who have no knowledge or regard for the thing we are hinting at. Have these pagans then become Christians in these secret symbols, because they carry the image of the Creator? Was the creation known to them? Was Moses their teacher, or God himself through created things? It is most clearly evident that these are the most secret matters and beyond the grasp of common pagans. 

If anyone sets aside those initial paradoxes—monstrous and contrary to nature (namely, about the Bull and the Dragon being both parents and children to each other, and other such things)—let them seek an explanation from these images; which we also shall briefly provide, bringing forward as few testimonies of more recent authors as possible. Regarding the first founder of the established Eleusinian solemnity, we notice a variation in the accounts. Some, like Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian author who described the mysteries in order to critique them.</note>, ascribe it to Melampus; others to Eumolpus; some to Eleusis, the prince of the city of the same name; certain others to the daughters of Danaus <margin>*The Eleusinian rites originated from the Egyptians.*</margin>; and others to Triptolemus. Whoever the author may be, there is no doubt that they draw their origin from the Egyptians. As for me, I agree with Eumolpus, for the reason that from the Eumolpidae <note>The hereditary priestly clan at Eleusis.</note> the sacred rites arose...

### Book 4 of the Egyptian-Greeks

[page] 191

...to the immense sea, the benign giver of all goods and gifts, it [the work] must flow back; it is considered and, as far as is humanly possible, prefigured through a representation. For without Him, nothing happens. Therefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note> says in chapter 2: *My son, I warn you above all things to fear God, in whom lies the effort of your arrangement; who himself confesses in chapter 1 that he possesses this art and science only by the inspiration of the living God, who deigned to reveal it to his servant.*

<margin>The images of the planets denote the parts of the physical work.</margin>
Then the individual images of the Sun, the Moon, and Mercury were carried by various figures—not as gods (otherwise the Creator would not be present, who is the God of gods), but as creatures. Nor were they intended as the celestial planets themselves, because among those, Mercury is of imperceptible operation compared to the others—Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, and Venus—and these others would rather have been joined with him then. Instead, they represent "terrestrial planets," <note>In alchemy, "terrestrial planets" refers to the seven metals: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Quicksilver (Mercury), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), and Lead (Saturn).</note> or rather the homogeneous subjects of a single art. Indeed, from the most ancient times, it was an accepted practice among the Egyptians to use the planets or "wandering stars" of the heaven to shadow forth the virtues or parts of the **philosophical work.** That is, they used well-known and visible lights to represent those things which were and ought to remain secret. They used designated signs for the things themselves, and images for the objects.

For just as in the **Art of Memory** <note>original: "arte memorativa"; a classical and Renaissance system of mnemonics where concepts are linked to visual images or physical locations.</note> a part is used to represent the whole (and vice-versa), the container for the contents, the instrument for the work, the effect for the cause, a word for a sentiment, and a letter for a word (or the reverse, according to the will of the creating artist), so also the most wise inventors and possessors of the philosophical secret used their own notes and signs or **hieroglyphic images** taken from known things. For unless the things used to represent the unknown were themselves known, both would remain unknown. However, nothing is more known to the sight than the Sun and the Moon; therefore, they very often utilized these two lights to illustrate their obscure and hidden matters, to which they joined a third as a servant: **Mercury.**

<margin>Nothing common is to be understood by the names and signs of the planets.</margin>
Nor indeed should it be thought that the ancients, by the sign of the Sun, meant the common metal gold; or by the Moon, silver; by Mercury, quicksilver; by Saturn, lead; by Jupiter, tin; or by Mars, iron. For this would not be a matter of great subtlety and would be of even less utility. Since for them, [the way] to the work...

### Book 4 of the Hieroglyphics

[page] 192

<margin>What the Sun and Moon represent in the work.</margin>
...we do not need the [common metals]; rather, the consensus of all true Philosophers testifies that their metals are not the common kind. They are one in genus, two in number, but many in power and virtue. They are homogeneous in essence and harmony, yet most diverse and discordant in quality; varied in color, but united in their final goal. Therefore, the image of the **Sun** denotes the active force of our subject; the **Moon**, the passive force; and **Mercury** acts as the receptacle for both. Thus, the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* is a 16th-century alchemical treatise famous for its series of twenty woodcuts depicting the "Chymical Wedding."</note> says: *The Sun is the male, the Moon the female, and Mercury is the seed,* and it calls these three "the water of those three." A little earlier, it is stated: *Both medicines are begun with the Sun and Moon; but for the red, the ferment <note>original: "fermentum"</note> is made with the Sun; for the white, with the Moon. The Sun is understood in two ways: in one way as the "water of the Sun," in the other as the "body of the Sun"; for the water of the Sun is volatile and its body is fixed, and the reverse is true of the Moon.*

Hermes reduces these to two when he says: *Its father is the Sun, its mother indeed the Moon.* Likewise, when he says, *That which is above is as that which is below,* <note>The most famous line from the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Hermeticism.</note> Hortulanus <note>A 14th-century commentator on the *Emerald Tablet* whose name means "The Gardener."</note> explains it thus: *Here, by "above" is understood the more worthy, and by "below" the less worthy, so that specifically one thing may be made from those three, or from the Sun and Moon one thing may be made whose parts are equal.* This is called the *conjunction* <note>The union of opposites, often represented as a marriage.</note> or the *sublimation of the Philosophers*; it is also called *exaltation* or *dignification*, because the Moon and Mercury are "dignified" [raised in status]. For when the union is made, the Moon is of as much dignity as the Sun and Mercury. 

They also called Mercury the **Dragon**, as the *Rosary* notes in the same place: *And I further notify you that the Dragon does not die unless he is killed with his brother and sister—and not by one alone, but by both together. The brother is the Sun, and the sister is the Moon.* From this it is clear that since this manner of speaking was common among the more recent writers...

### Book 4. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

It is very common that not only the **Sun**, **Moon**, and **Mercury** are understood by those images with respect to this art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" of transforming base matter into a spiritual or physical perfection.</note>, but also that the same things are signified by the **Dragon**, the son and father of the bull; we do not believe it necessary to demonstrate this more copiously in this place.
