We treated several matters regarding his solemnity in the first book when we discussed the Syrians, 

<margin>The Adonia.</margin>
and therefore we shall run through them more briefly here. Not only in Syria were the *Adonia* <note>The Adonia was a festival mourning the death of Adonis, often involving "Adonis gardens"—small pots of fast-growing, fast-dying plants.</note> usually celebrated with mourning and joy (where they tell the myth that the river called the Adonis stops its flow around these feast days), 

<margin>The Adonia celebrated among the Syrians.</margin>
but also in Phoenicia and Egypt, where these things first took their origin. The wailing and lamentation, which agitated the common people with great dejection and sadness over the believed death of Adonis, is clearly seen to agree in cause and principle with the mourning and wailing of **Ceres** seeking **Proserpina**, or of the Egyptians deploring the dead **Apis** <note>The Apis bull was a sacred animal in Egypt; when it died, it was mourned until a new bull with specific markings was found to replace it.</note> and longing for a new one. For why would these people mourn like madmen and torture themselves, unless they had some foundation in the truth of the matter? 

We know, however, that **Adonis** was never a man, nor was **Venus** his lover a goddess, nor was he killed by the impulse of **Mars**, much less that he was or is among the dead for six months in the embrace of **Proserpina** and for six months with **Venus**. We say the same of the abduction of **Proserpina**, who is imagined to remain by alternating turns of time with **Pluto** and her mother **Ceres**. But why did the Egyptians mourn a beast <note>original: "brutum"</note> that they themselves had killed? There was no reason, except that they might pass down their sacred mysteries to posterity with the greatest care and vigilance; and since the priests, knowing the true cause of the matter, appeared sadder at the death of the **Apis** (being anxious, of course, for the discovery of a new one), the common folk—as usually happens—turned that sadness into wailing, and that diligence into madness. The same thing appears to have happened regarding the loss of **Proserpina** and the death of **Adonis**, when understood allegorically. Did **Ceres** lose a daughter **Proserpina**, whom she never had? Does she grieve for one snatched by **Pluto**, who never existed, just as she herself did not?

### Book 4 of Hieroglyphics

[page] 195

Let us grant that **Ceres**, **Proserpina**, and **Pluto** existed, and that the one was abducted by the latter, making the former mournful—what is this to living and rational men? Let us grant that there was an **Adonis**, a **Venus**, and a **Mars**, and that the first was taken away by the trickery of the last, held in delight by Venus in death as he was in life; this could provide no cause for mourning or joy to men, unless they wished to imagine it for themselves. Yet we confess that in these matters, human minds—prone to superstition and blinded by the mists of the devil—slide very easily into most ruinous and detestable errors, unless that eternal Sun, the God of His Word (which is truth itself), graciously illuminates them with His rays. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at that the *Adonia* <note>The Adonia was a ritual festival commemorating the death of Adonis.</note> were performed with such great mourning throughout Syria, Phoenicia, and Egypt, without a manifest cause. Since, however, **Adonis**, the **Sun**, **Osiris**, **Pluto**, and **Jupiter** himself are held to be one and the same subject (as has been demonstrated thus far), and are commonly accepted as the great light of the world, once one of them is understood, the meaning of those remaining names becomes known—about which we have treated copiously in various places. 

We say, therefore, that **Adonis** is the **Philosophical Sun** <note>original: "Solem Philosophicum"; in alchemy, this refers not to the literal sun in the sky, but to the perfected "gold" or the "Sulfur of the Philosophers" that drives the transformation of matter.</note>, truly loved by **Venus**, who,

For this reason, he makes white roses purple with his own blood; certain poets sing charmingly of this "tincture" of Venus, among whom **Giovanni Gioviano Pontano** should especially be consulted in his proper place.

Let us grant, however, that the Greeks ascribed divinity to the sun, as is evident from the Athenians, who gave poison to Anaxagoras for asserting that the sun was a burning stone and not a god—as they also did to Socrates for thinking contrary to their gods. Yet this was done more out of a brutal affection and irrational persuasion than from the tradition of *Orpheus* or the Egyptians. For it is written that elephants in *Africa* salute the rising Sun and adore it as if with a certain devotion, and any rustic or wild peoples without any education have always worshipped the celestial lights, the Sun and Moon, as gods; thus, there would have been no need for Orphic instruction or the transfer of sacred rites from Egypt.

Furthermore, our discourse here concerns the primary causes of these solemnities and their true use, not the superstitions and abuses that came later. We concede that the Sun was worshipped as a God in this way and that sacrifices were made to it by the common people, but by no means by the wise; rather, they always used it to denote something hidden <note>original: "occultum quid"</note>—not the Sun of the heavens exposed to all eyes, which is the finest of creatures but not a god. Beyond these, we are not unaware that there were also countless other festivals among various nations, as well as among the Egyptians and Greeks; but since these are sufficient for our purpose and, having been explained, provide light for others...

There was a custom in Athens that several people, carrying lit torches, would run through the city one after another, and they would keep them unextinguished; however, he whose torch was extinguished yielded the victory to the next person. He who brought a burning torch to the finish line was the winner; if no one did, the victory remained unclaimed in the middle. Although some adapt this institution to the course of human life <note>A common metaphor where the "torch of life" is passed from one generation to the next.</note> (as we do not deny can be done), nevertheless, if we consider the reasons why **Prometheus**, **Vulcan**, and **Pallas** <note>Also known as Athena; the goddess of wisdom.</note> shared a common altar in the **Academy** <note>The grove or school in Athens founded by Plato.</note>, we are compelled to think quite differently.

<margin>Which gods shared a common altar.</margin>
For who is **Vulcan**? Is he not fire itself, or a worker around fire? Who is **Prometheus**? Is he not said to be the inventor of Medicine and other arts, as well as metallurgy? For of him, **Aeschylus** <note>A famous Greek tragedian.</note> says: *What should I bring forth,* says Prometheus, *how many benefits have been brought out by me that were lying hidden in the earth? Iron or silver or gold—whoever he is, unless he lies, who discovered them before me? No one, surely, unless he wishes to lie: all the arts discovered are the works of Prometheus.* Thus he spoke. This is the one who, having borrowed a spark of fire from the Sun, fixed it into human minds; this is he who showed the way to **Hercules** to the golden apples of the **Hesperides**; this is he whose statue was erected with a scepter in his right hand. Of him, **Orpheus** sings in his hymn: *Nourishing Prometheus, spouse of Rhea,* <note>original: "Rheæ conjunx alme Prometheu"</note> as if he were **Saturn** himself. Regarding **Vulcan** and **Pallas**, enough has been said above.

<margin>A mystical cause.</margin>
From these things, it appears there was truly a mystical cause why a common altar was erected to these believed gods, and why the solemnity of the **torch-bearers** <note>original: "lampadiferorum"; referring to the "Lampadedromia" or torch race.</note> was instituted in their honor. Since we have mentioned this matter before, we leave it here for any intelligent person to at least consider. From this Greek custom, the "eternal nourishment" of fire among the Romans seems to have taken its origin, which was done in reverence for **Vesta**, the virgin Goddess. For sometimes they interpreted **Vesta** as the earth, and more often as fire and the deity of fire, whose ritual of worship is handed down here: **Ovid**, in the 6th book of the *Fasti*, writes that **Vesta** had no image or statue among the Romans as other believed deities did, because fire in itself cannot be well-depicted; and therefore in her temple, the fire was tended and called "eternal."

<margin>*On the more notable contests and games of Greece.*</margin>

But enough of these things regarding festivals; now we turn to contests and games. Although there were various kinds of these among different nations, we shall nonetheless examine at least four of the principal ones celebrated by the Greeks. The purpose of establishing festivals, as has been said, was so that the secrets hidden beneath them would remain known to the wise but unknown to others, and furthermore so that the common people might be kept in political order under the form of religion and the fear of the gods. The same is seen in contests and games, as if they were confirmed by the gods themselves; and furthermore, that the more spirited might be trained and encouraged from leisure to business, from peace to war, for the acquisition of physical strength and health, as well as the pursuit of glory and fame.

But because Pallas <note>The Greek goddess Athena, associated with both strategic war and handicraft.</note> is fashioned as the goddess of wisdom and studies, and nonetheless a female warrior; and Apollo is the leader of the Muses, the inventor of Medicine, a Seer and poet, and nonetheless the slayer of Typhon <note>A monstrous giant in Greek mythology; Apollo's victory over such chaos represents the triumph of order.</note>, an archer and golden-armored soldier, and because he was once declared the victor in these very contests—we suspect not without cause that he has some right over these matters. 

And this is so because we find the true origin of these games—regarding the authors who first organized them at their own expense, authority, and judgment, as well as the special purposes for which they were dedicated—is wrapped in poetic fables and **Chymical allegories** <note>original: "Chymicis"; this refers to alchemy, suggesting the myths contain hidden chemical or metallurgical secrets.</note>. Regarding the first point, it is well-established that if an Emperor, King, or Prince begins a solemnity of this kind, his memory is never erased as long as the event endures, and it is celebrated in literature afterward. Yet now it does not come to mind which king or prince instituted those contests, or who possessed such authority that he wished or was able to summon other nations, whether near or far, to a single location.

<margin>The solemn festivals of the Greeks seem to have been instituted by private individuals.</margin>
It is therefore credible that these things were begun by private persons, and by such individuals who thought more of benefiting the common state than of looking to their own utility. And so that they might be held in greater esteem, the gods were said to have been the first victors in them; this will appear more clearly in the consideration of each individual. It is, however, worthy of admiration that among the entire Heathen <note>original: "Ethnicam"; referring to the non-Christian, ancient Greco-Roman world.</note> antiquity, no true, certain, and definitive boundary of time—which chronologists call an **Epoch** or an **Era**—existed before the beginning of the **Olympiads** <note>The four-year periods between the ancient Olympic Games, used by the Greeks as a calendar system starting in 776 BCE.</note>. From this it happens that almost all the deeds of the ancient kings (of whom it is clear there were many even before the Olympiads began) are rendered uncertain and doubtful.

<margin>The Heroic Age is <unclear>conjectural</unclear>.</margin>

<margin>1. The Olympic Games. Mercator <note>Gerardus Mercator, the famous cartographer who also wrote on chronology.</note> moves the Olympiads to the Year of the World 3154; the founding of Rome to 3178; and the Birth of Christ to 3929.</margin>
For from these men the entire lineage of gods and heroes was born and propagated. That contest was held every fifth year, or every fiftieth month, in the month called **Parthenius** <note>The "Virgin" month.</note>, or **according to Apollo** <note>original: "κατ’ ἀπόλλωνα"</note>; that is, when four years were complete and the fifth was beginning, so that an <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the ancient Greeks as a unit of time.</note> comprised a span of four years. It began after the fifteenth day of the Moon had passed—that is, at the **full moon**—once the solemn sacrifices had been performed according to custom. It was celebrated over five days with as many types of games: namely, **running**, **wrestling**, **discus**, **jumping**, and **boxing**. 

In these games, prizes of **wild olive crowns** were offered to the victors, and immense honor was paid to them; gifts were given by their fellow citizens, and many immunities and privileges were granted by the magistrates. These contests were called "Olympic" because **Mount Olympus** was near the place where they were held—specifically in the region of the Eleans, not far from the city of **Pisa** and the **Alpheus** river. See **Strabo**, Book 8.

He writes that the *Olympic* contests began after *Trojan* times, based on the argument that *Homer* made no mention of the *Olympic Games*, even though he mentioned several funeral contests <note>Funeral games were held in honor of a deceased hero, such as those for Patroclus in the Iliad.</note>. But if they wish to derive the games from **Hercules**, the son of **Alcmena** and **Jupiter**, the matter returns to the same point; much more so if it refers to **Jupiter** himself as the founder, who conquered the **Titans**; that is a far greater span of time, which extends back into "Never" <note>An idiomatic way of saying the time is so remote it cannot be historically recovered.</note>. But since so many and such great allegories have been attached to the primary origin, we think it not irrelevant that the poet-philosophers wished to hint at why and by which authors these games were begun: <margin>Apollo defeated Mercury in a race.</margin> 

If **Apollo** defeated **Mercury** in a race, we are more certain about both. For we know **Apollo** and **Mercury** from their genealogy, which we provided previously. The latter <note>Mercury</note> excels with his feet, the former <note>Apollo</note> with weapons; the latter killed **Argus** <note>A hundred-eyed giant</note> with a stone, the former finished **Python** <note>The great serpent of Delphi</note> with arrows. The one is winged, wearing <term>talaria</term> <note>Winged sandals, a traditional attribute of Mercury.</note>; the other is weighty and firm in golden shoes. Nevertheless, **Apollo** overcame **Mercury** in the race. 

If indeed the glory of establishing this contest is ascribed to **Hercules**, son of **Alcmena**, we do not object: because he owed so much honor to **Olympic Jupiter** as his father, and from such great spoils—namely those of the son of the **Sun**—he was able to provide for them. <margin>2. The Pythian Games.</margin>
The same find its place when speaking of the *Pythian Games*: it is established from historians and poets that these were second only to the *Olympic Games* in both antiquity and fame. They are said to have been established in honor of *Apollo*, because he pierced the *Python* at *Delphi* with arrows; the creature later rotted there unburied, from which [rotting] the name is said to be derived <note>The name "Python" was traditionally linked by Greeks to the verb *pythein*, meaning "to rot."</note>. Some take the *Python* for a robber, others for a massive dragon—even among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note>. For since the Pagans believed and presupposed that the god *Apollo* walked the earth and was very powerful with weapons and arrows (as he is depicted), and since they could not nor dared to deny this, yet meanwhile it seemed irrational to them that so great a god should receive such honors for merely killing a serpent—since they did not understand what kind of serpent it was, or what kind of *Apollo*—they explained it as best they could: namely, that he was an infamous robber or a dragon. 

But should we Christians, who do not recognize such an *Apollo*, be content with that answer? Not at all. Therefore, let us not explain these things so thoughtlessly as to say *Apollo* was a man who killed a robber or a dragon. For what would be new in this—a man piercing a serpent with arrows? Would this be worthy of such remembrance by the poets? Or of the celebration of such great games? Let us not believe it, I pray. For if those games had begun from such a lowly origin, the first authors would have been of the most abject mind and judgment; I speak of the beginning of the celebration, not its later success. 

The poets, however, imagine that the *Python*—previously called *Typhon* (by a transposition of letters)—was a serpent not far from the river *Cephisus*, which flows at the roots of Mount *Parnassus*. As *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a 2nd-century geographer and poet.</note> also says in his little book *On the Situation of the World*, it was born from the earth when *Juno* struck the ground with her fist (an act we have mentioned before, regarding how great a number of offspring he is the father of) <note>Typhon was often considered the father of many monsters in Greek mythology, born from the earth after Juno sought a son stronger than Jupiter.</note>, and was then killed by *Apollo*. And when it had wasted away from rot, it was named *Python*. These games were celebrated at the beginning of spring by all the *Cyclades* islands, as the same *Dionysius* records. Some attribute the authorship to *Diomedes* returning from *Troy*, when he had escaped the storm which [struck] the Greeks from...

### Book 4. Of the Egypto-Greeks.

[When a pestilence] was sent upon those returning from Troy <note>original: "Ilio redeuntibus"</note>, it is said that among the Troezenians they dedicated a temple to **Apollo the Incensor** <note>original: "Apollinis Incensoris"; Likely referring to Apollo as the bringer of heat or purification by fire.</note> and instituted the **Pythian** games in his honor. In these games, it was the most ancient custom that the most beautiful of all the hymns brought forward should be sung in honor of **Apollo**. But later, singing to the **Cithara** <term>Cithara: a professional version of the lyre, associated with the god Apollo</term> was instituted, along with contests for flute-players and pipers. Then other variations followed, which we pass over here. Monetary prizes were abolished, and a crown made only of laurel, which was held sacred to **Apollo**, was proposed as the reward. And there were almost the same athletic contests in the **Pythian** games as there were in the **Olympic** games, with the exception of the four-horse chariots. 

Others say the prize of this game was a palm branch, which the victors would carry in their hands wherever they were; others say it was the winter oak <note>original: "aesculum"</note>, as the laurel had not yet been discovered. Others say certain apples consecrated to the God were usually given to the victors, as *Ister* wrote in his book *On Crowns*. At first, the **Pythian** games were held every ninth year, but later every five years, because that is how many nymphs, called the **Parnassides**, were said to have offered gifts to **Apollo** when he had slaughtered the beast. 

In the first **Pythiad**, in which the gods themselves competed, they say that **Castor** won the stadium sprint, **Pollux** won at boxing, **Calais** in the race, **Zetes** in the armed race, **Peleus** with the discus, **Telamon** in wrestling, and **Hercules** in the pancratium <term>pancratium: an ancient martial art combining boxing and wrestling</term>; and they were crowned with a branch of laurel. Those hymns which were composed and sung in praise of **Apollo** were called **Paeans**. Moreover, their rhythm was generally that which is preserved by **Sophocles** in this poem, in *Oedipus the King* <note>original: "Oedipode Tyranno"</note>:

->O Healing Delian Paean,<-

### Book 4. Of the Egyptians and Greeks. 205

The **Dragon** is composed of the four **Elements**, and not in a literal sense—as if it were merely earth, air, water, or fire—but it is a single nature that contains within itself the nature and properties of the four Elements. This **Dragon** is read to have been slaughtered at the roots of Mount Parnassus, because our **Apollo** came forth from Parnassus and dwells upon its peak with his sisters, the **Muses**; thus, at its roots, he finishes off the serpent with his arrows. Truly, this beast was worthy to be killed by so noble a hunter, since it has so many <term>triformed offspring</term> <note>These are likely the three stages or components of the alchemical "Great Work" often symbolized by triple-headed figures.</note>, which we numbered above, who would easily remove an inexperienced person from the world as if they were guilty of parricide.

**Ovid** relates that, after the flood of **Deucalion**, the earth produced this **Python** on account of its "putrid humidity"; and this is not without reason. Because from the "stony seeds" of **Deucalion** and **Pyrrha**—the bones of the Great Parent <note>Refers to the myth where the survivors of the Great Flood threw stones (the "bones of mother earth") behind them to create a new race of humans.</note>—while the Sun was heating the earth with its rays, this putrid animal **Typhon** <note>The author uses Typhon and Python interchangeably here to represent the state of "nigredo" or alchemical decay.</note> arose. Regarding what is said of **Diomedes** returning from Troy, it tastes of history, unless a fable lay beneath it; more on him below. 

If the **Pythian Games** were supposed to have been instituted by **Diomedes**, they would be far more ancient than the Olympic games; indeed, they would even precede this world, which was established by the Creator not yet six millennia ago. In that primordial time, **Osiris**, **Isis**, **Apollo**, **Castor**, **Pollux**, **Calais**, **Zetes**, **Peleus**, **Telamon**, and **Hercules** are placed by the Egyptians as gods—and as even more ancient beings descended from gods, if it please the gods <note>original: "si dijs placet"; a common idiom meaning "if you can believe it" or "heaven help us."</note>. 

It also appears from the hymns that this is a poetic introduction, and proceeded from men of letters rather than men of arms. For the Musical god was honored with musical honors by the poets who loved him; hence the laurel remains, even to this day, the reward and prize for those who sound forth hymns. Concerning the apples proposed as a <term>prize</term> <note>original: "bravio"; a reward in a contest or race.</note>, it is plausible, but only if they were brought from the gardens of the **Hesperides**; otherwise it would have been ridiculous to offer apples to such great heroes, as they are things usually given to children. 

That the nine **Parnassian nymphs**, that is, the **Muses**, offered gifts to **Apollo** when he had slaughtered the beast, is most true. For one-tenth part of the earth is said to remain at the bottom with nine parts of water, according to the number of the "9 Eagles," as is shown in the figure of **Senicris** <note>Likely referring to "Senior" or Senior Zadith, a famous 10th-century Arabian alchemist whose "Table" or "Figure" was a staple of alchemical study.</note>. These nine Nymphs, who also appear to be **lymphs** <note>A pun on the Latin "lymphae," meaning both water-nymphs and clear spring water.</note>, offer gifts to **Apollo**: but not before he has slaughtered the **Python**.

### Hieroglyphics, Book 4.

Whoever explains these things otherwise than the reality of the matter allows, understands nothing of **hidden letters** <note>This refers to "hermetic" or alchemical secrets encoded in myth.</note>; indeed, they barely understand the "first three" <note>Likely the three alchemical principles: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>, even if they are otherwise learned in all other things. Concerning the first victors, we have spoken elsewhere and will speak in what follows. Why **Apollo** is called *Ieius* <note>original: "Ieius". An ancient epithet for Apollo, often associated with the ritual cry "ie," but here linked by the author to his role as a healer.</note> is taken from Etymology, because he is a **healer**; and why the **Paean** <note>A song of praise or triumph, specifically associated with healing and protection.</note> is sacred to him, because he is a **soldier**; namely, a warrior with medicine, by which he conquers diseases. For **Philosophical Medicine** is the conqueror of all human diseases that can be healed in any way. 

The reason that is added—why **Apollo** is decorated with hymns—is plausible to those who know: because he sang the praises of **Jupiter** after **Saturn** was deposed. For unless **Saturn** were cast down from his kingdom into **Tartarus**—that is, the **first blackness** <note>original: "prima nigredo". This is the first stage of the alchemical "Great Work," involving the decomposition and "death" of the matter.</note>—**Jupiter** would have no power or praise. Therefore, **Saturn** was rightly deposed, or rather even disemboweled by his son **Jupiter**, because it was fitting in the <term>Philosophical art</term> <note>A common synonym for Alchemy.</note>, not in Politics. In the former, there is no crime of impiety, but a reward of knowledge; in the latter, it would be a detestable and horrific parricide. 

The **purple garments** that **Apollo** puts on, we admire most greatly: because it is necessary to be dressed in them if the **Paean** is to follow. But we do not sing the **Paean** to **Apollo** (who exists nowhere except among the Philosophers), but to the **Giver of Apollo**—at whose birth that pagan **Apollo**, the spirit of darkness, fell silent—that is, to **Christ**, the victor over all false deities and the greatest triumpher.

# Book Five.

## ON HERCULES’
### Labors.

**T**he fame of the virtue, strength, and immense labors of Hercules has spread so greatly throughout the entire world that there is not a single corner in the four cardinal points or regions of the world where he is not known, or where his name is not on everyone's lips and held in honor. Hence, when a certain man in a gathering of most illustrious men took it upon himself to sing the praises of Hercules in a poem, another silenced him with this Spartan <note>original: "Laconico". The Spartans, or Laconians, were famous for their "laconic" or pithy, brief style of speech.</note> wit <note>original: "dicterio", a sharp or witty saying.</note>, saying:

> Who is ignorant of the praises of Hercules?

Therefore, we consider it untimely and almost absurd—indeed, impossible—to take it upon ourselves to demonstrate that Hercules (who for so many centuries past has been accepted and recognized as a most excellent Hero) either did not exist at all, or at least existed only in the minds of Poets and Philosophers as an "idea" <note>The author refers to the Platonic "Idea," suggesting Hercules might be viewed as a mental archetype rather than a historical man.</note> of the most hardworking tamer of monsters and tyrants. For our part, we are content to let it stand that there was a Hercules, by whatever name he might be called—whether Egyptian, or Idaean <note>Refers to the "Idaean Dactyls," a group of mythical beings from Mount Ida often associated with an early version of Hercules.</note>, or Germanic <note>original: "Alemannicus". Early modern scholars often tried to find local versions of Hercules in German or Celtic history.</note>, or of some other nation. For we know that every age and every region of the world produces its own "Hercules," figures who are most industrious both in war <note>original: "Marte", referring to Mars, the god of war.</note> and in skill <note>original: "arte".</note>, so that not—

### Book 5 of the Hieroglyphics

[...every age and] time <note>The text here completes a sentence from the previous page, likely "omnisque aetas et tempus."</note>, it would be superfluous to recall other fabricated or fictional heroes from the far reaches of the underworld. However, we could easily prove that this very Hero, to whom so many such great labors are said to have been commanded, hardly ever existed—not indeed by searching historical monuments (of which there are hardly any, except the allegorical tales of the Poets), but from consideration of the subject itself and the labors he is said to have endured. For these labors are of such a kind that, in part, they do not befit a man of such great spirit due to their triviality and worthlessness; and in part, they far exceed human strength and all reason. Instead, they match the characteristics of all the gods and goddesses of the **golden genealogy** <note>The "Golden Genealogy" refers to the lineage of the primordial gods from the mythical Golden Age, suggesting Hercules is a cosmic archetype rather than a man.</note> mentioned before. Thus, these stories depict *Hercules* in his own living colors more effectively than any other writers ever could.

<margin>*Painting is silent Poetry; Poetry is a speaking picture.*</margin>
For as the most skillful paintings are said to be a kind of silent Poetry, so the Poetic faculty itself can rightly be valued as a speaking picture. From this source—namely, the fictions of the most ancient Poets—we have drawn everything we know about *Hercules* in these recent centuries. Let the historians who lived after the times of *Hercules* write what they wish; hardly any of them reached the age of *Homer*, much less that of *Orpheus*, the leader <note>original: "Coryphaei." This term refers to the leader of a chorus in ancient Greek drama, used here to mean the foremost or supreme poet.</note> of the Poets. Yet even they were found to be by no means contemporaries of *Hercules*, such that they could establish a history of his deeds without suspicion of fiction.

<margin>*The works of Orpheus.*</margin>
It is most certain that *Orpheus* was the very first to transfer fictions and allegories about gods and heroes from *Egypt* to *Greece*. Among other works, he composed those which he himself recounts at the beginning of the *Argonautica* <note>The *Orphic Argonautica* is an epic poem, often attributed to Orpheus in the Renaissance, telling the story of Jason and the Argonauts from Orpheus's perspective.</note>, including a work on the labors of *Hercules*. He wrote similarly about the giants fighting with *Jupiter*, about the abduction and grief for *Proserpina*, about the wanderings of *Ceres*, about the mourning of the *Egyptians* for the sake of *Osiris*, about the sacrifices of *Venus* and *Minerva*, and other matters of this sort, which were then spread to the *Greeks* as the deeds of gods and heroes.

<margin>*Before Orpheus, hardly any Greek writer exists.*</margin>
If, therefore, *Orpheus* is the first author of these things, and no *Greek* writer exists before him (unless perhaps a fictitious one)—and much less any writer of other nations (I always except the *Israelites*)—how they do babble, those who talk so much about the "Heroic Age," claiming to know which persons of gods and heroes lived then, what they performed, and what [was to be spoken...] <note>The text ends with "fanda," likely part of the phrase "fanda nefandaque," meaning "things right and wrong" or "things to be told and not told."</note>

<summary>The author argues that Hercules is a poetic allegory rather than a historical man, tracing the origin of his myths back to Orpheus, who imported these stories from Egypt to Greece.</summary>

### Book 5. Egyptian-Greeks.

[...reached the age to see whether they] performed speakable or unspeakable deeds, how long they lived before our own time, and similar matters. Let those backwards judges of things they do not understand be silent, or let them produce for us other writers who are truly older than Orpheus. It is not enough to bring forward a writer who is far younger than Orpheus and Homer, but who extends their own fictions—their chronologies and the deeds of fabricated characters—far beyond the time of Orpheus. There is no doubt that many such writers were found among the Greeks in those times, and not only among the Greeks, but among other nations as well. I do not wish to say this as if I am calling all those ancient records of the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnicorum*</note> into doubt, but so that at least the errors of certain writers may be recognized. These authors, in order to prove that their city or race originated from the gods, sat at home and fabricated long genealogies of kings descended from the gods, inventing deeds for them that look back more than a thousand years.

<margin>A statue with a golden tongue was erected for Berosus, according to Pliny, Book 7, chapter 37.</margin>
We know that Berosus <note>Berosus was a Hellenistic-era Babylonian writer and astronomer who wrote a history of Babylonia.</note> is quite ancient among the Pagans, and similarly we know many others mention Abraham, the father of the Israelites. However, those writers received much through tradition from either the Church Fathers and the Chaldeans, or the Jews. But as for what they hold regarding those gods and heroes, they drew it from their own writers—who were rarely eyewitnesses, and most often drew from their own imaginations like spiders spinning webs <note>original: *tanquam aranei hauserunt*; a metaphor for creating something entirely from one's own internal thoughts rather than external facts.</note>.

<margin>The empty glory of the Egyptians concerning their antiquity.</margin>
In this regard, the Egyptians have snatched the prize from all others, leaving behind an example of empty vanity in their claims of antiquity. Some of their more recent writers shamelessly claim that gods and heroes reigned in Egypt for eighteen thousand years. Nor is that enough; there are some who attribute a hundred thousand years to Egypt because it possessed the knowledge of Astronomy and Geometry. Who could hold back laughter at this? Who does not have the "nose of a rhinoceros" <note>A classical idiom (from the poet Martial) referring to a sharp sense of irony or the ability to sniff out a joke or a lie.</note>? What boy would not mock those old men, delirious with age? But it is not our place to provide an answer to such obvious lies, since these stories consume themselves, just as octopuses <note>original: *Polypi*</note> in hunger are said to gnaw on their own feet.

<margin>Horus is called the Sun by the Egyptians.</margin>
If Horus <note>original: *Orus*</note> is the last of the gods who reigned over the Egyptians, since his father is Osiris, and Osiris's father is Saturn, and Saturn's father is Uranus <note>original: *Cælus*</note>, who will be his father? None, because according to the testimony of Boccaccio <note>original: *Bocatio*; likely referring to Giovanni Boccaccio's *Genealogia Deorum Gentilium* (Genealogy of the Gods of the Gentiles).</note>...

## Hieroglyphics, Book 5.

<margin>Mercator <note>Gerardus Mercator (1512–1594), the famous cartographer, who also published a significant work on chronology.</note> counts 3,494 years from the Year of the World <note>original: *A. M.* for *Anno Mundi*, a calendar system based on the biblical creation.</note> to Alexander the Great.</margin>
Caelus <note>The Roman god of the sky, equivalent to the Greek Uranus.</note> is without a father. The entire sequence of gods, according to the Egyptians, is Caelus, Saturn, Osiris, and Horus; and these are the gods who reigned for so many thousands of years. After these, it is told that human kings reigned, 475 in number, up to the time of Alexander the Great. If ten years were attributed to each of these, it would make 4,750 years during which humans reigned in Egypt. However, from the creation of the world to Alexander, only 3,629 years are counted; from the Flood, 1,973 years; and from the first reign of Nimrod <note>A biblical figure mentioned in Genesis as a great king and "mighty hunter."</note> to the same Alexander, 1,842 years are numbered. In this small span of time—not yet two thousand years since the Flood—how could 475 Egyptian kings have reigned, unless we attribute only four years to each? If indeed they count four months for a whole year, as they are often said to have done, the total sum of years would be far less than the former, but the number of kings would still not correspond. But if they calculate a month for a lunar year, we might grant that by the time of Alexander they had kings over a span of 20,000 years. We are not greatly troubled by this number; for just as the deeds of Hercules <note>The legendary Greek hero known for his immense strength and twelve labors.</note> are told as monstrous, so too is his incredible birth related; of which Orpheus writes in the *Argonautica* <note>An epic poem attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus, detailing the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts.</note> in this manner:

> *Here, first, the strength of Hercules is seen by me: once*
> *Alcmena bore him, joined with heavenly Jupiter,*
> *When Phoebus <note>A common title for Apollo, the sun god.</note> lay hidden for three long nights in a row*
> *Continually, and the Sun lacked its day, the suns their light.*

<margin>The fictions of dreamers.</margin>
For although Alcmena was already pregnant by Amphitryon <note>Alcmena's husband; in myth, Jupiter disguised himself as Amphitryon to seduce her.</note>, yet so that she might also conceive from him, Jupiter is said to have joined three nights into one, a whole space of time which he consumed in producing Hercules. By this fiction of the poets, a sin is committed not only against the truth of the matter itself, but against piety toward the gods, nature and its order, good morals, and the institution of civil life. But the poets seem deserving of excuse if their intent is considered rather than their words; for since they wished to express an effect that was not common, but the best, they chose the best cause, [describing] the strongest of men...

<header>Book 5. The Egypto-Greeks.</header>

<page-num>213</page-num>

...[first], they imagined him born not from a man but from a god, and that not in the usual way, but after such a long interval of time that a thousand others could have been born. Thus they imagined Pallas <note>The goddess Athena, often referred to as Pallas Athena.</note> born from the brain of Jupiter by an extraordinary birth, signifying her supreme wisdom and the sharpest intellect. Because Hercules had to embody and signify strength and persistence, he is described as being fathered by the most robust of gods, namely Jupiter, and born after an extended pregnancy. For the poets, or rather the original Egyptian authors, do not concern themselves with the common laws of nature or morality in their stories, as long as they can effectively express their intended meaning. From this come the many adulteries, the various forms of lust, and the monstrous vices committed even by the gods they invented—acts which they even sing of with praise and celebrate with hymns in the town squares. It is as if they were admitting that those about whom they invent such grand tales are not truly gods, but were merely human (as some priests have confessed), or are thought of as gods "manufactured by human hands," a concept we recognize from Hermes’s discussion in the *Asclepius* dialogue <note>A famous text from the Hermetic tradition where the character Hermes Trismegistus describes how humans "make" gods by drawing divine power into statues.</note>.

Hercules was subsequently born in Thebes to Jupiter and his mother Alcmena, as has been said. He had a brother, Iphiclus, who was younger by a single night—the son of Amphitryon—and who was known for his remarkable speed and lightness of foot. To provide a clear reason for the many labors <note>The famous "Twelve Labors of Hercules," a series of impossible tasks he was forced to perform.</note> that he alone would have to endure, they imagined that these were imposed on him by fate in the following manner: While Hercules was in his ninth month in the womb, and Eurystheus <note>The king who would eventually command Hercules to perform his labors.</note>—the son of King Sthenelus of Mycenae and Archippe—was in his seventh month, Jupiter declared that whichever of the two was born first would rule over the other. Consequently, Juno caused the seven-month-old Eurystheus to be born early, while Hercules was born later on the first day of the tenth month. Because Hercules was the son of a rival mistress <note>original: *pellicis*</note>, Juno hated the newborn child with all her might.

<margin>Eumolpus on the mysteries.</margin> However, Eumolpus <note>A legendary figure often associated with the Eleusinian Mysteries in Greece.</note>, who wrote a book on the mysteries, recorded that although Hercules was initially hated by Juno because his mother was a mistress, she was later appeased by Pallas. Indeed, at Pallas's urging, Juno even offered her milk to the infant, which made him immortal. They then tell the story that the Milky Way <note>original: *via lactea*</note> was formed in the heavens by the spilling of this milk, when Hercules [was violently...] <meta>The catchword "violen-" suggests "violenter" (violently). This refers to the myth where the infant Hercules bites Juno's breast and she pulls him away, spraying milk across the sky.</meta>

### Book 5 of the Hieroglyphics ###

<page-num>204</page-num>

<margin>*The constellations of astronomy are derived from the fictions of the golden gods.*</margin>

...[He] sucked Juno's breast more violently; a story which others attribute to Mercury, as we mentioned above. For the poets wished that even the heavens should bear the traces of Hercules. Hence, they imagine not only that the **Milky Way** <note>original: "viam lacteam"</note> was created by him, but they also derive nearly all the stars or constellations from the "golden gods" and heroes, and from their works or great deeds. This is evident in those twelve signs of the zodiac and many others. On this subject, one may consult Ovid in his pagan *Fasti* <note>A Latin poem explaining the origins of Roman holidays and constellations.</note>, and another "Christian Ovid" named Novidius <note>Likely referring to a medieval or Renaissance author who "moralized" or Christianized Ovid's myths.</note>, as well as many others. 

On the night following his first day of birth, it is said that two most ferocious snakes were sent against Hercules by Juno; these he strangled with his hands, crushing them and showing the power of his strength at the very threshold of life. Later, when he had grown, although he possessed the most noble seeds of his nature implanted within him, he was nonetheless unable to bring any of them into action without the discipline and exercise of teachers. Therefore, he obtained individual instructors for each of the arts he was required to learn. 

He learned the art of the javelin from Teutarus the Scythian shepherd, or, as others prefer, from Rhadamanthus. According to some, he learned from Thestiades or Eurytus. From Linus, the son of Apollo, he received instruction in letters; however, Hercules brought death upon him as a <term>didactrum</term> <note>A fee or payment for instruction.</note> when Linus attempted to beat him. He learned music from Eumolpus; wrestling and other athletic arts from Harpalycus, the son of Mercury and Phanope; the driving of chariots from Autolycus; and from Amphitryon himself, the skill of riding. From Castor, he learned to fight in armor. In matters of astronomy, however, he had that most wise and excellent man, Chiron <note>The centaur famous for mentoring many Greek heroes.</note>, as his teacher.

<margin>*The eight teachers of Hercules.*</margin>

These eight individuals each contributed their own labor to the education of a single Hercules. For just as many nights were required for his conception, so were many teachers required for his instruction. By the former, it was provided that he should exist and live; by the latter, that he should live well. But what sort of man Hercules would eventually become, one might ask: was he merely a fable wandering through the mouths of men, or was such a hero ever truly born outside of allegory?

<margin>*The nature of the highest of the pagan gods.*</margin>

That Hercules was such a great man, or rather a semi-god, was easily persuaded to the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note>. They believed that the god Jupiter, the son of Saturn, had lived on earth and committed all kinds of adulteries, debaucheries, homicides, and other things of that nature...

# Book 5 of the Egyptian-Greeks #

<page-num>205</page-num>

...that he [Jupiter] committed [adultery], that he lay with the daughters of many kings and gods and sired children by them, among whom they considered Hercules to be one—the one into whom Jupiter had conferred all the strength and vigor of his own body. Since Jupiter is presupposed to be the most powerful of the gods and as if omnipotent, they did not judge it difficult or impossible for him to produce and present to the world a son who was the subduer of so many monsters and the achiever of deeds otherwise incredible. Consequently, they accepted all the deeds of Hercules as actual facts and not fictions. As to how this opinion reached the minds of the common people, it can be inferred in part from the circumstances mentioned previously.

<margin>
Franciscus Junius in the preface to his *Hebrew Grammar*.
</margin>

There is no doubt that the name of **Jove** <note>original: "Iovis"; the author argues that "Jove" is a linguistic corruption of the Hebrew "Jehovah."</note> was retained among the pagans from the name **Jehovah**. Since Jehovah is omnipotent, and was destined to send His Son into the world to destroy the monstrous works of the Devil—that is, Cerberus <note>The three-headed dog of Hades, representing the powers of death and hell.</note>, the Underworld, and other related things—as was known among the more learned pagans through shadows or even, as it is said, from the clear prophecies of the **Sibyls** <note>Ancient prophetesses whose verses were often interpreted by later Christian scholars as pagan "premonitions" of Christ.</note>, this could have provided the occasion for the fiction concerning the strength and invincible fortitude of Hercules, the son of Jupiter. 

Toward this also seems to point the fact that this same Hercules is imagined to have spent three days and nights in the belly of a whale, just as one reads of **Jonah** <note>The author is likely conflating the myth of Hercules rescuing Hesione from a sea monster with the biblical story of Jonah.</note> in the Holy Scriptures, who was a figure of **Christ**, who was one day to remain for the same amount of time in the heart of the earth and then rise again. And since Hercules is said by others to have lived in the time of **Samson** <note>A biblical judge of Israel famous for his superhuman strength; many Renaissance scholars believed Hercules was a Greek retelling of Samson's life.</note>, perhaps many attributes of the latter were falsely ascribed to Hercules. Samson, that most robust hero, was undoubtedly a figure and type of Christ the victor, who would triumph over the Devil and all His enemies. 

Such things, I say, borrowed from the true Israelite history, perhaps provided the occasion for many fictions to be added to the **labors of Hercules**,

<margin>
Many things were added to the labors of Hercules.
</margin>

so that the Egyptians themselves or other pagans might appear to possess so great a Hero. Whether these things are so or not, we believe the first origin of this allegorical fiction concerning the labors of Hercules stems from elsewhere, and is older than Samson himself, or even **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>. For since the latter makes mention of Hercules—specifically [naming] him, along with **Prometheus** and **Mercury**, to **Isis** as a prefect of Egypt...

        ...established by Osiris, the name of Hercules appears to be of the most ancient memory. And if he is perceived by associated or parallel things, or as they say, "known by his companion" when he is not recognized by himself—or by effects from causes, the disciple from the masters, the doer from the deeds—we do not doubt that the allegory of Hercules, fashioned from so many and such great labors (for if we deemed them worthy of historical faith, we would be not only more insane than the Heathens, but even deprived of sacred faith), graphically depicts the persona of the **Artificer** <note>In alchemy, the "Artificer" is the practitioner or chemist performing the Great Work.</note> who wishes to investigate and perfect the most secret secret of the Egyptians. Although this may appear obscure at first glance, I shall make it shine most clearly, God willing, once all the clouds of doubt have been scattered and removed—first in a general sense, and then specifically regarding each individual labor.

        <margin>The Parents of Hercules.</margin> If we consider the parents of Hercules, his father is the chief of the **Golden Genealogy** <note>Likely referring to the lineage of "Golden" or divine principles in the alchemical process.</note>. Whither the father is directed, there also the son is referred. Now, it is established from the third book concerning **Jove**, who he is, and of which sons he is the father. Those things demonstrated there are so firm that they can in no way be undermined, even by one who prefers to be a Heathen rather than a Christian (provided, however, he does not turn history into fiction), and they should not be repeated in this place. Therefore, Hercules is such a son as his father is, but in a different respect: the latter [the father] designates the internal agent of the Art—namely the principal subject—while the former [Hercules] designates the external agent, namely the **Artificer** himself. And indeed, he does not represent the whole Artificer, but rather the operation of his hands, and his invincible constancy and strength in investigating and perfecting that which is required.

        For since, besides this, there is considered in the Artificer a subtle, natural, and non-sophistical intellect, as well as wisdom, these are foreshadowed through **Minerva** or **Pallas**, as has often been said before regarding **Jason**, and later regarding **Ulysses**. For these three seem to depict the **Philosophical Artificer**: namely, **Jason** represents what must be investigated, how it should be treated, and by what art it must be overcome; **Hercules** represents with what constancy of mind and body the same thing ought to be sought, labored upon, and perfected. The title "Chrysopoeia" means "Gold-making."</note>: *where with ivory comb...*

...established by Osiris, the name of Hercules appears to be of the most ancient memory. ### Hieroglyphics, Book 5

...the operation of the body, as well as the hands, is required in a true and perfect craftsman; Geber <note>original: "Geber in sum: perfect: cap: 4" — referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan's 'The Height of Perfection,' a foundational alchemical text</note> in the *Height of Perfection*, chapter 4, says: ***Therefore, we say that if anyone does not have his organs complete, he will not be able to reach the completion of this work by himself; for example, if he is blind, or missing limbs, since he is not assisted by the members through which this art is perfected, serving as the ministers of nature. If, however, the craftsman’s body is weak and diseased, such as the bodies of those with fever or leprosy, whose limbs fail them, or those laboring at the end of life, or the decrepit age of the elderly, he will not reach the completion of the art.*** Thus he spoke. On constancy and perseverance, the same author says in chapters 5 and 7: ***It is also necessary,*** he says, ***that he insist diligently on the work until its consummation, so that he does not leave the work cut short; for he would not acquire profitable knowledge from a diminished work, but rather despair and loss.*** We shall not bring further examples here. How difficult this art is, though true, is demonstrated by the rarity of true craftsmen, in addition to their own testimonies, in which they assert that many things are presupposed for attaining the perfection of this art. For Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> in the *Rose Garden*, book 2, chapter 5, says: ***In this matter, three things are to be sought: namely, the subtle wit of the craftsman, the labor of the hands, and judgment; which indeed requires wealth, wisdom, and books.*** Similarly, Lull <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> in the *Theory of the Testament*, chapter 31, says: ***And therefore, son, I tell you, that three things are required: namely, a subtle wit—natural, not deceptive—the operation of the hands, and free judgment; and this requires wisdom, wealth, and books. Wisdom for knowing how to do it; wealth for having the power to do it; and books for opening a diverse understanding, which is found among many peoples.*** Thus Lullius. These things certainly seem to require the dangers of Jason and the labors of Hercules, nor can they be perfected without the wanderings <note>original: "erroribus" — literally wanderings or mistakes, referring to the Odyssey</note> of Ulysses. If anyone desires more concerning the difficulty of <term>alchemy</term> <note>original: "chymiae"</note>, let him consult the books of others on this matter. For us, let it suffice here to have demonstrated that Hercules—whom we left in his cradle (already in his tender age practicing the strangling of the philosophical serpent <note>In alchemy, the "serpent" often represents the raw, chaotic matter or "mercury" that must be fixed or subdued by the chemist</note>) or to be instructed by so many of his masters—is understood to be the most industrious craftsman of the philosophical work. <margin>The labors of Hercules.</margin> In addition to the father and kinsmen of Hercules recognized in the golden genealogy, he himself... to Osiris...

*This is a metaphor; just as the strong Lion, the king of the animals, grows weak through its infirm flesh—for on every fourth day it naturally suffers a quartan fever <note>A recurring fever occurring every four days, here used to describe a periodic weakness in the material.</note>—so the natural Lion grows weak and is eclipsed through its flesh, which is tempered by the nature of the moon. Thus says the author:*

From these things it is sufficiently clear what the Lion is in the **Art** <term>Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art"</term>, and why it is so often used as its primary subject. The author cited last also says that the Lion is the Sun, which has a lunar nature joined to itself; hence it is clear why this lion is said to have fallen from the Moon. For in truth, the Lion—or the Sun of the Art—falls from the Moon. 

But regarding what is said of the **spittle of the Moon** <note>original: "sputo Lunae" — Alchemists used this term to describe the white, frothy substance or "mercurial foam" that appears during certain stages of heating.</note>, it might perhaps be considered strange to think this is where that Lion was generated. However, if our own authors are consulted, it will be clearly established that they frequently mention the "spittle of the Moon." Thus the author of the *Aurora* <note>*Aurora Consurgens*, a famous 15th-century alchemical manuscript attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note>, in chapter 12, says: *Some of the Philosophers have placed the entire secret in it, and have called it by various names on account of the excellence of its nature; just as it is written in the book of the "Assembly of the Philosophers" <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum" — one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>, because some called it by its place of origin, such as gum or **spittle of the Moon**, and some by its color, such as blood.* 

Here it should be noted that the author says it is called "spittle of the Moon" from its place of origin; by which he seems to refer to the Lion generated in the "place of the Moon" from foam; for "spittle" is used and understood to mean "foam." If we consult the *Assembly*, the spittle of the Moon will be found in many places. For Astratus says: *He who wishes to attain the truth should take the humor of the Sun and the spittle of the Moon.* Likewise, Pythagoras: *You must understand from the Assembly that Sulfur, and lime, and alum (which is from apples), and **Kuhul** <term>Kohl or Antimony; here referring to the dark mineral form of the matter</term>, and the spittle of the Moon, and combustible spittle—all these things are nothing other than sulfur water and "burning water" <note>likely referring to aqua ardens or strong acids used in dissolution.</note>.* 

And Anastratus: *In addition to these things, I say that nothing is more precious than the red sand of the sea, and it is the spittle of the Moon, which is joined to the light of the Sun and congealed.* Belus also says: *Some have named this same water the "spittle of the Moon," and others the "heart of the Sun."* 

From these examples brought forward, it is sufficiently clear what sort of Lion this is, and what sort of Moon it is from whose foam or spittle he is said to be generated. Likewise, it is clear what the Herculean labor of slaughtering this beast entails: it is indeed a Philosophical labor. For he overcomes it not from afar with arrows, but at close quarters with a club—which he afterwards consecrates to Mercury—and with his bare hands...

## Book 5 of the Egyptian-Greeks

...slaughtered or cast into the fire. It is said, moreover, that Creon was the king of Corinth, whose daughter Glauce Jason took to wife after Medea; but she perished, having been infected with poison by the latter.

<margin>
3. The Hydra of Lerna.
</margin>

From here, Hercules is called by Eurystheus to slay the immense and formidable Hydra, which possessed many heads and lived in the Lerna marsh of the Argive and Mycenaean territory. This creature had been reared beneath a most spacious plane tree at the spring of Amymone <note>A spring in the Lerna region of Greece, named after a daughter of Danaus; in alchemy, such springs often represent the "mercurial water" or solvent</note>. It had seven heads according to some, nine according to others, or fifty according to still others. If one of these heads was cut off, the original number would immediately be doubled, unless someone had immediately cauterized the stump of the severed neck with fire. They say that the Hydra's venom was pestilential to humans, infecting both the waters and the air, and that the beast itself devastated the flatlands in its attacks. When Hercules approached it with burning torches, aided by his charioteer Iolaus, a crab <note>original: "cancer"</note> sent by Juno came to the Hydra's aid, but it was finally crushed by him. It is established from the myths that the Crab and the Hydra were translated into the Heavens by Juno.

<margin>
It appears that Astrology arose from the myths of the Egyptians and the Greeks.
</margin>

Here it should be noted that Astrologers assign to the sign of Cancer <note>The Crab</note>—which is unequal to its celestial sign in both position and size, being out of its proper place and far too small—many traits taken from the nature of the crab as a backward-moving creature <note>original: "retrogradi piscis" — literally "backward-walking fish," a common early term for crustaceans</note>. They do the same for the lion, the bull, the ram, the virgin, the twins, and all other constellations, as well as for each individual Planet according to their own judgment. Yet they ought to consider whether God imposed that nature and name upon said stars, or whether men did so by their own will. If it were men, for what reason? Was it because it suited the nature of those stars, or for some other reason? Thus they would find that all those names originated from myths, and that myths come from earthly things, not heavenly ones. They do not signify anything regarding the stars of the firmament or the Planets of the higher World, but were devised and introduced concerning other hidden matters <note>The author is arguing for an "Euhemerist" or alchemical origin of the zodiac: that the stars were named after earthly stories (alchemical processes) rather than the stars having intrinsic "crab-like" or "lion-like" powers</note>.

<margin>
From where the construction of celestial figures depends.
</margin>

Geometry can also divide the Heavens into twelve equal celestial signs according to the poles of the Zodiac, or into just as many houses <note>The twelve divisions of the astrological chart</note> according to the equator and the poles of the World, or according to the horizon and the Zenith. But what can these divisions impart to the stars in terms of effects? No... <note>original: "nihil" — the text continues: "nothing..."</note>

### Book 5 of the Hieroglyphics

...nothing, I think, whatever proof is sought from experience, for there is none. I wished to give this warning so that the abuse of Astrology—which was derived from the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note> together with so many superstitions—might be avoided, and the true and legitimate use of Astronomy might be proven.

<margin>The reason why certain powers are ascribed to certain stars among the Pagans is clear from these allegories.</margin>

For the ancient Pagans, who truly believed that the Hydra, as well as the Crab, were raised to the stars by Juno, and likewise that all other animals migrated into the celestial nature of the gods, attributed to those constellations the strength and power of those animals as if by their own right. For if Achelous <note>A Greek river god who wrestled Hercules; he famously transformed into a bull during the fight</note> was a Bull, and was afterwards translated into Heaven and arranged into certain stars, he would possess something of the bull’s virtue; and so it goes for the rest. This was the foundation of the Astrological doctrine propagated from the Pagans to us; if this cannot be perceived from these examples, it could easily be demonstrated in an entire book, if necessary. 

But to return to the matter: the very name indicates that the Hydra is an aquatic Serpent, or one living in water. Yet it has many heads, and when one was cut off, the number of the previous ones would grow; the only remedy was to burn it with fire. Even if Hercules had been exactly as he is imagined, it would nevertheless be apparent that this is an Allegory. Why say more? Our Serpent in the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, the "Great Work" of transforming matter</note> is congealed from water. The books of our authors are full of this description. 

Basilius Valentinus <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, supposedly a Benedictine monk, though his writings likely date to the 1600s</note>, in *Of Occult Philosophy*, chapter 1, relates among other allegories how Mercury was born: he says that a serpent or hydra, called Orcades, was cast out from the waters, and from its jaws a vapor and fiery smoke exhaled; the other things he adds need not be brought up here. 

Furthermore, there are infinite passages attesting to our hydra which we shall pass over, transferring here at least the single testimony of Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, a Majorcan philosopher; many alchemical texts were attributed to him posthumously</note>, which is proper and relevant to this matter. In *The Theory of the Testament*, chapter 3, he says: 

*“The fourth is a certain substance proceeding from its mineral, and within itself it is more closely related to the nature of metals; it is named by some vitriol <note>original: "calchantis"</note> and glassy azoth <note>Azoth is the "universal solvent" or essential spirit of matter in alchemical theory</note>. It is the earth and mineral of metals, and by another name it is called Vrisius—shining and white, red in secret, black and green in public. It has the color of a poisonous lizard, and is immediately ge-”*

...generated from quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term>, the substance mentioned above, impregnated by the said hot and dry sulfurous vapor, which in its dissolution becomes a "frozen lizard." From this comes the form and appearance of the pungent <note>original: "fatentis," likely "foetentis" or stinking, a common alchemical description of sulfurous vapors</note> *Spirit* in the mixture, whose mineral heat is multiplied—this heat is the very life of the metal. The Centaurs destroyed.

But it is asked: how did this knowledge profit Hercules? It can be answered that as he was heading toward Mount Atlas and the Astrologer who carries the heavens <note>the Titan Atlas</note>, he had need of it so that he might hold up the sky while Atlas inquired about the golden apples of the Hesperides. Or, as I believe more truly, it was so that he might recognize the "central and subterranean stars" <note>The "inner stars" or hidden properties of metals</note>, and observe the Sun, Moon, and Mercury in conjunction together, with Saturn positioned in Capricorn and Venus in Taurus, or vice-versa.

From that same region, on Mount Cyllene, Mercury was also born; for this reason, Mercury is a "countryman" to that boar. *...day and to their caves, and take from them the honored stones.* <note>The author is quoting various alchemical authorities to show that the "matter" of the Stone is found in "mountains."</note>
*Rosinus says: The Rebis is born in two mountains. And soon: The mountains, dragons, and springs of the earth give the Rebis.* <term>Rebis: From the Latin "res bina," meaning "double thing," a symbol of the union of opposites—like spirit and body or sulfur and mercury—often depicted as a hermaphrodite.</term> *Rhazes says: Contemplate the highest mountains, which are on the right and on the left, and ascend there, for our stone is found there; and in the other mountain, which bears every kind of pigment and spirit, or species, it is likewise there. Morienus says: Climb the high mountains planted with trees, for there our stone is found and is hidden. Hermes says: Take the black stone, the stone from the mountains of India; what is inside, put outside, and what is outside, put inside.* <note>This is a famous alchemical maxim referring to the transformation of a substance's hidden properties into visible ones.</note> *And Maria says: Take the white herb, clear and honored, growing upon the little hills.* All the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists.</note> testify likewise that our matter is drawn from mountains; thus many of the wild beasts tamed by Hercules are named after mountains, such as the previously mentioned *Lion of Cithaeron*, the *Lion of Helicon*, and likewise the *Erymanthian Boar*. Let it suffice to have given this warning once.

<margin>7. The Stables of Augias cleansed.</margin>
Afterward, when Augias, King of Elis and son of the Sun, possessed a stable of three thousand oxen that was completely stuffed with dung, Eurystheus ordered Hercules to clean it in a single day. When Hercules arrived there, Augias made a pact that he would give Hercules a tenth part of all the animals if he cleaned that stable in the same day. Once it was cleaned, when Hercules demanded his payment and Augias refused to give it, Hercules slew him with arrows. From his spoils, as we have said, he established the Olympic Games in honor of Olympian Jupiter. Though this labor was the most lowly and unworthy of such a hero, it was a very great task, as is apparent from the proverb it inspired concerning matters of the greatest effort, work, and care. For who is greater than Hercules, the son of Jupiter? And what is more lowly than cleaning a manure-heap? Nevertheless, this burden was imposed upon him, and with the necessity that he complete in a single day what would have been easier for many men to do over a longer time. Lest anyone think there were only a few animals, the number is recorded as three thousand. There are some who add that the stable had not been cleaned for many years, so much so that the oxen were standing on a heap of dung that reached the top level or the rafters. From this, it can be concluded that this labor, which would have been too much for three thousand other men, was commanded of and completed by Hercules alone. ### Book 5: Of the Graeco-Egyptians

...as it is often said, but Hercules alone is bound by incredible labor. Thus, he had already undertaken such a nocturnal labor to be completed in a single night, which he could not have refused even if it had taken many; indeed, he had also undergone the tiring out of the hind by running, and the tearing apart of the lion with his hands—tasks which to have laid low with javelins or arrows would have been a matter of greater skill than labor. Thus, the condition and the law added to the labors always seem to have increased the magnitude of the Herculean tasks, so that it was not enough that they were done, but that they were done both usefully and in such a specific time. 

Fables tell that these oxen belonged to **Augeas**, the son of the **Sun**, which he undoubtedly received from his inheritance; for it has been handed down to memory that the **Sun** had very many oxen and sheep in his own pastures. Now, what is understood by "oxen" we have said under the declaration of **Apis** <note>original: "sub Apis declaratione". Apis was the sacred bull of ancient Egypt, here linked to alchemical symbolism.</note> and elsewhere—namely, the **Philosophical matter**. Since this matter is found in dung—that is, it is vile in appearance and surrounded by many superfluities from which it must be purged by the Philosopher—it is not unsuitably handed down that this stable-work was imposed upon **Hercules**. Nor should one think that this is accomplished without labor and stench. 

<margin>Stercutius</margin> <note>Stercutius was a Roman deity associated with dung and the manuring of fields; here, the author links the god's name to the "filthy" start of the alchemical process.</note> Regarding its vileness and discovery, all authors agree under the duties of **Stercutius** or the dung-heap, of whom we shall cite a few. **Morienus** says: *The wise, however, have disposed and said: if you find what you seek in a dung-heap, take it; but if you do not find it in the dung-heap, take your hand away from your purse <note>original: "tolle manū à marſupio". This is a warning to alchemists not to waste money on expensive, exotic ingredients, as the "true" matter is common and cheap.</note>: for every thing that is bought at a great price is found to be deceitful and useless in this kind of art.* 

So says **Avicenna** in the first discourse, chapter two, *On the Soul*: *We have found it written in the book of **Aristotle** which he made concerning stones, where he says: "Two stones lie in the dung, one stinking and the other well-scented; they are little valued in the eyes of the people. If the people knew their value, they would hold them honorably; but because they do not know their value, they despise and leave them upon the dung in stinking places, and he who joins them together, therein lies the mastery."* <note>While attributed here to Aristotle, this quote comes from pseudo-Aristotelian alchemical texts common in the Middle Ages.</note>

And **Gratianus**: *And if you find in the dung that which pleases you or is useful, take it nonetheless.* 

And **Merculinus** in the *Rosarium* <note>Referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum" (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical florilegium.</note>: *There is a hidden stone, buried in a deep spring, vile and cast out, covered by filth or dung.* 

That it is vile, of little price, and not rare, **Arnoldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist.</note> says in the *New Light*, chapter 1: *They sell it openly for the smallest price.* 

And **Count Bernard** <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a legendary 15th-century alchemist.</note> says: *It is turned before the eyes of the whole world, yet no one of those who are in the world has known it...*

in the world; *The Rose Garden of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosar: Phil:" referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> says: "Even if I were to call it by its true name, the ignorant would not believe it to be so." > *By any force; for I saw this with my own eyes.*
> *But when he struck the bronze rattle with his hands,*
> *Standing upon a high lookout point, immediately they*
> *Left the shore with a cry and fled far away.*

If anyone interprets this labor of Hercules literally, or even according to morals or common physics, they are trifles...

No one fails to see that these stories are most trifling—indeed, they are absurdities and childish toys. For why would such a great Hero be said to drive away birds with the **rattle of Archytas** <note>original: "crepitaculo Archytæ." Archytas was an ancient Greek philosopher credited with inventing a child's rattle; here, it is interpreted as an alchemical tool</note>, when they could not be driven off by arrows? One would be considered contrary to nature, the other contrary to reason. 

But if one adapts this to the **philosophical work** <note>the "Great Work" of alchemy, or the *Opus*</note>, to which it uniquely points, it is the most beautiful and evident of all the labors. Indeed, I dare to assert that among almost all more recent authors, there exists hardly a more secret or distinguished example of the foundation of the **Art** <note>the "Art" refers to alchemy</note> than this very story, which has been misunderstood through so many ages of the world and yet handed down even to us. 

I call as witnesses those who are not imaginary—not "map-sailors," or those swimming on bark, or those who write only after greeting a single book through a lattice—but those who truly recognize that kind of <term>Rattle</term> <note>original: "Crotalum," a clapper or rattle</note> fashioned by **Vulcan**, as well as the **Stymphalian birds**. 

Regarding these birds, many philosophers have made mention, sometimes calling them "volatile parts" likely to flee, and sometimes "flying birds." So too they speak of the **Rattle**, or the "philosophical copper," which is the fixed thing that "fixes" or stabilizes them. The author of the *Council of the Sun* <note>original: "consilij con: sol:" likely referring to the *Consilium Coniugii*</note>, **Constans**, says in the *Assembly*:
> *Care for nothing else except how there are two quicksilvers: namely, the one fixed in copper, and the volatile one fleeing in Mercury.* 

And **Invidus** <note>A name appearing in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says that this sulfur—that is, the quicksilver—is accustomed to flee and is sublimated like a vapor. 
> *For it is necessary to retain it and restrain its flight with another quicksilver of its own kind—that is, of copper—for if it is not mixed with the white or red sulfur of its own kind (that is, gold or silver), it will undoubtedly flee.* 

The same author says a little later: 
> *And Eximidius says: "I tell you truly, there is no **tincture of Venus** <note>referring to the essence or transformative power of copper</note> except in our copper."* 

And regarding the figure of **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century alchemist</note>, he says: 
> *The two birds are homogeneous, that is, of one nature, and they are the Stone of the Wise. The male is without wings—that is, he cannot fly—because fire of itself cannot destroy him, nor can he exhale in the fire; no salt, spirit, or alum can move him, except for our so-called **eagle**. But the winged bird is the female, who is consumed along with the corrupting bodies.*

**Lull** <note>Ramon Llull, a major figure in medieval alchemy</note> says it best in *The Theory of the Testament*, chapter 57: 
> *Therefore, with such water, we fix the little birds flying in the air by the power of our Stone.* 

Therefore, aided by the art of **Vulcan** <note>the god of fire and smithing, representing the alchemist's furnace</note> and the instinct of **Pallas** <note>Athena, representing wisdom/intellect</note>, Hercules (or the craftsman) can drive away the **Stymphalian birds**, which have arisen from the rotting lake. Driven—
