...[they] are said to be driven away <note>The word fragment "gatæ" likely completes "purgatæ" (cleansed) or "fugatæ" (driven off), referring to the Stymphalian birds from the previous page.</note> when they no longer appear to be flying. Some add, among whom is Timagetas, that these birds possessed iron wings and claws, just as the Harpies <note>monstrous winged creatures from Greek myth</note> possessed golden ones. This is a marvelous thing, and it clearly declares the nature of the birds; namely, that they are metallic, though in this context the description refers more to their violent force than to their actual physical substance. 

From here, Hercules went to Crete: <margin>9. The raging Bull of Crete is captured.</margin> For a most furious bull was wandering there, sent into the fields by the wrath of **Neptune** <note>god of the sea</note>. It breathed fire from its nostrils, killed anyone in its path, and laid everything to waste. By the command of Eurystheus, Hercules betook himself there, and having soon captured the bull, he brought it back to him. What is signified by bulls has already been repeated often; for even if this one scatters fire from its nostrils, it is of the same rank as those bulls tamed by Jason and many others <note>In alchemy, the "bull" often represents the raw, potent earth or the "fixed" part of the matter that must be tamed by the "fire" of the work</note>. 

Soon after, he was sent to tame the horses of Diomedes: <margin>10. The horses of Diomedes are slaughtered along with him.</margin> Now, **Diomedes** was the King of Thrace, the son of Cyrene and **Mars** <note>god of war</note>. He possessed the most ferocious horses, to whom he would expose his captured guests to be torn apart. Hercules captured this man and, by the law of retaliation, cruelly exposed him to be mangled by his own horses, and afterwards he slaughtered the horses themselves. 

It is a wonder that Hercules attempted anything against Mars and his son, since Hercules seems entirely dedicated to Mars on account of his vigor and fortitude. However, it must be noted that he received some help and aid from **Pallas** <note>Athena, goddess of wisdom</note>, **Vulcan** <note>god of fire and smithing</note>, and even **Mercury** <note>god of messages and commerce, associated with quicksilver</note>, but nothing from Mars. For he was instructed in many arts by the son of Mercury, frequently warned by Pallas, and obtained his tools from Vulcan—to say nothing of Linus the son of Apollo, or Chiron the son of Saturn. Therefore, after the end of his labors, he dedicated an altar not to Mars, but to Pallas, and consecrated his club to Mercury. 

It is most certain that the same **philosophical subject** <note>the primary material used in the alchemical Great Work</note> is denoted by the horses. Since this subject possesses almost all the names in the world, why should it not also be called "our horse"? Thus **Rhasis** <note>original: "Rhases," a prominent 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician</note> says in his epistle: *The covering of the horse is our white mantle, and our horse is the strong lion hidden under the mantle.* Because Diomedes is the son of Mars and the grandson of Jupiter, he seems to be a partaker in the "golden genealogy." For this reason, he is imagined to be hostile to Hercules on account of his grandmother **Juno**. His horses are said to [devour] guests or unknown newcomers...

<margin>11. The olive tree.</margin>
It is also a sign of Herculean strength, which is related [in history] that in the territory of the Epidaurians, taking an olive tree by hand, he bent it around so that it took that circular shape, so that it was called "versile" <note>turnable or rotatable</note>, not far from the temple of **Diana Coryphaea** <note>the "Peak-dwelling" Diana</note>. For unless this bending or encircling of the <term>philosophical vessel</term> <note>the glass retort or flask</note> is done, it will not contain the <term>volatile spirits</term> <note>substances that easily vaporize</note>, as the philosophers hint in many places; namely **Morfoleus**, **Mundus**, **Astratus**, and others in the "Crowd" <note>referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> and elsewhere. Therefore, since this work is necessary to the art, the ancients rightly expressed it through the likeness of some Herculean labor. Now, the olive is sacred to **Pallas** <note>Athena, goddess of wisdom</note>, as is the art. **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says in his *New Light*, chapter 8: *"Who, then, shall make such water? Certainly I say, he who knows how to make glass: for this material is nothing other than what wants to be joined to itself; for it has in itself everything it needs."* By these words he hints that this matter requires nothing except its own inclusion in glass.

Who would doubt that the Amazons once existed, when so many and such great writers...

## Book 5. Egypto-Greek [Hieroglyphics].

<note>The first letter of the page is missing, likely an ornate initial from the preceding page. Reconstructed as "S".</note>

[S]cholars believe—though not in those things said to have happened in that Heroic age <note>The mythical era of demigods and heroes</note> long before the world was founded by our Creator—that we should therefore accept these tales as things never actually done, but very often spoken of, invented, and yet always believed. The most ancient Egyptians, situated far from these places, invented these stories and inserted them into their writings; the Greeks borrowed from them, and from the Greeks, everyone else followed. We previously related that these places, situated toward the West and Hesperus <note>The evening star, associated with the West/evening</note>, were celebrated for their metal mines. Therefore, they were sought out and occupied first of all by the Phoenicians, a maritime people. This gave rise to the allegory invented about the cattle to be led away from Iberia <note>Ancient name for the Spanish peninsula</note>.

But let us contemplate these cattle more closely: who is their possessor or master, or of what color and excellence are they? We shall easily recognize them. 

<margin>
*Who*
*Geryon is.*
</margin>

That triple-bodied Geryon, the son of Chrysaor, possessed these cattle. Some imagine him to have been a king of Iberia or Spain, and called "triple-bodied" because there were three brothers united and in harmony in their kingdoms. I confess these things are said, but they can by no means be proven. Thus the Heathens explained it, for they had never seen a triple-bodied man in the natural world, and they did not want the deeds of Hercules to seem like mere fables. 

But why is Geryon the son of Chrysaor <note>original: *Chrysaoris*, whose name means "Golden Sword"</note>, who was born from the blood of Medusa? Why did he have a dog with two heads and a dragon with seven heads? Why were the cattle purple-red <note>original: *punicei*, a deep reddish-purple associated with the final "red" stage of alchemy</note>? All these things, beyond what was said before, point toward an allegory. 

And so as not to linger here too long, Geryon is that one—as we have also mentioned scattered elsewhere before—of whom the *Author of the Marriage* <note>Likely referring to a Hermetic text on the "Chemical Wedding"</note> says, following Hermes:

> *I saw three faces—that is, spirits—born from one father; that is, from one offspring, because they are of one kind. Of these, one is in fire, the second in air, and the third in water.*

This is because Hamuel, the commentator on Senior <note>Senior Zadith, a famous 10th-century Arabian alchemist</note>, says:

> *The water of life is triple, because it is one thing in which they [the elements] are: namely air, fire, and water, in which the soul has arisen. This they call "gold," and they call it "divine water." These faces their father joined—the "father" meaning one kind, because they are homogeneous.*

So he says. The same is found in the rhymes of a certain philosopher, who says of those three faces thus united:

> *But by the grace of God they always remain, and together they triumph in a magnificent kingdom.*

### Book 5 of Hieroglyphics.

<margin>
A king despoiled of his cattle and life by Hercules.
</margin>

A father and son sit together on one seat, and the face of an old master appears in the middle, visible in a blood-red cloak. From these final words, one may judge the scarlet or purple color—the supreme red or "Tyrian" hue <note>original: "Tyrio"; referring to the famous and expensive purple dye of Tyre</note>—of the cattle of Geryon. For this color is appropriate for those cattle when they have reached a mature age. A dog and a dragon <note>The two-headed dog Orthrus and the serpent-like guardian of the cattle</note>, the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, were assigned as their guardians; enough has been said of them previously. 

If someone says that Hercules truly led away cattle of such a color, let him please himself; it does not please me. For if Hercules had existed in the natural world as such a great hero, would he have been a mere cattle-thief <note>original: "abactor boum"</note>? Would he have wanted, or even been able, to slaughter a king and his people for such a reason? Would he have driven cattle across such a vast distance, through the greatest part of the earth? Shall we believe they were purple back then, and have since ceased to be? These are considered the "nonsense of nonsenses" <note>original: "Nugæ nugarum"</note> if viewed as history; but if viewed as allegory, a serious sequence of truths presents itself. 

Or should we also believe—as those same pagan writers add—that Hercules then separated Libya from Europe and gave entry to the Mediterranean Sea <note>A reference to the creation of the Strait of Gibraltar, supposedly formed when Hercules broke the mountains apart</note>? If we were all lying in our cradles, we might be persuaded by them—those chattering old women, the writers and poets of ancient paganism. The "Pillars of Hercules" are held to be of the same truth as the "Pillars of Dionysus" or "Osiris." For in this way the Egyptians, staying at home and making offerings to their Vulcan <note>The god Ptah, whom the Greeks identified with Hephaestus/Vulcan</note>, "subjugated" the whole world: to the West through the "Egyptian Hercules," and to the East through Osiris, by erecting pillars and markers of their travels and victory. 

Nor was it enough for Hercules to have fought in Iberia <note>Ancient Spain</note> for such precious cattle and to have slaughtered a king, but he also suffered many adversities on his journey.

For since Hercules represents the Sun, the cold Earth restores by contact those things which have been scorched by excessive heat; wherefore it calls Antaeus himself back to life. For in this way we are taught that cooling medicines are to be applied to hot ailments, but not violent ones, lest an abscess form due to antiperistasis.”* <note>term: antiperistasis: A concept in pre-modern science where a quality (like heat or cold) is intensified when surrounded by its opposite.</note> 

So says he. We certainly judge these things to be true in themselves, and very well known even to those only slightly instructed in the school of physicians. However, we do not believe these are the sort of dogmas that ought to be hidden under the shadows of allegories—both because they are evident to common people on their own without fables, and they are not found to be of great subtlety. Even donkeys and sheep, the most stupid of beasts, [seek relief from] excessive heat...

Everything that is said, written, fashioned, or painted can be adapted to a commonplace of either *Ethics* <term>Ethicæ (Ethics)</term>, *Physics* <term>Physicæ (Physics)</term>, or mythical history; <note>The author is listing the three common Renaissance ways of interpreting myths: as moral lessons (Ethics), as metaphors for natural processes like weather (Physics), or as distorted accounts of real kings (History).</note> this is not a matter of great skill, but rather of memory. But to restore secret things to their own proper nature, truth, and homogeneity—this is the task of a man of genius and a lover of truth. For one thing is predicated of one truth, and one truth of one and the same thing, and not of another, properly speaking.

<margin>
Very diverse attributes given to Hercules in the exposition.
</margin>

How therefore will Hercules now be the Sun of the sky, now a hero of the earth, or a King of Egypt, or any other? How will he signify a contrariety in *Physics*, then something in *Ethics*, and a little later a historical person? How will he be the son of Jupiter, the governor of Egypt, the tamer of monsters, the specimen of virtue, and yet the perpetrator of so many vices and adulteries, thefts, robberies, and murders? All these things do not agree with a single truth, but are most contradictory, unless one wishes to say and believe everything about everyone, true and false simultaneously.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whatever is said here about Hercules, the same ought to be understood regarding Jason, and the whole genealogy of the gods and goddesses, and all the allegories and fables explained thus far.

...folly, so that there is no need to explain these fables now according to morals, now according to common Physics, and a little later according to the doctrine of another science in a most intricate and foreign way. Let them therefore be silent and make a sacrifice to Egyptian Harpocrates <note>The god of silence, often depicted with a finger to his lips.</note>—those who take it upon themselves to explain things of which they do not grasp even the shadow, and do not blush to teach others what they themselves have never learned. Meanwhile, like ungrateful mules, they attack by kicking and reviling the mother of all sciences—the oldest and most genuine after the most holy doctrine of God—and are in no way willing to recognize her even among the common sciences; I mean <margin>Alchemy is the mother of sciences.</margin> **Alchemy** <term>Chymia (Alchemy/Chemistry)</term>, the parent of Medicine (the most useful art for the human race) and the Queen of the remaining arts. What if these supposed and stinking censors of God's gifts were deceived by their own judgment? Those who would, if they could, extort from God's hand with insults that which they themselves have never received—just as the fox took the cheese from the crow’s beak with flatteries—when they write thus:

->*O deceptive art, hated by good men, how pleasantly you kill*<-
->*those captured by your sweetness? An impious Siren to the mad:*<-
<note>original: "Ars fallax invisa bonis dulcedine captos / Iucundè ut perimis? dementibus improba Siren." The author is quoting a critic of alchemy who views the "Great Work" as a dangerous delusion.</note>

And the many other things the same author vomits forth bear witness to his ignorance and dog-like eloquence <note>original: "canina facundia," a Latin idiom for snarling or cynical speech.</note> rather than to any doctrine of secrets or a benevolent will. That the character of Antaeus is a fiction is evident, even without anyone pointing it out. For he is the "Son of the Earth"—that is, a most obscure being without father or mother, born from the brains of poets—who could easily equal twenty other men of common stature, and is to be compared to a massive tower. Mention of him is also made in the administration of the offices of Egypt, along with Busiris, Hercules, Prometheus, and Mercury, who were left with Isis as governors by Osiris when he was about to set out for India. 

However, he signifies the <term>stone-making power (lapidifica virtus)</term> of transmuting his own mother into himself whenever he touches her; a force which arises when the total of the **fixed** <term>fixi (fixed element)</term> exceeds the total of the **volatile** <term>volatilis (volatile element)</term>, as we have discussed extensively elsewhere. <note>In alchemical theory, Antaeus represents the "fixed" principle (Earth) which grows stronger whenever it touches the ground, while Hercules represents the "volatile" or purifying force that must lift it up to transform it.</note> Afterwards, Hercules, having set out for Egypt, killed Busiris, the son of Neptune and Libya, along with his sons, <margin>25. He killed Busiris.</margin> because he had sacrificed strangers to his father Neptune.

We have already dealt with Busiris; Tithonus is imagined by others to be the brother of **Laomedon** and the father of **Memnon**, the lover of **Aurora** <note>The Roman goddess of the dawn.</note>, and belongs to the same class of symbols as the rest. This Eagle is said to have been struck down by Hercules. 

We have already frequently mentioned what kind of figure Prometheus is, as well as his lineage and name. We understand the **Eagle** to represent **volatile and penetrating matter** that reaches the interior, which the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists or "Philosophers by Fire."</note> have mentioned in many places. They interpret the Eagle as being like **water**, as **Senior** <note>Referring to the 10th-century alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel, known in Latin as Senior Zadith.</note> does in the figure of the ten eagles and others. They provide a reason: just as the feathers of an eagle easily take on gold if they are gilded, so too this water easily becomes golden. Indeed, the eagle’s feather corrodes other feathers just as the eagle itself devours other birds; thus, it is the <term>Philosophical Water</term> <gloss>aqua Philosophica: a specialized alchemical solvent, often an acidic substance used to break down metals</gloss>. Hence **Basilius Valentinus** <note>A famous, likely pseudonymous, 15th-century alchemist.</note> says: *The swift bird from the South, almost from the East, tears the heart from the chest.* This Eagle is struck by Hercules with arrows,

Therefore, either **Theseus** the king of the **Athenians** (though others describe his life) is entirely fabulous along with his ancestors, or if he is real, then false parents and deeds are ascribed to him. This is because that **Hercules** is imagined to have lived in the time of **Saturn** and **Osiris**, whom we have already sufficiently discussed.

**Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were central to medieval Western thought.</note> truly testifies of himself that he put so much labor and study into this divine art that he spent more on oil for working late at night than others spent on wine for drinking; and for that reason, he knows those things which he knows above others. 

The same man, in proving the truth of the art (Chapter 1, Book 2 of *On the Soul*), brings forward three kinds of arguments: one dialectical from philosophy, another from sophistry, and a third deduced from the nature of vision and the eyes. Regarding the last of these, he says: *“If I did not see gold and silver, I would say that the mastery was nothing; but because I see it, I believe and know that the mastery exists.”*

### BOOK SIX.

# ON THE TROJAN
## Expedition.

<margin>
Christian cities that assert these claims have drawn them from Heathenism and its false histories, and they continue to promote them.
</margin>
**T**o wish to unravel the destruction of the city of Troy or to call it into doubt—when so many cities exist that claim to have been built by Trojan refugees as their founders after the war—would be <note>original: "Æthiopem dealbare," a classical idiom meaning to attempt the impossible or to labor in vain.</note> **to wash an Ethiopian white** or to entirely **lose both oil and effort**. For that reason, we do not take so much upon ourselves. Nevertheless, we believe we can point out, succinctly and powerfully as if with a finger, how close this matter is to a fable or to a history that never actually happened. We do this with the protestation that we leave everyone to their own free judgment, especially since this can be believed (or not) without any wounding of one’s conscience. Nor indeed do we willingly submit what we are about to say to the "more-than-natural" sharpness of those Critics who might easily scatter these and similar arguments with the winds of words, even if the truth of the matter remains unmoved. Instead, we propose and leave these things to be judged by the devoted students and lovers of <term>secret physics</term> <note>original: "Physicae secretioris." In this context, it refers to alchemy or the hermetic study of nature's hidden forces.</note>. A certain <term>Dictys of Crete</term> <note>Dictys Cretensis was the purported author of an "eyewitness" diary of the Trojan War, which was widely read in the Middle Ages but later viewed as a literary forgery.</note> <term>plays the Cretan</term> <note>original: "cretizat." A wordplay based on the ancient proverb that "all Cretans are liars." It means to lie or deceive.</note> by claiming that he was present at the Trojan war while it was being waged. But because his work does not savor of such great antiquity (which would extend beyond the age of <term>Hesiod</term> and <term>Homer</term>) but rather seems to have borrowed everything from them, we view him as a fictitious and legendary writer who published that work under a false name and with a different intention...

...we set aside. The first reason why the destruction of Troy is seen as akin to a fable is this: all the founders of Troy are mythical and trace their origin from a genealogy of fictitious gods. Take, for instance, **Tros** or **Laomedon**, for whom **Neptune** and **Apollo** pledged their labor for a fixed price to build the city walls. This was done on the command of **Jove** <note>Jupiter, king of the gods</note>, either because they had tried to bind Jove along with the other gods, or because Jove had killed the **Cyclopes** with his arrows. Similarly, **Ovid** writes in the *Epistle of Paris* that the Trojan walls were built while Apollo played his lyre, using these verses:

> *You shall look upon Ilion, and walls fortified with high towers,*
> *Built by the melody of Phoebus’s lyre.* <note>original: "Ilion aspicies, firmataq; turribus altis / Mænia Phœbeæ ſtructa canore lyræ." Phoebus is a common title for Apollo, the god of music and light.</note>

**Virgil** records that those same walls were once fashioned by the hand of **Vulcan** <note>The god of fire and smithing</note>. If this is true, as we have suspected, then it was achieved through Vulcan’s arts, which cannot exist without fire. Neptune, who is considered the god of water, brought aid to Vulcan; this is because we generally require both water and fire in human affairs, so much so that without them we can accomplish almost nothing. For this reason, those who were "forbidden water and fire" <note>original: "interdicebatur aqua et igne," a Roman legal formula for banishment</note> were effectively deprived of civil life and the ability to live among men. Thus, in that craftsmanship—which **Homer** undoubtedly discovered in **Egypt** and passed down to posterity—at least fire and water are required, represented by Vulcan and Neptune, or their specific gifts. As **Aros** and **Calib** <note>These likely refer to Arisleus and Khalid, famous names in alchemical literature</note> say: "In all our work, <term>mercury</term> (which represents water) and fire are sufficient for you in the middle and at the end." But they are not enough in the beginning, because other things are present that must be removed through the power of Vulcan <note>meaning the intense heat of the furnace</note>.

Indeed, it is no more incredible that stones ran toward the walls themselves when they were being founded and arranged themselves in order after Apollo played his <term>lyre</term> <note>original: "Cythara," a stringed instrument like a harp</note> in rhythm, than it is to believe that when **Orpheus** sang, the stones, wild beasts, and even the trees moved from their places and ran to him in amazement. Or that the ship ***Argo*** held its course straight while he sang, but wandered aimlessly through the waves when he was silent, as was discussed above. These were articles of faith for the Heathens, but they are not so for us. However, the logic of Troy is far different from that of the city of Athens. For the latter was for some time the mistress of Greece and nurtured many brilliant minds, and it was well enough known for its arms and letters while it flourished, as is clear from historical records. But Troy ceased to exist at the very moment it had barely begun. The writings of many have spread word of its destruction, but concerning its kingdom and the deeds of its kings, there is nothing at all, except for what pertains to its ruin. For he himself—**Laomedon**—is imagined to have built Troy, a city so famous and populous, yet his own son witnessed its destruction.

*As if it were possible, speaking politically, for a very large city to be founded by one man, which possessed such strength that it could resist such a powerful army of Greeks for so long. For the growth of great cities, a royal seat frequented over a long period of time is most effective, in addition to other advantages of the region. Hence hardly anything great begins as such from the start; rather, that which is meant to endure very often arises from a small origin. As the common saying goes: "What is made quickly, perishes quickly." Thus Troy is imagined to have been founded by Laomedon and to have grown into such a great city so quickly that it is presumed not only to have been the most populous and powerful, but also that all the more refined arts, the metalworking arts, and the pictorial arts were invented there.*

This could not have happened in so small a span of time, namely that of a single king. But just as it was raised to the sublime peak of dignity, so it was soon reduced to ashes by the one and same author; so that the poet truly said of it: *There is a field where Troy once was.* <note>original: "Est campus, ubi Troia fuit." A common poetic variation of "Troja fuit," signifying total erasure from history.</note> For it was destroyed while the ashes of its builder, Laomedon, were still present, as will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, if one inquires carefully into the origin of Laomedon himself, he will be found to be mythical, along with all his ancestors. That is, he traced his descent from those who never existed in the nature of things—namely those believed to be mostly Gods, descending from Heaven and Earth, as was shown above in Book 3.

It is well-established that the Phrygians had a different idiom than the Greeks, because Phrygia is on the furthest coast of Asia Minor, which the Greeks did not inhabit in those ancient times before the age of Alexander the Great; rather, it was inhabited by the Colchians and Egyptian colonists (as we have cited before), who used a language very different from the Greeks. <margin>
A wondrous story regarding the antiquity of language.

this is evident from the history recorded by **Herodotus** <note>The Greek historian, often called the "Father of History"</note>: that a certain king (an Egyptian) <note>Pharaoh Psammetichus I</note>, when there was a dispute among neighboring nations regarding the antiquity of their languages—each claiming their own was the oldest—gave a newborn child to a certain shepherd living in the wilderness to be raised. He commanded that no one should utter a single word in the boy’s presence, and that the shepherd should observe which word he would pronounce first of all. Since the boy was nourished on goat’s milk, and after a year and a half the shepherd approached the now-hungry child, the boy began to cry out, "**beccum, beccum**," as if he desired to eat. When this was reported to the king, he inquired what "beccum" signified; it was discovered that **Beccum** in the Phrygian language denotes "bread," which the boy had been requesting. And so, the honor of the most ancient language remained with the Phrygians. However, the Egyptians responded with an objection: they said it was no wonder that the word **beccum** was the first uttered by the boy, as he had often heard it repeated by his nurse, the goat <note>suggesting the word "beccum" mimicked the "bleating" of the goat</note>, and thus he had learned it before all other vocal sounds. Since, therefore, the names of all the Trojans are Greek, it is easily apparent from this that they were given to them by Greek parents...

<margin>3. Argument: From "causes without which not" <note>A logical term (*causa sine qua non*) meaning indispensable conditions</note>, which are fictitious and fabulous.</margin>

The third argument is that the causes concurring to the siege and destruction of Troy are fictitious and fabulous. For just as the chick is potentially inside the egg, and the apple tree is inside the apple, so the entire expedition of the Trojans and Greeks lies hidden and exists by virtue within the apple and the egg. 

Take away the apple and the egg—as if they were merely the <term>desserts</term> <note>original: *repotia seu bellaria*, referring to the sweets or drinking-bouts at the end of a feast</note> or second courses of a table—or imagine those two things never happened or were not so, and the whole Trojan expedition is subverted. For if there were no Egg, there would be no Helen—the prize of such great labor and the most beautiful of women—who indeed, contrary to human custom, was hatched from an egg like the white daughters of a swan, nourished on "cock's milk" <note>A classical proverb for an impossible luxury or an exquisite delicacy</note>, and born from Jupiter as her father. 

And if the Apple of <term>Eris</term> <note>The goddess of Discord, who threw a golden apple "for the fairest" among the gods</note> did not exist, there would be no contention for the prize of beauty among the goddesses Juno, Pallas <note>Athena</note>, and Venus. Nor would Paris have been the judge of goddesses, nor Venus the cause of the promise of Helen, nor would Paris be her abductor and adulterer, nor Menelaus with the Greeks the seeker of her return, the avenger of injury, and the depopulator of Troy. In short, when the cause is removed, the effect is also removed. What then? If we remove the gods and goddesses themselves—Neptune, Apollo, and Vulcan, who founded Troy; or Jupiter, who...

Therefore, if *Helen* had not been immortal, she could undoubtedly not have endured through so many generations." 

These are his words. We, however, deny that she was immortal, unless they prove it by some other argument. Therefore, she did not endure; and whatever is said about *Helen* and the Trojan War fought on her account is recognized as a fable. This is further supported by the fact that Servius, along with others, records that *Helen* was first entrusted by *Theseus* to *Proteus* in *Egypt*. ### Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics

<margin>
**Aulus Gellius, Book 3, Chapter 11.**
Seven cities compete for the ancestry of the illustrious Homer: Smyrna, Rhodes, Colophon, Salamis, Chios, Argos, and Athens.

...he enumerates the people of Smyrna, Chios, Salamis, Colophon, and others. There are some, says **Aulus Gellius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman author who collected diverse historical and literary anecdotes</note>, who say he was an Egyptian; **Aristotle** reports that he was born on the island of **Ios**. Thus, everything regarding **Homer** is left in uncertainty, even though some have used plausible conjectures regarding his date. Therefore, if it is not most truly established from **Homer**, or some other writer even older than him, when that so-famous destruction of **Troy** occurred, it does not prevent the story from being a fable—rather, it truly proves it so. 

For times must correspond to times, just as events to events and persons to persons, if the truth is to shine forth. The reality will be clearer with examples: from history, it is known which kings were reigning in **Egypt** and in what year **Moses** was born. Likewise, we know when **Christ** was born, who ruled the world, and what happened under both preceding and following Emperors. We know under which consuls **Corinth** was destroyed, **Carthage** was overthrown, and all other countless events. From this, it is impossible that, if **Troy** had been destroyed, there would not exist a certain memory of the time and persons, which would have extended to those who followed them. 

However, the fact that **Homer** wrote that **Aeneas**, a fugitive from **Troy**, sought out Italy, served the **Roman** writers greatly for the expansion of the authority of their city. Since from the descendants of this same **Aeneas** they derive—if you please!—**Romulus**, at least on his mother’s side, while assigning him a father far more noble than a man: namely the god **Mars** himself. And since **Aeneas** is said to have been born of the mother **Venus**, they gladly recognized in **Romulus** a maternal lineage from **Venus** and a paternal one from **Mars**. It was as if it were something magnificent to have a city founder born beyond the human fashion, whom they therefore afterwards numbered among the gods.

For Rome, fictional ancestors descending from the gods were added so that its origin would be more noble.
</margin>

Is it lawful for gods to be joined to human women, but a sin for human men to be joined to goddesses? A harsh condition, or rather one not to be believed: that what was permitted to Mars in his intercourse by the right of Venus, is not permitted to Venus herself by her own right. Yet both are confirmed by Roman authority." And soon in Chapter 4: "Someone might say: Do you really believe these things? I truly do not believe them. For even their most learned man, Varro, almost confesses these things to be false, although not daringly nor confidently."*

**And in the same place:** But whether **Venus** could have given birth to **Aeneas** from her intercourse with **Anchises**, or **Mars** could have fathered **Romulus** from his intercourse with **Ilia**, the daughter of **Numitor**, let us leave that undecided <note>This quote is likely drawn from Saint Augustine’s *City of God*, where he critiques the absurdity of pagan myths</note>. So he says: It is therefore a wonder that in such great light of the Christian faith, it is still believed and taken for truth that Troy was founded and destroyed in the manner described, and that from its remains such a great kingdom—namely the Roman—arose like a new **Phoenix** from the ashes; since all those stories concerning Troy are fables, as are the "greater gods" of the nations. 

If, however, someone believes that Troy existed or stood without such a condition or destruction connected to the gods, he certainly will not satisfy the Pagans <term>Ethnici</term> <note>The author uses 'Ethnici' to refer to the ancient non-Christian Greeks and Romans</note>, but will attempt to protect a house built in the air without pillars from the harm of the winds. For the gods of the nations are established as the foundation of all that Trojan construction and destruction; without them, there will be no Troy, and no authors to build or destroy it. 

Hence, those who truly embrace the Christian faith are altogether blind and deprived of the light of reason if they meanwhile presuppose or believe that Troy was built or destroyed by so many gods; for while we are indeed faithful Christians, we conquer and uproot Troy even by our silence. Conversely, if we assert its reality along with the Pagans, we also silently assent to their gods and renounce Christianity. 

<margin>
5. Reason: From the Place.
</margin>

The fifth reason is taken from the place, which never existed; where it should be known that some take Troy to be the province in which the city of **Ilium** was located, others take it for the city itself—which is the opinion that has prevailed—and say **Ilium** refers to the citadel, **Phrygia** to the region, and **Troy** to the city. Regarding the region, there is no doubt that it once existed, as we have often mentioned, and still exists, although called by another name. But regarding **Troy**, it is disputed. 

We do not deny, meanwhile, that a place can perhaps be designated where **Troy** is presumed to have stood, but this became known from **Homer's** description; he, like other poets, wrote wonders about certain places, mountains, seas, springs, rivers, forests, and islands: how gods were born in them, what memorable things they performed, on which rock they sat, and many such things, all of which the Pagans [held] in mind... <note>original: "præ men..." — the sentence is interrupted by the page break</note>

### Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks

...blindness of mind <note>The previous page ended with "mentis," the first part of the phrase "blindness of mind"</note> they accepted and embraced these things as true, especially those people for whom a certain god was fashioned by the Poets as a **fellow-countryman** <term>sympatriota</term> <note>From the Greek 'sympatriotes', meaning someone from the same country or city</note>, as we mentioned previously regarding the **Thebans**, **Rhodians**, **Delians**, and others. 

But even if the locations remain—serving as monuments and traces of those things the Poets remembered—it does not follow that the things attributed to the gods are entirely true. For although the Poets could invent everything—namely the characters (whether gods or men), the time periods, and the deeds—as if they were historical and plausible, they could not or should not have invented the locations as if they were speaking of another world. Since places are immobile, practically immutable, and everlasting, the human mind would have inquired where those places were where such things were said to have happened. If it had not found them in the world, it would have immediately recognized the story as a fable. 

On the contrary, when the **Pagans** <term>Ethnici</term> heard a specific place named, they were not concerned about the characters, their deeds, or the timing, because those three things seemed changeable and, as it were, invisible. They did not deny such gods as the Poets fashioned, but instead accepted them as lustful, adulterous, incestuous, and marked by every crime, led by a certain insane persuasion. Thus, the Poets were allowed to invent whatever they pleased regarding the gods and to perform it in stage spectacles, yet they were by no means allowed to do so regarding men. **St. Augustine** disapproves of this in Book 2, Chapter 13 <note>Refers to *The City of God*</note>, saying: 

*The Greeks,* he says, *think they rightly honor stage actors because they worship the gods who demand those stage plays; the Romans, however, do not allow stage actors to dishonor even the plebeian tribe, much less the Senatorial court. In this dispute, a reasoning of this sort settles the heart of the question:* 

->**The Greeks propose:** If such gods are to be worshipped, surely such men ought also to be honored.<-
->**The Romans assume:** But such men are by no means to be honored.<-
->**The Christians conclude:** Therefore, such gods are by no means to be worshipped.<-

And in the following Chapter 14, he says: *Next we ask why the Poets themselves, the composers of such fables, are prohibited by the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BCE</note> from damaging the reputation of citizens, while they hurl such shameful insults at the gods? Why are they not considered dishonest, just as the stage actors are? By what logic is it right that the madness of poetic fictions and disgraceful gods...*

<summary>The author argues that the use of real geographic locations in myths was a trick to make divine fables seem plausible. Citing St. Augustine, he highlights the logical inconsistency of Roman law, which protected citizens from slander but allowed poets to blaspheme the gods.</summary>

### 256 Hieroglyphics Book 6.

...should the actors be called liars, while the authors are honored? <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "an mentiuntur actores, honorentur auctores?"</note> Or perhaps the palm should rather be given to **Plato the Greek**, *who, establishing with reason what a city ought to be, judged that Poets, as enemies of cities, should be driven out; for he bore the injuries against the gods with indignation, and did not want the minds of citizens to be darkened and corrupted by fictions.* <note>The author is paraphrasing Saint Augustine’s "The City of God," where Augustine discusses Plato’s banishment of poets from his ideal Republic.</note> Thus far Augustine. *Since these things are most true, who but a total **Pagan** <term>Ethnicus</term> would admit those Gods, or the influence which is ascribed to them by Poets in specific places that actually exist?*

It does not escape our notice that both ancient and more recent Geographers assign a specific location for **Troy**, where it is presumed to have stood; and there are those who testify that the **Turks**, who live near those places, report that marble is still dug up from the subterranean ruins of Troy to be used for decorating houses. However, there is no doubt that these signs are highly unreliable. Even if they are real, they can only testify to buildings that once stood there, not to the specific Troy built by the gods and destroyed by the Greeks. 

For what magnificent work could have remained underground if that Troy really stood, since that age recognized humble huts and shacks <term>mapalia</term> <note>A term used by Roman authors for the temporary huts or movable dwellings of North African nomads, here used to suggest primitive architecture.</note> rather than palaces and marble houses? Furthermore, the walls are said to have been built by **Apollo’s** lyre, and in the very short time Troy is written to have stood, such great buildings as Poetic fame describes could not have been constructed. 

Moreover, it is well known that the city of **Troas** (from which the inhabitants are also called Trojans), which is mentioned in the sacred writings of **Saint Paul**, stood in that place around the time of **Christ**. But who will affirm for certain that this was the remains or a colony of that other ancient Troy? Who can say the marble dug up there was not from this more recent city rather than that most ancient one? 

Who would not instead guess that this city was built according to **Homer's** description long after his time? We have noticed this happening in countless other cases, so that Homer rightly earned the name of **Prophet** <term>Vates</term> among the Pagans. For the things he invented, they either embraced as having already happened, or they imitated them as things to be done. 

They claim **Phrygia** was named after **Phryxus**, who—as the fables go—reached **Colchis** with the ram that **Mercury** made golden, traveling either through the air or through the waters; and when he had lived there, he gave his name to the region. **Apollonius** also mentions this ram in Book 2. <note>Referring to Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the 'Argonautica'.</note>

### Book 6: The Egyptian-Greeks

...the **Argonauts** <note>The author is likely quoting from a poetic source like Valerius Flaccus’s *Argonautica* or a similar mythological compendium</note> in these verses:

> *As I believe has long since reached your ears,*
> *How Phryxus reached the kingdom and the walls of Aeëtes:*
> *A ram carried him, which the Cyllenian <note>original: "Cyllenius"; an epithet for the god Mercury, who was said to be born on Mount Cyllene</note> soon made golden;*
> *Even now, that golden fleece hangs from a golden oak,*
> *Which occasionally rustles gently in the breeze.*

It is clear, therefore, that **Colchis** <note>A region on the Black Sea, modern-day Georgia</note> and **Phrygia** <note>A region in central Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey</note> are regions very close to one another, and the name of one is often given to the other, and vice-versa. This indicates nothing other than that both fables—the one concerning the **Golden Fleece** of Phryxus (from whom Phrygia is said to be named) and the one concerning the **Trojan expedition** (which is said to have taken place in Phrygia)—were invented and introduced to describe one and the same thing. 

Just as there is almost a single meaning for both allegories, the same characters are also invented for both; however, they are arranged so that the children or grandsons of the Argonauts participated in the Trojan War, which is established as being a hundred years more recent than the voyage of the Argonauts. This is despite the fact that—as we have also mentioned before—**Castor and Pollux**, along with **Helen and Clytemnestra** (who were produced from two eggs in a single birth), were present for both events. <note>The author is pointing out the chronological impossibility in Greek myth: the same generation of heroes appears in events supposedly separated by a century.</note> 

A single ram, I say, explains that entire war: what it was really about. It was not, as the saying goes, about **goat’s wool** <note>original: "de lana caprina"; a Latin idiom for arguing over something trivial or non-existent</note>, but about the skin of a golden ram which **Mercury** had gilded. This ram brought fame to both Phrygia and Colchis, the explanation of which we have sufficiently dealt with previously. 

It is a wonder how the **Mythologists** <term>Mythologi</term> <note>Scholars who interpreted the hidden meanings of ancient myths</note> twist themselves in explaining what ought to be understood by the "Ram of Phryxus." They bring forth twenty different meanings, not one of which fits the nature of the matter. Just as they are all erroneous and depart from the truth, they also mutually cancel each other out. They say it was called a "golden ram" because the "advice of wise men should be considered golden." But this is completely wide of the mark; such an explanation is not even "leaden," nor is it worth marking with red chalk or ink <note>original: "nec rubrica, nec atramento notanda"; a way of saying the idea isn't worth writing down</note> for it to enter the eyes and minds of the wise. 

**Midas** made this same place, the land of Phrygia, famous by his "golden wish," which we mentioned in Book 2 along with the Golden Fleece; and **Ovid** writes in the *Metamorphoses* concerning the **Pactolus** <note>A river in Lydia/Phrygia famous for its gold deposits</note> of Midas...

<summary>The author argues that the Golden Fleece and the Trojan War are actually the same allegorical story set in the same region, noting the chronological contradictions in Greek mythology. He mocks contemporary scholars who provide overly simplistic moral explanations for these myths.</summary>

# On Hieroglyphics, Book 6

...[the river] having been made gold-bearing by the washing, he relates it in this way:

> *The king entered the water as commanded; its golden power stained*
> *The river, and passed from the human body into the stream.*
> *Even now, having absorbed the seed of that ancient vein,*
> *The fields grow stiff with gold, their sodden clods turning pale.*
<note>original: "Rex iussa succedit aqua..." These lines are from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book 11, describing how King Midas rid himself of the "golden touch" by bathing in the River Pactolus.</note>

Although this method of "tinting" <note>Referring to the alchemical or transformative coloring of the water</note> does not align with the laws of nature, it sufficiently declares what the ancients intended to suggest by it—namely, the same thing signified by the **Golden Fleece**, the occupation of <term>Troy</term> <note>original: "Trojae"</note>, the abduction of <term>Ganymede</term>, and other similar tales. From this source, King <term>Midas</term> is also handed down to us as the wealthiest man of his time. He is the one who—while Mount <term>Tmolus</term> in <term>Phrygia</term> was judging the singing contest between <term>Phoebus</term> <note>Apollo, the sun god and patron of music</note> and <term>Pan</term>—refuted the victory being awarded to <term>Phoebus</term>. As a result, he was given the ears of an animal <note>Specifically, the ears of a donkey, a punishment for his "poor hearing" of the music</note> by <term>Phoebus</term>. Therefore, let <term>Tmolus</term> and the river <term>Pactolus</term>, the <term>Ram of Phryxus</term>, and <term>Midas</term> serve as witnesses that <term>Phrygia</term> abounded in veins of gold, and thus provided the setting for the narration of many fables.

To these we shall add <term>Ganymede</term>, likewise a Phrygian, who is said to be the son of <term>Laomedon</term>, King of the Trojans. He was carried up into heaven by **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> in the form of an eagle, so that he might serve the god's cups in place of <term>Hebe</term> <note>The goddess of youth and original cupbearer to the gods</note>. Under this fable, <term>Cicero</term> <note>The Roman orator and statesman</note>, in the first book of his <term>Tusculan Disputations</term> <note>original: "Tusc. quæst."</note>, suspected that some secret truth was contained, when he said: *Nor do I listen to Homer, who says that Ganymede was snatched by the gods on account of his beauty, so that he might serve Jove’s cups. It is not a just reason why such an injury should be done to Laomedon. Homer was making these things up and transferring human qualities to the gods.*

<margin>Homer transferred human affairs to the Gods.</margin>

By these words, <term>Cicero</term> confesses that <term>Homer</term> invented the things he wrote concerning the abduction of <term>Ganymede</term>. In the same way, we know that <term>Homer</term> did this throughout his entire work—not only in this one instance—but that he directed every single detail toward a different goal than what the literal words suggest. Others attempt to relate this act of **Jove** to history, saying that **Jove** was a king of **Crete**, a most immoral man who abused boys and kidnapped the daughters of foreigners. They claim that <term>Tantalus</term>, King of the Phrygians, kidnapped <term>Ganymede</term> (the son of King **Tros**, the founder of the Dardanians) for the king's favor, so that **Jove** might abuse him, according to <term>Orosius</term> <note>A 5th-century Christian historian</note> in his first book. However, it appears from all circumstances that these explanations were devised by others and rest upon no truth. <term>Lactantius</term> <note>An early Christian author and advisor to Constantine</note> also thinks this way about **Jove** in his first book: *What Ju—*

The author cites Cicero and Ovid to demonstrate that these stories were poetic inventions intended to convey deeper physical or philosophical truths rather than literal history.</summary>

<header>Book 6. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.</header>

...[Ju]piter, who in solemn prayer is named **Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Optimus Maximus," the traditional Roman title for Jupiter</note>, is he not discovered to be almost a parricide from his very first cause and childhood? For he expelled his father <note>Saturn</note> from the kingdom and, in his greed for ruling, did not wait for the end of the decrepit old man. When he had seized the paternal throne by force and arms, he was provoked to war by the **Titans**, and once they were conquered, he consumed the rest of his life in debaucheries and adulteries. I omit the virgins whose honor he diminished, for that is usually judged a tolerable offense; but I cannot pass over **Amphitryon** and **Tyndareus**, whose homes he rendered full of disgrace and infamy <note>Jupiter disguised himself as these men to seduce their wives, Alcmene and Leda</note>. Truly, it was the height of impiety and crime that he snatched a royal boy <note>Ganymede</note> for the purpose of lust. For it seemed too little to him that he was so stained and foul in overpowering the modesty of women, unless he also did injury to his own sex. 

These are the words of *Lactantius* <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD), an early Christian author who critiqued pagan mythology</note>. However, it is sufficiently clear from what has been said before that **Jupiter** was neither a man, nor a God, nor a King of **Crete**; for he had been celebrated with many monstrous fictions and allegories by the **Egyptians** long before the **Greeks** had learned anything of that religion first brought to them by **Orpheus**. We have sufficiently proved that neither he, nor his parents or ancestors, nor his brothers, sisters, sons, grandsons, or descendants, ought to be—or even can be—counted among either gods or men.

As for what is related concerning **Ganymede**, it pertains to **Chemical Hieroglyphics** <note>Alchemical symbols or allegories</note>. In these, **Ganymede** is not interpreted as the bringer of winter rains or the cupbearer of **Jupiter** (representing the Air), nor as the celestial sign of **Aquarius**; rather, he represents that which is carried upward by the eagle—that is, the **fixed** substance which is raised to the highest dignity by the **volatile** <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to stable solids, while "volatile" refers to substances that easily vaporize or transform</note>.

<margin>
6. *The Reason.*
From the six conditions or fatal requirements without which *Troy* could not be conquered.
</margin>

The **sixth reason** is the firmest of all, and is drawn from the Conditions or Requirements without which **Troy** could not be besieged. For six "fatal" things are celebrated in total, which were necessary to occur and had to be sought out by the **Greeks** before they could emerge as victors over the **Trojans**. 

The first of these was that the seer **Calchas** had pronounced that **Troy** could not be taken without **Achilles**, nor without his son **Neoptolemus**. The second was that the **Palladium** <note>A sacred wooden statue of the goddess Pallas Athena</note> would have to be stolen from **Ilium** <note>Troy</note>. The third, that one of the bones of **Pelops** <note>A legendary king whose shoulder was said to be made of ivory</note> must be held at **Troy** before it could be conquered. The fourth, that the ashes of **Laomedon** <note>The father of King Priam of Troy</note> must be snatched from the gate.

Fifth, that there was a need for the arrows of **Hercules**; Sixth, that the horses of **Rhesus**, King of **Thrace**, must be driven away before they could drink from the river **Xanthus**. At first glance, these things would appear fabulous <note>meaning mythical or unbelievable</note>, were they not repeatedly insisted upon by **Homer** and those authors who, after him, recorded the Trojan disaster. But how could things so diverse and foreign to the purpose contribute to the storming of a city or the destruction of a race? Why are these things said to benefit the **Greeks** and hinder the **Trojans**, unless perhaps by magical power or supernatural virtue? We read in the monuments of Sacred Scripture how the walls of **Jericho** <note>original: "Hierochuntis"</note> 
<margin>Joshua ch. 6.</margin>
were cast down by the **Israelite** people at God’s command, by marching around them and the repeated sound of trumpets, and the way was opened for the victorious **Israelites**; yet we do not remember anything of the sort happening among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note>. This is held to have most truly been done by the **Lord of Hosts**; those other things are fashioned as if they had been done. The former was handed down by the most sacred writings, the latter by the fables of poets. But so that it may become more clear that these things are not only fictional, but for what purpose they were finally fashioned, we shall inquire more broadly into each of them and their circumstances.

The first was the presence of **Achilles** and his invincible courage against the **Trojans**.
<margin>1. Requirement: Achilles and Neoptolemus. Secrets.</margin>
**Achilles** is fashioned as the son of **Peleus** and **Thetis**. (**Peleus** comes from *pēlos* <note>Greek: πηλός</note>, meaning clay or mud, just as **Thetis** signifies water). For **Peleus**, as **Isaacius** <note>Isaac Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine scholar known for his commentaries on mythology</note> has left in writing, on the advice of his father **Chiron**, caught **Thetis** while she was hiding in the form of a cuttlefish in **Magnesia**, a place in **Thessaly**. All the gods came to celebrate their wedding on **Mount Pelion** (where our **magnesia** <note>A reference to "Magnesia Philosophorum," a key substance in alchemy</note> lies hidden, and from which it was originally named), except for **Discord**, who, being angry at this, threw a golden apple into the midst of them all with this inscription: *Let it be given to the most beautiful* <note>original: "detur Pulcherrimæ"</note>. This apple <note>The author likely intends a pun here, as the Latin "malum" means both "apple" and "evil"</note> was the beginning of every evil for the **Trojans**. For at this wedding, two seeds were sown, or the principal causes for the destruction of **Troy** were provided: For first, **Achilles** was generated from them; and second, **Paris** was chosen as the arbitrary judge, who judged **Venus** most worthy of the Apple—having been corrupted by her with the promised gift of the most beautiful **Helen**. From this, the rages of the remaining goddesses flared up against the **Trojans**, both because of **Paris** the judge and because of **Aeneas**, the son of **Venus**; and then followed the abduction of **Helen**.

# Book 6. Of the Egypto-Greeks.

->Page 261<-
->Signature Ll 3<-

They write that **Helen** bore several children by **Paris**, from which it is clear she was still younger than fifty; but how was **Pollux**, who emerged from the same egg as she, present with the **Argonauts** about 100 years before they sought the Golden Fleece <note>original: "vellus aureum"</note>? Or how was **Achilles** born at this wedding <note>the wedding of Peleus and Thetis</note>, who later took his own son **Pyrrhus** with him to **Troy**? From this it follows that at minimum 40 years after the apple of **Eris** <note>The "Apple of Discord" thrown by the goddess of strife</note> was thrown, **Achilles** struggled at **Troy**. If the duration of the siege is added to this, as well as the age of **Helen** at the time of the **Argonautic** expedition, they would make **Helen** no less than 180 years old by the time **Troy** was finally conquered and the adultress was recovered by the **Greeks**. Nor does it follow that **Helen** was very young even then, because she was said to be still a maiden when abducted by **Theseus**, though she was later restored to her parents. But we think it is superfluous to examine these points too scrupulously, since the matter is sufficiently established as being fictional in itself.

**Helinandus** <note>Helinand of Froidmont, a medieval chronicler and monk</note> tells that **Jupiter** loved **Thetis**, but when he was warned not to father anyone by her who might expel him from his kingdom, he gave her as a wife to **Peleus**, the King of the **Peloponnese**, brother of **Aeson**, and uncle of **Jason**. When all the goddesses were present at their wedding, except for **Discord**, she became angry and threw a golden apple into the midst of the goddesses with the inscription mentioned before. **Fulgentius** <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a late antique mythographer</note> maintains that through these three goddesses the poets understood three types of life: namely, through **Venus**, the voluptuous life; through **Juno**, the active life; and through **Pallas**, the contemplative life. But it is not likely, based on all the circumstances, that these moral things are the *primary* meaning intended; however, we do not deny that they fit perfectly as a *secondary* meaning.

From the aforesaid, therefore, it is established that **Achilles** is the son of **Peleus**—that is, of "mud" <note>the author derives Peleus from the Greek "pelos," meaning clay or mud, a common alchemical reference to the "First Matter"</note> or of **Mount Pelion**—and of **Thetis**, the goddess of the sea or water; the grandson of **Chiron**, the great-grandson of **Saturn**, and the great-great-grandson of **Sky and Earth**. For thus must he be who ought to be chosen by a philosopher to complete his work; without these ancestors, he will hardly be of a noble nature. <margin>Ulysses is an artist powerful in counsel.</margin>

### Book 6 of the Egypto-Greeks.

...devoid of scrutiny and intellect, those who can scarcely understand common speech, and who similarly learn ordinary works with difficulty; those who easily conceive every fantasy, and what they believe to be the truth is entirely fantastical, deviant from reason, full of error, and removed from natural principles. Their brains are filled with many vapors <note>original: "fumositatibus"; in early modern medicine, these were "smoky" residues of digestion thought to cloud the mind and cause confusion</note>, and they cannot receive the true intent of natural things. They possess a fickle soul, moving from opinion to opinion and from desire to desire—like those who believe one thing now and desire it without any foundation of reason, but a little later believe and desire something else entirely. They are so fickle that they can scarcely complete the smallest part of what they intend, but instead leave it unfinished. They cannot see any truth in natural things, no more than beasts; they are like those who are deranged, insane, or children who despise science and do not believe it exists. Science likewise despises them, and repels them from the goal of this most precious work. They are slaves serving money, affirming this wonderful science themselves, yet they fear to incur any expense; therefore, although they affirm it and investigate it according to reason, they never arrive at the experience of the work because of their greed for money: ***To these people, therefore, he says, our science does not come: For how could one who is ignorant, or who has neglected to investigate science, easily attain it?*** And in chapter 6, he affirms that those oppressed by extreme poverty, even if they possess the knowledge spoken of thus far, are forced to postpone this most excellent mastery <term>Magisterium|The completion of the Alchemical Great Work, or the philosopher's stone</term> due to a lack of resources. Others, who are curious but detained by various cares and anxieties of this world, never reach the end of the art even if they possess everything else. Thus the same **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy</note> in chapter 7, under the form of an Epilogue, describes the true craftsman as a **Ulysses** <note>The hero of the Odyssey, used here as a symbol of the patient, wise, and enduring seeker</note>, whose words may be seen in that place. # Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics.

->Page 264<-

...any time in the whole art of **Alchemy** <term>Alchemy; the original uses "Chymia," which at this time referred to the sacred science of transforming matter</term> will he produce anything, even if he were to work forever. He might, *by sheer chance* <note>original: "Fortè fortunâ"</note>, arrive at some result in the art, *just as a blind man hits a sparrow with an arrow*, but otherwise he could not reach it. Ulysses, therefore, has been sufficiently described as to which gifts of the mind he ought to possess, so that Troy might be occupied chiefly by his counsel, as is evident in the speech of Ulysses against Ajax in *Ovid’s Metamorphoses*: it was by his effort alone that whatever was successfully achieved at Troy by the Greeks was carried out. His first praise is that he brought Achilles; for the sake of this business, which he took upon himself, he set out to explore the enclosures of the maidens in the habit of a merchant. Thus, having finally found Achilles, he led him—unwillingly—to Troy, together with his son Pyrrhus, *a youth with red hair* <note>original: "iuvene rufi capillitij"</note>. But to what purpose is all this? We confess that these matters are the most secret in Alchemy, handed down by Homer with marvelous artistry. For there is a certain subject in the nature of things without which the philosophical Artist can achieve nothing; and that subject must be sought out with Ulyssean intelligence. He is properly called Neoptolemus <note>Neoptolemus is another name for Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles</note>, and he is born of Achilles with *fiery hair* <note>original: "ardentis capillitij"; the name Pyrrhus is derived from the Greek "pyr," meaning fire</note>. How he is born, however, one must proceed just as *Thetis* proceeded with Achilles.

<margin>The Secret of Secrets.</margin>
This is the **secret of secrets**, scarcely ever expressed in clear words by the philosophers; yet if you survey the corresponding passages of this treatise—at Rhodes, regarding Adonis, and very often elsewhere—you will notice it. There is one among all the moderns <note>original: "neotericis"; referring to recent or contemporary alchemical authors</note> who delivers this secret most openly. Since this is the Key of the whole art, I shall provide his words here: *It is mineral,* he says, *it is equal, it is continuous, it does not vaporize unless it is excessively excited; it partakes of sulfur, it is taken from elsewhere than the matter; it destroys, dissolves, and gathers all things; likewise it congeals and calcinates; it is artificial to find, and it is a shortcut without any expense, or at least a very small one.* Let the rest be seen in the works of its author, who is well known. If our Ulysses, therefore, possesses Achilles, he will also acquire Pyrrhus; for the father is brought along for the sake of the son. But from where, you ask, will this Achilles be summoned? One must look to the parents and the birthplace of Achilles: his father is Peleus, and his mother is Thetis.

# Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks.

->Page 265<-

**Thetis**, as you will recognize from her names and omens, was sought by **Peleus** while she was hiding in the form of a cuttlefish <note>original: "sepiæ"</note>; the cuttlefish is a well-known aquatic genus which, when it is captured, stains the water with ink. The location of this myth is **Magnesia**; hence our **Achilles** is called "Magnesia" by some. Regarding this, Flamel, citing Democritus, says: *For whitened Magnesia does not allow bodies to be broken, nor the shadow of Venus to be introduced.* And soon after: *What is Magnesia but the whole composite?* And: *Behold the beautiful Magnesia, and marvel at how through one thing it brings about a multitude.* And Dardaris says among the crowd: "Furthermore, know that *the body of bronze is governed by Magnesia.*" Mosius says: "*Living Mercury* <term>Argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for quicksilver or mercury</term> *is Magnesia.*" Pythagoras says: "*Therefore, you must not leave that Magnesia without the mercury.*" For when they are joined, it is the strongest composition, which is one of the ten. Pandulphus, Belus, Astratus, Rasson, and many others in the crowd have mentioned the same, whose sayings we omit. Indeed, Pythagoras defines the whole art in this way: *And it should be known that the science of this art is nothing other than the sublimation of vapor and water, and the joining of mercury to the body of Magnesia.* Nor does it matter that some think this name was given to it out of envy <note>The "envy" of the philosophers refers to their habit of using "deck names" or code words to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note>. Whence Rasson says: *This is indeed our greatest secret, which the envious have called Magnesia for the sake of the secret itself.* Therefore, diligently cook this Magnesia in its own vessel *until the whole is coagulated and contains itself.* Thus, once you have obtained the Magnesia, or Achilles (or **Pyrrhus** <note>Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, is associated with the color red (from the Greek 'pyr' for fire), symbolizing the final 'rubedo' or reddening stage of the Great Work</note> arising from him), who is fostered under the fire by his mother’s industry and educated by his grandfather **Chiron**—who instructed so many heroes, and among them his cousin **Jason**—so that he may truly become our Pyrrhus and our salamander, it is then permitted to approach the occupation of **Troy**.

<margin>What is understood by the destruction of Troy.</margin>

By the siege of Troy and its reduction to ashes, nothing else was mystically and secretly intended by **Homer** than the period and circuit of the **philosophical vessel** <term>The alchemical furnace or "athanor" containing the glass vessel where the transformation occurs</term>, in which **Helena** and **Paris** (the principal matter) are contained, tightly enclosed, and surrounded by their own vaporous and digesting fire. Helena is the one for whom the struggle takes place, in whose lap the idle adulterer Paris hides. For in one single subject there is a double power, active and passive, male and female, with which there concurs...

### Hieroglyphics. Book 6

->Page 266<-

**Achilles**, however, was killed through treachery by **Paris** in the temple of Thymbraean **Apollo**; thus lies that bravest of the Greeks, slain by the most cowardly and effeminate Trojan. Yet it was necessary for it to happen this way; for our fire must finally be extinguished by its own water, and water has the primary power of acting, specifically in the dissolution <note>original: "solutione"; the process of breaking down a solid into a liquid state</note>. And then it is necessary that **Achilles** die, but afterwards, when the color is already changing to the best, all of **Troy** is occupied by the art and knowledge of **Pallas** <note>The goddess Athena, representing wisdom and craft</note>, plundered, and reduced to ashes—ashes which are nevertheless most dear and not to be despised. For from them the immortal **Phoenix** <term>Phoenix: the mythical bird that rises from its own ashes, representing the rebirth of the alchemical stone in its perfected state</term> is born and lives again; from those remains, I say, colonies are sent to foreign shores—**Aeneas**, **Diomedes**, **Antenor**, and others—who found and take possession of new kingdoms.

<margin>The summary of the Homeric work.</margin>

This is the summary of the whole Homeric work concerning the destruction of **Troy**, the details of which we will make clearer in the following sections. **Helen** and **Pollux** are produced from one egg, male and female; thus **Helen** and **Paris** reside in one bedchamber, and they comprise our philosophical **Marcasite** <term>Marchasita: a term used here not for the mineral iron pyrite, but for a specific stage of the "raw" matter being refined</term> under one name. **Achilles** and our **Pyrrhus** <note>Achilles' son, also known as Neoptolemus</note> is the **latten** <term>laton/latten: an alloy similar to brass, used by alchemists to represent the "copper" or impure stage of the metal before it becomes gold</term>, our **magnesia**, our fire. Thus a war arose between the marcasite and the magnesia, in which the former dominates first, but later the latter.

Do you wish for examples from the authors? See **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist</note>, who says: *And likewise **Mary** <note>Mary the Prophetess, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says: "There is nothing that can take away its darkness or its color from the latten; but **Azoth** <term>Azoc/Azoth: the essential "mercury" or universal solvent sought by alchemists</term> is like its covering, namely first when it is cooked down; for it both colors it and makes it white, and again the latten dominates the Azoth and makes it red."* Another Philosopher also says: *That Azoth cannot substantially take away the color from the latten, or change it, except as far as the sight is concerned, but the latten can take away its substantial whiteness from the Azoth, because there is in it a wonderful strength, which appears above all colors.*

So says **Morienus**. Therefore, **Achilles**—or his son **Pyrrhus**, taking the place of his deceased father—is the latten, and **Paris** with **Helen** is the Azoth. First **Achilles** falls, as was said, because the Azoth covers and devours the latten; but afterwards **Pyrrhus** dominates with his red hair <note>Pyrrhus means "flame-colored" or "red-haired" in Greek, symbolizing the final "Red Work" of alchemy</note>, who overturns all of **Troy** and brings everything to his own...

And this is said not without reason; because like a <term>Pyrisous: a mythical creature believed to live in fire</term>, or a <term>pyrausta: a winged insect said to live in the flames of a furnace</term>, or a **salamander**, our **Achilles** must live in the fire and not be consumed. For it was not enough for **Achilles** to have been instructed by his mother and his grandfather **Chiron** <note>The centaur tutor known for his knowledge of medicine and hunting</note> to be able to fight against the fire, but the shield of **Vulcan** was also necessary for him. He himself had previously slain **Hector**, the bravest of the Trojans, whose corpse was ransomed by the Trojans for a weight of gold equal to it; thus, when he was slain by **Paris** in the temple of **Apollo**, his corpse was likewise balanced with gold. For since these heroes are entirely golden and almost all descended from golden gods, they are matched with gold not undeservedly. They also recall that his bones were stored in a golden vessel, which **Bacchus** had bestowed upon **Thetis**, and that **Medea** married him after death in the **Elysian Fields** <note>The final resting place of heroic souls; here used to signify the state of perfection or the final "conjunction" of the work</note>. **Bacchus**, or **Dionysus**, being a golden god who granted the golden wish to **Midas**, is clear from what was said before; therefore, he blessed **Thetis** with that vessel. The reason he married **Medea** in the **Elysian Fields** is that our **Achilles**, though dead, grows young again and becomes a healer of the sick—that is, relieving the bodies of men from various languors and ailments, he brings to them a new life, just as **Medea** herself is said to have done with her medicines <note>original: "pharmacis"; Medea was famous for her potions that could restore youth</note>, as was mentioned before. ### Book 6. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

->Page 268<-

...but he is also said to have been instructed in the medical art—besides the skill of plucking the lyre, the use of herbs, expertise in hunting and javelining, and the laws of equity and prudence—as **Staphylus** <note>An ancient Greek historian who wrote on the affairs of Thessaly</note> writes in the second book of *Thessalian Affairs*. Nor was this without cause; for nine **Eagles** <note>In alchemy, "eagles" often represent the process of sublimation or the volatile spirits of a substance</note> with a tenth part of black earth, or the **Muses** with **Apollo**—that is, the **Nymphs** and the Waters <note>original: "Lymphæ"; a play on words between Nymphs and the Latin word for clear water</note>—moistened his body with their tears; for thus it is fitting. Whence it is also said that when he was carried to **Troy** and descended from the ship onto the land, he stirred up a fountain of waters. 

His spear was of great strength, because it is thought to be steeped in hot poisons, for which reason a wound made by it could not be consolidated <note>meaning healed or closed</note> except by its own application to the wound. In this, he expressed the magnetic power of the **weapon salve** <term>weapon salve: (unguentum armarium) a controversial 17th-century medical theory where an ointment was applied to the weapon that caused a wound, rather than the wound itself, to heal the patient through "magnetic" sympathy</term> mentioned in our own time. **Lull** <note>Raymond Lull, a 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> in *The Theory of the Testament*, chapter 81, mentions a lance of this kind under Allegory in these words: 

*“Son, take a little of our air and of the earth, and pierce its side with a sharp lance, entirely hot, and you will see coming out of its belly so much black and burnt bile <note>original: "cholera nigra"; representing the nigredo or black stage of alchemy</note> that it will have the power of poisoning and infecting the whole world.”* 

And soon after he describes our **Pyrrhus** <note>The son of Achilles, also called Neoptolemus; here symbolizing a specific stage of the chemical process</note> in this manner: 

*“And the nature of this red head is a substance very subtle and light, and in temperament very hot, dry, and sharp: And this is Pyrrhus with the red head, or Achilles Pyrisous <note>original: "Achilles Pyrisous"; meaning Achilles 'born of' or 'saved from' fire</note>.”* 

The same **Lull** depicts **Helen** and **Paris** excellently in the same chapter when he says: 

*“After these things, add to them two parts of white feet: The nature of those white feet is a substance moderately coarse, and in quality moderately cold: And through this property it shares black eyes; it is still in a moderately subtle substance through its moist and hot quality.”* 

Thus **Lull**: The encroaching blackness represents **Paris**, because it extinguishes the **red head**; but afterward **Helen** with **Paris** and the rest of the **Trojans** is entirely rooted out by that redness—whether you call it *laton* <note>An alchemical term for base metal or "impure gold" undergoing purification</note> or **Pyrrhus**—so that redness dominates after all other colors are defeated. Those who have caught a scent of the true **Secret** <note>original: "Arcano"; the hidden goal of alchemy</note> will be my witnesses that this is the genuine explanation of the **Trojan War**; they who, like **Ulysses**, after many wanderings...
