### Book 6. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

->Page 269<-

...things might recognize our **Achilles**. Nor should it seem a wonder to anyone that a **Philosophical work** <note>In this context, the "Philosophical work" or "Great Work" refers to the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> was described by **Homer** through a battle or the siege of a citadel or city, since this allegory and manner of description is most suitable to this work. This is because in our work there are two things, the **active** and the **passive** <note>original: "agens & patiens"; the fundamental dual principles in alchemy, often represented as masculine and feminine or sulfur and mercury</note>, and between them a continuous war, until one subdues the other, and the **Greeks** with red hair <note>A reference to the *Rubedo* or Red Stage, the final phase of the alchemical process</note> rule over the **Trojans**. 

In this manner, **Dionysius Zacharius** the Frenchman—who testifies that he wrote in the year 1548, or shortly after—took a most elegant allegory from an **Emperor** besieging a **Prince** in a certain town. This was based on a true history, as it had occurred in **Germany** in nearly that same time and manner three or four years earlier; and thus, though perhaps unknowingly, he truly expressed the **Trojan War** in his work. 

However, to pass over all the others who use this same similarity (of whom there are very many), we will bring forward the testimony of **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist and monk, though the works attributed to him likely date to the late 16th century</note> on this matter, who in his description of **vitriol** <term>vitriol: a term for various sulfate minerals, considered a primary ingredient in many alchemical recipes</term> concludes thus: 

*“And I say this for memory: that if **Paris** can protect the noble **Helen** without interruption, so that the noble city of **Troy** is no longer destroyed by the **Greeks**, and **Priam** with **Menelaus** are not afflicted by sadness from this, then **Hector** and **Achilles** will become harmonious to obtain the royal blood without war, and to possess the **Monarchy** with all their grandsons and posterity, amplifying their domains with great riches.”* 

To these things is added that other learned men have undertaken philosophical thoughts concerning this **Trojan War**. While we were publishing these things, and the copperplate engraver had already reached the sixth book, we were advised by a certain friend and most learned man of a treatise recently brought from **Germany** (not unlike our argument) titled ***Achilles Redivivus*** <note>original: "Achilles Redivivus," meaning "Achilles Revived"</note>, in which **Achilles**, **Chiron**, and other persons are reduced to a certain medicine. If this is so, although it has not yet happened that we have seen it ourselves, we congratulate ourselves on it, and we place the truth about the **Trojan expedition** before the reader with all the more pleasure:

### Book 6. The Egyptian-Greeks

...<note>The OCR "cinné" appears to be a garbled transcription of the name **Galaton**, a painter mentioned by ancient sources</note> **Galaton** once depicted **Homer** as vomiting a great froth from himself, while all the other petty Greek poets crowded around him to lick up his spit. For through these streams, drawn from that fountain of Homeric poetry, superstition and monstrous opinions regarding the gods were channeled into the minds of the Greeks, then later to the Latins, and eventually to the nations of the whole world.

This **Palladium** <term>Palladium<note>A sacred statue of the goddess Pallas Athena, believed to protect the city that possessed it.</note></term>, because it was entirely a work of fiction, has excited many doubts—not only concerning where it came from, as we discussed previously, but also whether it was seized by the Greeks or truly carried away by **Aeneas** along with the rest of the Trojan gods and brought into Italy. *Ovid, in the 6th book of the Fasti*, leaves this in doubt, yet asserts that in his own time the **Palladium** was kept in Rome within the temple of the goddess **Vesta**; *Titus Livy* agrees with this in his account of the Second Punic War.

They say it was a <term>fatal object<note>original: "fatale"; meaning an object tied to the destiny or "fate" of a kingdom.</note></term>, such that wherever it was moved, the seat of empire would follow. For this reason, these items are called <term>sacred fated things<note>original: "sacra fatalia"</note></term>. It is said that three cities perished while they were in possession of it: first **Troy**, then **Lavinium**, and finally **Alba**. This last city was founded by **Ascanius** (from which the Albans descend) and is said to have been the mother-city of **Rome** before it was destroyed by **Tullus Hostilius**.

However, the more common opinion is that the **Palladium** was snatched from the Trojan citadel by **Diomedes** and **Ulysses** and carried off to the Greeks. For these men—as *Virgil* records in the *2nd book of the Aeneid*, and *Augustine* recalls in *Book 1, Chapter 2 of The City of God*—"having slain the guards of the highest citadel, seized the sacred image, and with bloody hands dared to touch the virginal ribbons of the goddess." 

*Dictys of Crete* <note>The purported author of a "first-hand" account of the Trojan War that often contradicts Homer by being more cynical</note> tells that **Antenor** the Trojan, a traitor to his own country, after he had plotted the betrayal of **Troy** with the Greeks, persuaded **Theano** (who was the priestess of the temple of **Minerva** or **Pallas** where the **Palladium** was kept) to hand the statue over to him. She did so, and **Antenor** then delivered it to the Greeks. In a similar way, this same **Dictys** and **Dares the Phrygian** <note>Another author of an alternative, anti-Homeric history of the war</note> report that **Aeneas** was an accomplice in the betrayal of the city of **Troy**, although **Virgil** attempts to excuse **Aeneas** from the charge of betraying his fatherland by claiming he was unaware of the plots. 

Then, after the destruction of the city, they say a great contest arose over the **Palladium** between **Ajax** and **Ulysses** (just as there was a contest over the arms of the slain **Achilles**), with each of them seeking the statue and citing his own merits in the war. **Agamemnon** favored **Ulysses**...

# Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics

This was because when **Ajax** wanted to kill **Helen**—the source of so many evils—**Ulysses** intervened to free and save her. However, the army and the rest of the common crowd favored **Ajax**; nevertheless, **Ulysses** obtained the **Palladium**, a result that **Ajax** took very poorly. Afterward, **Ajax** was found dead in the night, slain by a sword. When a sedition arose in the army against **Ulysses** because of the death of **Ajax** (for which he was held in suspicion by the troops), **Ulysses** fled by sea. He left the **Palladium** in the care of **Diomedes**, from whom **Aeneas** is said to have received it in Italy, as **Solinus** <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman geographer and compiler.</note> records in Book 3, Chapter 2. 

But since there is such a great conflict of opinions—with authors always setting themselves in opposition to one another, and every writer adapting everything (whether fact or fiction) to his own mindset and purpose, if only to seek honor for his own nation—we cannot agree with any of them. Instead, we say that all these stories depend on **Homer**. Just as so many poets borrowed their works or songs from him, so too did **Dares the Phrygian** and **Dictys the Cretan** <note>Dares and Dictys were the supposed authors of "eyewitness" accounts of the Trojan War; in the Renaissance, they were often cited as historical alternatives to Homer's poetry, though they are now known to be later literary inventions.</note> receive them from the same source. They wrote what appeared to be histories of the Trojan War to seek glory for their own people, though neither of them was actually present at the war, despite their false boasts.

<margin>What the **Palladium** signifies.</margin>
But what, after all, **Homer** understood by this **Palladium**, we will briefly add: It was explained sufficiently above what is signified by **Pallas** <note>The goddess Pallas Athena, representing wisdom and strategy.</note>. Since the **Palladium** is derived from her in both name and form, it is easily apparent what **Homer** wished to <term>shadow forth<note>original: "adumbrare"; to represent vaguely or through allegory.</note></term>: namely, that wisdom and the highest subtlety of genius must be present in the artist, so that relying on this, he may be secure in the completion of his work. For **Ulysses**, in this entire <term>Allegory</term>, is regarded as the artist endowed with the sharpness of reason, by which he accomplishes all the most difficult business. 

His first labor concerned the discovery of **Achilles** and his induction to Troy; his second was to inquire, through a more subtle investigation of the mind, by what means Troy might be occupied—namely, by the seizing of the **Palladium**. Therefore, it is useless to ask about clearly fictional things—such as where it came from, whether from heaven or from the imagination of **Minerva**, and where it remained. The statue is assigned to **Ulysses**, who is strong in prudence, rather than to **Ajax**, who is outstanding in physical strength. This is because the "subtlety of the artist" is required here, not the magnitude of labor or physical power, which concerns the labors of **Hercules**...

Whether **Tantalus** was punished for his lack of restraint in speech <note>Referring back to the previous page's mention of Tantalus revealing divine secrets.</note>, or for some other reason, it is beyond doubt that this entire narrative contains fable and allegory, and that it refers back to those very same Hieroglyphic traditions we mentioned previously. And **Cicero**, **Seneca**, and **Papirius** also mention it. So says he. But if the truth of the matter and the fables that cling to each of these persons are considered, they will all be seen to lead back to **Jupiter**, who was the father of **Tantalus**, who fathered **Pelops**, who fathered **Thyestes** and **Atreus**. All of these events provided the occasion for devising allegories about **Pelops**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the mythical remains of Pelops, specifically his ivory shoulder/bone, transitioning from the literal myth of the Trojan War to an alchemical interpretation of "bones" and "ashes" as metaphors for the "fixed" elements of the Great Work.</meta>

-> ### Hieroglyphics: Book 6. <-

...gave: It is remembered that his bone was of extraordinary size, which was also obtained by Ulysses, just like the rest. But why was this said to be useful or necessary for the capture of Troy? Without a doubt, it is because the craftsmen <note>The "artifices" or alchemists.</note> wished to indicate that a certain thin substance is required for the work, which is as if dead and a remnant from the metallic body, just as a bone is from a human body. For just as bones in the body of an animal or human support the flesh, humors, vessels, and spirits, acting as the base and foundation of a house; so also in the Philosophical work <note>The "Great Work" of alchemy, the process of transmuting base metals into gold or creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> one fixed thing contains all volatile or non-fixed things and binds them together so that they may deservedly be called one substance.

Hence in *The Rising Dawn* <note>original: *Aurora consurgens*, a famous medieval alchemical treatise often attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note>, it is said in chapter 20: *That the tincture is by nature of the volatile things; and that which firms and fixes the spirit itself is fixed, perpetual, and unburnable; and it is called the sulfur of the Philosophers: or ash extracted from ash, as Senior <note>Zadith Senior, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were translated into Latin.</note> says: That which is fixed, fixes fugitive things.* And soon after: *Earth fixes, water whitens, air penetrates, fire colors; Likewise: Earth is left there so that the other three elements may be able to take root in it; if it were not there, the elements would have no foundation upon which to build the new treasure house.* 

And the author of the *Counsel of the Marriage* <note>original: *Consilium coniugii*, an alchemical text.</note> says, quoting Gratianus: *Fire in the air is its light; From bone comes lime <note>original: "calx," a powder produced by heating a substance.</note>; he intends the drying out <note>original: <unclear>exiccatone</unclear>, likely "exiccatione" or drying</note> of that shining moisture, so that it may be turned into ash: of which Aziratus says, "And how precious is this ash": Air in the egg becomes spirit.* From here also the fourth requirement was the ashes of Laomedon <note>Laomedon was a King of Troy; his ashes were mythologically significant for the city's safety.</note>, to be seized from the sixth gate.
<margin>4. Requirement: The Ashes of Laomedon.</margin>
For since ash is made from bone, as authors say and as is evident through experience, bone and ash are two substances necessary for the Philosophical work. They have mentioned ash in countless places; Bonellus says in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba*, referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: *That nature, from which moisture has been taken away, when it is left through the nights, appears similar to a dead thing, and then that nature requires fire, until the body and its spirit are turned into earth, and then it becomes a powder similar to a dead man in his tomb.* After these things are done, God restores to it spirit and soul, and with all infirmity removed, our nature is strengthened and improved. It is necessary, therefore, to burn that thing without moisture, until it becomes ash, which ash is fit to receive the spirit, soul, and infused tincture.

-> ### Hieroglyphics: Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks. <-

Observe, my son, the teaching: just as painters are unable to paint with their colors until they turn them into ashes and pulverize them; similarly, Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to alchemists, who called themselves "Philosophers of Nature."</note> are often unable to compose medicines for their patients <note>In alchemy, the "sick" or "ailing" metals are base metals like lead that need to be "healed" into gold.</note> unless they are broken down and pulverized. Because if you govern this ash subtly, many things will proceed from it, for that which you are—like a human being—possesses both a body and a spirit. The same is indicated by Custos <note>likely an alchemical authority or a specific text like the "Custos Veritatis"</note> and many others, as is clear to those who read them: without ash, nothing is accomplished in the chemical art. For two pots and ash can do a great deal here. But the ashes of a certain specific individual (as also <unclear>bones</unclear>) are required; namely, those of Laomedon.

As King of Troy, he is said to have built the walls of the city with Apollo and Neptune—or even Vulcan—as his workmen, as we mentioned before. He is said to have been slaughtered by Hercules, as we explained under the account of his fourth labor. Thus Laomedon, the founder of Troy, was deprived of life on account of that very city. For when he did not give the agreed-upon wages to the aforementioned workmen, he was harassed by a sea monster <note>original: "Ceto", the Cetus or sea-beast of Greek myth</note> from which his daughter Hesione was freed by Hercules. But since he did not give the promised horses to Hercules either, he was killed, and his ashes were preserved in a certain Scaean gate. These ashes also seemed necessary for the destruction of Troy, and therefore they were secretly carried away from there by Ulysses. 

Thus, authors often report that the end of the Philosophical work bears witness to its beginning, and vice versa; that it begins with one thing and ends with one thing. Because for the capture of Troy, the arrows of Hercules were required,
<margin>5. Requirement: The Arrows of Hercules.</margin>
who, dying on Mount Oeta between Thessaly and Macedonia, gave his arrows as a gift to Philoctetes. He commanded him, having received an oath, not to reveal the location of his body’s remains to anyone. But when the Delphic oracle <note>The famous oracle of Apollo at Delphi, which provided cryptic prophecies.</note> afterward warned the Greeks that Troy could not be captured without the arrows of Hercules or the ash of his body's remains, Philoctetes was found. When questioned about Hercules, he denied knowing anything, and when he was pressured, he remained silent but pointed to the place with his foot. Ulysses, having received these arrows from Philoctetes, brought them to the Greeks. They say these arrows were infected with poison; when Chiron the Centaur once handled them, admiring their length by chance, one fell on his foot, from which he received a lethal wound, but he is said to have been healed by the centaury herb <term>centaurea herba</term> <note>A medicinal plant named after Chiron, known in folk medicine for its healing properties.</note>. No one fails to recognize that these stories are allegorical: the arrows of Hercules were given to Philoctetes...

### Hieroglyphics: Book 6.

...just as the club is to Mercury; with this [the club] Hercules fought against so many monsters hand-to-hand, and with those [the arrows] from a distance. With the club, he cut down and softened things that were fixed and resisting; with the arrows, he pierced and slowed from flight those things that were fleeting and volatile. Every Philosopher <note>In this context, "Philosopher" refers to an alchemist or "Philosopher of Nature."</note> stands in need of these two instruments or modes of operation, as has been shown often above; just as he needs two waters, one of which fixes the other and dissolves it in mutual turns. 

Therefore, at Troy, little could be accomplished without the arrows of Hercules. For the greater labor is spent in halting that which is fleeting and volatile, piercing it as if with arrows (from which comes "fixation" among the Chemists <term>Chymicos: Early modern alchemists who sought to "fix" volatile substances like mercury into solid form</term>), as is seen in Apollo piercing the Python, Diana piercing Orion, Atalanta the boar, and similar instances, which we have treated in their proper places. 

The sixth and final requirement is held to be this: 

<margin>6th Requirement: The horses of Rhesus must be led away.</margin>

That the horses of the King of Thrace, after he was slain, had to be led away before they drank from the river Xanthus; without this being duly performed, Troy could not be occupied. We might not undeservedly judge these things to be ridiculous and very similar to the fables usually told to boys by their nurses, were they not handed down by so many and such great writers—Homer and his followers. 

What do bones, ashes, and arrows have to do with occupying a city? What does bringing away horses before they drink from a certain river matter? Yet we have seen from the foregoing that these things were not devised without cause. Now, the Xanthus was a river of the region of Troy, whose power is celebrated as being such that it dyes animals drinking from it with a yellow color; for "Xanthus" <note>original: "Xanthus" — derived from the Greek word for yellow or golden-haired.</note> denotes yellow. 

This color, perhaps, seemed undesirable in these horses; therefore, precautions had to be taken so the horses would not drink the water of that river. Thus they recount that Neptune brought the horses Xanthus and Balius to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, which are believed to have come to Achilles by hereditary right. 

<margin>A King slaughtered for the sake of horses.</margin>

But it might seem a wretched thing, were it not a fable, that a King had to be slaughtered just to lead away some horses—and indeed a Thracian King, fierce and warlike, who could be so easily overcome by Ulysses <term>Vlyfse: The Latin name for Odysseus, the clever hero of the Odyssey</term> alone or with a few companions without any resistance. Was it easier to kill the King of Thrace and snatch away his goods by force than to overcome the Trojan Phrygians, who were considered cowardly, yet in whose occupation...

# Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks.

...so many years are said to have been consumed; these things seem contrary to nature and reason if we consult history: For one does not hunt hawks with doves, but rather the latter with the former; we do not hunt dogs with hares, but the opposite. But if these things are reduced to their true **Hieroglyphic** <note>In this context, "hieroglyphics" refers to the symbolic emblems used by alchemists to hide their secrets in plain sight.</note> sense, they will not be absurd, but possible and necessary before Troy can be occupied. And if one looks closely at the sayings of the **Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers" are the alchemists or natural philosophers who studied the secrets of matter.</note>, we notice that they warn practitioners to see to it that they do not acquire redness instead of whiteness, or whiteness instead of blackness, at the beginning of the work. For a reddish or yellowish color is not appropriate at the start, but is considered a failure among the **Philosophers**. 

Hence, **Count Bernard** <note>Bernard Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist.</note> warns that we should not acquire the color of a wild poppy <note>original: "papaveris sylvestris"</note> by using too much fire in place of blackness; and **Zacharius** <note>Denis Zachaire, a 16th-century French alchemist.</note> teaches us to avoid the "poison" in the first stage of the work, which usually appears in the second. Likewise, **Isaac** <note>Isaac Hollandus.</note> says the color of crushed brick is useless at the beginning. After the perfection of the work, however, everyone insists on the colors yellow, purple, red, and Tyrian <note>Tyrian purple was the most precious dye of the ancient world and represents the final, highest stage of the alchemical process.</note>, as **Cerus** says in the *Assembly of Philosophers*: *Govern it by cooking, until a most excellent Saffron color is produced.* <note>original: "Regite ipsum coquendo, donec Crocus fiat excellentissimus."</note> **Ardarius** says: *And behold, the Tyrian stone shall appear to you;* <note>original: "Et ecce apparebit vobis lapis Tyrius ;"</note> **Borates** says: *Grind it with its own water until the Saffron becomes similar in color to gold:* <note>original: "Terite aqua sua donec Crocus fiat in colore auro similis :"</note> And thus others mention that the golden and **Xanthic** <note>Yellow or golden-hued.</note> color ought to be present at the end of the work, not the beginning; it is useful there, but harmful here. 

And so it must be thought regarding the Horses of **Rhesus** <note>The text spells this "Rheli," a likely variant for Rhesus, the Thracian king whose horses were a key omen in the Trojan War.</note>: they must be led away to Troy before they turn yellow <note>The myth states Troy could not fall if the horses drank from the river Xanthus ("Yellow River") and ate the grass of the Trojan plain.</note>. And these are those six memorable requirements without which Troy could not be occupied or destroyed. To these, not without merit, a seventh should be added:

<margin>**The Trojan Horse.**</margin>
Namely, that **Trojan Horse** filled with armed men and led into the city after the walls had been cast down. It was called the invention of Pallas <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note>, because it could be seen as a stratagem devised by a subtle wit—unless it were joined with such great danger, and proved the Trojans to be of excessive simplicity (if not to say stupidity) for demolishing their own walls while the enemy remained in their land, and thus they themselves led into the city those by whom they could be conquered. But this clearly proves it to be a fiction in several respects, though it might be excused otherwise; since similar...

# Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics.

->Of the Hieroglyphics.<-

<margin>*The sacrifice of Iphigenia.*</margin>
...just as we have experienced examples of ships in our own time being successfully guided through: So too, the story of Iphigenia, the daughter of Agamemnon, offered as a sacrifice to Diana because of the winds being hostile to the army, is entirely a fiction and something very close to a fable. Likewise, everything contained in the entire *Iliad* and *Odyssey* is allegorical, partly explaining the physical and secret works of nature, and partly the political, instructing kings and public or private figures in many matters. This is why Homer was so highly valued by **Alexander the Great**, who placed the book under his pillow at night and called it a "royal manual" <note>original: *viaticum*, literally "provisions for a journey"</note>; he was similarly valued by other great and learned men of every age. Indeed, the highest artistry of the human mind seems expressed in Homer's work—unless one considers the many great evils and <note>original: *miara*, Greek for "vile" or "abominable" things</note> foul deeds mixed in with the good, such as the adulteries of the gods, thefts, murders, robberies, and other things. It is not likely that such a great man truly attributed these to the gods; rather, he brought them forward through poetic license and an allegorical mode of writing, so that the wise might separate the kernel from the shell <note>original: *nucleum á cortice*</note>, the good from the evil, and turn it to their own use. Thus, we assign a fourfold use to Homer, as we also do to **Orpheus**;

<margin>
*The fourfold use of the Homeric Work:*
1. *Hieroglyphic.*
</margin>
The first is the **Hieroglyphic** <note>The primary layer of hidden alchemical meaning</note>, secret, profound, and latent; this primary use regards the most hidden works of nature which we have discussed. Only **Philosophers** <note>In this context, the "Philosophers" are the alchemists</note> and those aware of the true **Chemistry** <note>Alchemy</note> look into and admire this; others neglect it and do not notice it beneath the shadowy cover.

<margin>2. *Political.*</margin>
The second use is **Political** <term>Political: From the Greek *politikos*, relating here to the conduct of the state, personal ethics, and civic duty</term>, ethical, moral, historical, and economic. This secondary use instructs kings, leaders, magistrates, and every individual in morals and common life. Many have noticed this layer and have looked upon it as having something of the divine.

<margin>3. *Poetic.*</margin>
The third we leave to the **Poets**, who embrace the idle fables, inventions, and traditions about gods, heroes, and other things in a unified way;

<margin>4. *Grammatical.*</margin>
The fourth we assign to the **Grammarians**, who observe the ornamentation, the outward trappings <note>original: *phaleras*, referring to decorative medals or stylistic flourishes</note>, and the flow of the speech and interpret it for others. Hence Homer—who was most falsely considered a beggar, when in fact he was a man highly skilled in politics and most experienced in conducting great affairs, which does not befit a beggar but rather one excelling in talent and the gifts of fortune—has given so many gram-

[gram]marians <note>The word completes "grammaticos" from the previous page</note> throughout Greece, so much so that even **Alcibiades** <note>A flamboyant Athenian statesman and general</note> is said to have struck a certain man with a blow for mocking **Homer**, adding this sharp jest: "Will you call him a beggar, or a vain man, who supports so many of his own interpreters and makes them rich?" <note>original: "Tune ipsum mendicum, aut vanum nominabis, qui tot alit sui interpretes & dites facit?"</note> From so many reasons and arguments brought forward and explained thus far, it is clear enough that the **Trojan Expedition** contains little or nothing of historical truth, but a great deal of allegory. It was introduced for the sake of its secret meaning <note>original: "intellectum arcanum"</note> rather than its common literal sense. 

<margin>⨁</margin> Nonetheless, we do not deny that a second, third, and fourth use—as we have just mentioned—can be attributed to it. For nothing prevents one from mixing a bit of truth into allegories and fictions, though conversely, it would be improper to thrust fictional elements into true events. Just as leaven <note>yeast</note>, mixed into even the smallest portion of pure wheaten flour, makes the whole mass sour and fermented, so too do even a few false or fictional elements make a true history suspect and strip it entirely of its credibility. Thus, if poets like **Orpheus** and **Homer** perhaps mixed some truth into their fables and allegories regarding places, things, or people, it does not follow that these stories are true or should be taken and understood exactly as they sound, as many of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note> did. Therefore, if someone encounters such things in the works of said poets, this will not make their fictions true, except to the most thoughtless reader.

<margin>·</margin> Hence, if Troy had been a city in the most ancient times and was destroyed, it would not have happened in the way it is described. For the things handed down by the poets, or by the historians who followed them in time and style of writing, are of such a nature that they ought rightly to be called into doubt and traced back to their origin—namely, the allegorical one, as we have done. 

It remains now to briefly run through the return and wanderings of **Ulysses**, since he is, as has been said, the persona of the **Artist** <note>In hermetic texts, the "Artist" or "Artifex" usually refers to the alchemist performing the Great Work</note>, prevailing in intellect as much as **Hercules** did in strength. Therefore, if all things are considered well, whatever was famously achieved at Troy will be seen to have been accomplished by his counsel and effort. Ulysses was powerful not only in intellect but also in the labor of his hands, as **Aelian** <note>A Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> notes in Book 7, Chapter 5; Ulysses himself testifies to this in the *Odyssey*, Book 15, with these words:

->*The wisdom of the Ithacan is not in doubt, yet he still prays*<-

<note>original: "Non dubia est Ithaci sapientia, sed tamen optat / Fumun de patrijs posse videre focis." From Ovid's *Epistulae ex Ponto*.</note>

Regarding the reason why he fled, which we mentioned above, we shall add nothing further here. Therefore, first of all, he was carried by a storm to the coast of the **Cicones**, a people of Thrace. Afterward, he went to the **Lotus-eaters** in Africa, where, when his companions had tasted the fruit of the lotus, they forgot their fatherland and refused to return to the ships. From there, he went to Sicily to the cave of **Polyphemus**, whom he blinded along with twelve companions. After that, he held his course to the island of **Aeolia** and the **Laestrygonians**, the most savage people of Campania, and soon to the island of **Aeaea**, where the sorceress **Circe**, daughter of the Sun, transformed his companions into beasts. By her, he fathered **Telegonus** and **Ardea**. Afterward, he descended to the **underworld**, consecrating a pillar to **Pluto** and **Proserpina**, so that he might learn from the prophet **Tiresias** there what things he must do. Then, carried to the **Island of the Sirens**, he plugged the ears of his companions with smeared wax and ordered himself to be bound to the ship's mast. Passing from here through **Scylla** and **Charybdis**, not without some loss of his companions, he arrived again in Sicily, where the daughters of the Sun were guarding their father’s flocks...

### Book 6. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

...whom when his companions slew <note>This refers to the companions of Ulysses killing the sacred cattle of the Sun god, Helios, an act of sacrilege that led to their destruction</note>, almost all perished in a shipwreck. He himself, having seized the mast of the ship and clinging to it for nine days, was tossed by the waves of the sea until he was carried to the island of **Ogygia**. There he was received in hospitality by the nymph **Calypso**, and having stayed for seven years, he also fathered sons by her. Then, by the command of the gods, setting sail from there, he was shipwrecked again near **Phaeacia** by the impulse of **Neptune** because of the fate of **Polyphemus** <note>Ulysses had blinded Neptune's son, the Cyclops Polyphemus, earning the god's wrath</note>. Having received clothes and companions from her as a gift, he was set down in **Ithaca** with gifts while sleeping. There, having assumed the habit of a beggar, he returned to **Penelope**, who is said to have borne him a son, **Polyporthus**, after the defeat of Troy, in memory of his father's virtue—since that name signifies "the destroyer of the city" <note>original: "Polyporthum". From the Greek "ptoliporthos," an epithet of Ulysses meaning sacker of cities.</note>. 

<margin>The wanderings of Ulysses concerning his return to his fatherland:</margin>

And these are the wanderings of **Ulysses** concerning his return to his fatherland, which appear to have extended beyond a decade. Since the Trojan siege lasted just as long, Ulysses lived twenty full years outside his fatherland, entangled in many errors and misfortunes. Having finally overcome these, he obtained the name "destroyer of the city" from the son born to him. These things are well enough known in themselves, since they are entirely fabulous and fictional stories produced by the Poet <note>Homer</note> to demonstrate in a multifaceted way what errors and evils human life is exposed to, and also what things the **artists** <note>The "Artifices" or alchemical practitioners</note> become subject to before they reach the final goal. For he who has not wandered is said not yet to have begun. And **Bacasser** <note>A philosopher-character in the "Turba Philosophorum," an influential early alchemical text</note> says in the *Turba*: *"The right path,"* he says, *"is not discerned except through error, and nothing generates more grief in the heart than an error in this art and work."* <note>original: "Rectum, inquit, non nisi errore discernitur, & nihil magis dolorem cordi generat, quam error in hac arte & opere."</note> Since the commentaries of others exist concerning these detours and difficulties of the art, and daily examples testify to them more than enough, we add nothing further here for their demonstration.

Therefore, whether **Troy** actually stood and was destroyed in reality, or whether it is merely a fiction—and the same is to be understood concerning the **labors of Hercules**, the sacred contests, and matters pertaining to the gods—it is all the same to us, since nothing is carried or reaped by us from that history alone. But if, on the other hand...

<header>Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics.</header>

Whichever side we ought to join, a thousand proofs convince us that none of these things truly existed, although they are treated by the Pagans in almost as many books as if they had been real. If, however, we consult all the writers concerning where they drew such great and numerous things, we will return to the six previously mentioned authors of all Pagan religion—or rather, idolatry—(*Orpheus*, *Linus*, *Musaeus*, *Melampus*, *Homer*, and *Hesiod*). And if we inquire where these men obtained them, we will observe that they all draw their origin partly from the **Egyptians**, and partly from their own minds in imitation of **Egyptian** doctrine and teaching. 

The **Egyptians**, in truth, received all their teachings from **Isis**, and she from **Mercury** and **Vulcan**, as we have already related before. But if someone, led by their own persuasion nonetheless, affirms that all those things ought to be said and understood as referring to true and certain persons, and believes that history is contained within the fables themselves, we do not strongly oppose them, provided that they in turn grant us this: that an **Allegory** can be hidden beneath a true history—that is, that the most secret matters, which must be passed down figuratively, are not rarely covered under the veiled form, as it were, of true teaching. 

If anyone seeks an example of this matter, let them inspect the books of that great **Physician of Amiens** <note>Referring to Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a celebrated French physician whose work *De abditis rerum causis* sought to explain phenomena that could not be accounted for by the four humors, often touching on occult or "hidden" powers of nature</note> concerning the **hidden causes of things**, and judge whether he does not hide another kernel beneath that husk—which to many seems very hard—or whether he does not interweave the most secret works of nature and art with the theorems and precepts of common medicine gathered from authors, in such a way that his intention is recognized only by the most perceptive. 

Thus even those most ancient writers (in whose time not even the name of **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymia". In this context, it refers to the Hermetic art or Alchemy</note> was widely known), if they handed down certain true things in their writings, it is nevertheless certain that most of what they brought forth was fictional, and things which far outweigh the truths by their own weight; under these fictional and allegorical things, who will demonstrate that those **Chemical** secrets do not lie hidden, which we have so far sufficiently rescued from their darkness and placed into the light for all who are intelligent? In this kind of writing, disregarding all other matters, if someone attempts to reduce those fabulous tales to [literal] truth, and considers all the authors along with himself to be ignorant of **Chemistry**, nor [perceives] anything of a **Chemical** sense...

<summary>The author argues that Greek myths originated from Egyptian wisdom and serve as alchemical allegories. He uses the physician Jean Fernel as a modern example of how secret knowledge is often hidden beneath the "husk" of conventional writing.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the sixth book, which explores the Egyptian and Greek foundations of alchemy. The text picks up mid-sentence, likely referring back to Natalis Comes (a famous 16th-century mythographer) as "the Mythologist," arguing that if earlier authors were allowed to interpret ancient myths according to their own judgment, the current author should be granted the same right to provide an alchemical interpretation.</meta>

# Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks. 285

...that [the Mythologist] once hid in his own writings; let him use his own judgment as much and wherever he wishes. Nonetheless, so that we may be allowed as much as he and others, he will be bound to concede this to us by the *right of Retaliation* <note>Latin: *iure Talionis*; the principle of reciprocity, suggesting that if one person can interpret myths one way, another has the equal right to offer a different interpretation.</note>. And now, just as Natalis, under the mythology of the Sun, gives thanks to God in these words: 

*“A clearer and more abundant declaration of the fables, because it was reserved for my times, is the reason why I should give immortal thanks to* **ALMIGHTY** *God the Redeemer, by whose benefit it has been granted to me to open these foolish ramblings of the ancients which contain nothing truly religious, but to demonstrate that they are only fictions for explaining philosophical matters”*; 

So we also, with the same devotion of soul, heart, and mouth, give as much thanks as we can conceive in our minds to the same **TRIUNE GOD**, because he has most mercifully granted us that by which we could bring back to their true origin these allegories, fables, and mysteries of the Egyptians, Greeks, and all antiquity—once held as the most secret of secrets, as they still are (and devised not concerning common things known in the world, but concerning those things which by their own right ought to be hidden), from which the idolatries, darkness, and errors of so many nations have overflowed like most abundant springs—and to reconcile them in one line of truth and an immovable point with a certain irreproachable harmony (which is the property of truth). 

Since all these things agree in nothing else than that truly golden saying, the **MEDICINE OF SOUL AND BODY**, may the Highest, **BEST AND GREATEST** <note>Latin: *Optimo Maximo*; a title originally for Jupiter, adopted by Christians for God.</note>, and uniquely that **THRICE-GREATEST** <note>Latin: *Trismegistus*; usually referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy, here applied to Christ as the ultimate healer.</note> Physician of soul and body, **JESUS CHRIST**, grant us to use this for the glory of his name and for the benefit of ourselves and our neighbor for a very long time, and after this, grant us Eternal Life. May He—who like the **STONE** torn from the high **MOUNTAIN** without hands <note>A reference to the prophecy in Daniel 2:34, which alchemists frequently identified with the Philosopher's Stone and Christians with Christ.</note>, and the cornerstone rejected by the greater part of the world or the nations, has been made our own—be blessed forever: **AMEN.**

->**Decorative Endpaper**<-

[This page contains no text. It is a full-page illustration of decorative <term>marbled paper<gloss>paper decorated with a swirling, stone-like pattern created by floating pigments on a liquid surface and then transferring them to a sheet of paper</gloss></term>.]

<note>The design shown here is known as a "snail" or "curl" pattern. This style was created by using a comb-like tool to swirl the floating ink into small circular spirals before the paper was laid down. These colorful papers were highly popular in European bookbinding during the 18th and 19th centuries, used both for aesthetic beauty and to hide the structural elements of the book's binding.</note>

->**Decorative Endpaper**<-

[This page contains no text. It is a full-page illustration of decorative <term>marbled paper<gloss>paper decorated with a swirling, stone-like pattern created by floating pigments on a liquid surface and then transferring them to a sheet of paper</gloss></term>.]

This page features a complex "snail" or "curl" pattern in a palette of vibrant orange, charcoal grey, and ochre yellow swirls against an off-white ground.

<note>The design shown here is a characteristic and well-preserved example of traditional bookbinding. The "snail" or "curl" style was created by a craftsman using a comb-like tool to swirl floating ink into small circular spirals before the paper was laid down. These colorful papers were highly popular in European bookbinding during the 18th and 19th centuries; they were used both for their aesthetic beauty and to hide the structural elements of the book's binding, such as where the leather of the cover is glued to the boards.</note>

<summary>This page consists of a decorative marbled endpaper featuring a vibrant "snail" pattern in orange, grey, and yellow, a classic element of historical book arts.</summary>
<keywords>marbled paper, endpaper, bookbinding, snail pattern, decorative arts, 18th century, 19th century</keywords>
